title: Patch a SharePoint people picker field from Power Apps
shortDescription: Save a selected person from a combo box into a SharePoint person column.
fullDescription: A reliable pattern for patching single-value SharePoint person fields from Power Apps using the claims object SharePoint expects.
problemStatement: Power Apps person values do not save correctly when the app sends only a display name or email address to SharePoint.
whenToUse: Combo boxes connected to Microsoft 365 users
whenNotToUse: Multi-person fields without adapting the table shape
Dataverse user lookups
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm the SharePoint column allows one person.
Use a combo box that returns Mail and DisplayName.
Patch the full expanded user object, including Claims.
Refresh the record or collection after save.
commonMistakes: Patching only the email string.
Using UserPrincipalName when the combo box returns Mail.
Forgetting to lower-case the claim email in tenants with mixed casing.
Leaving out Department, JobTitle or Picture. All six properties must be present, even when empty.
troubleshooting: If the field saves blank, inspect the combo box selected record shape.
If SharePoint rejects the value, confirm the column is not multi-select.
If the Patch reports 'The specified user could not be found', the Claims value does not match an account in the tenant. Guests need their full user principal name, which contains #EXT#.
If Blank() does not clear the field, turn on formula-level error management in the app's settings.
If the combo box shows nothing while typing, isSearchTermRequired is true and the search text is empty until the user types.

faqs.question: Why does Patch need a Claims value for a person column?
faqs.answer: SharePoint identifies users by a claims string, not by email alone. The format i:0#.f|membership| followed by the lower-case sign-in name tells SharePoint which account to resolve.

faqs.question: Can I patch a person column with only an email address?
faqs.answer: No. The connector expects a record with Claims, DisplayName, Email, Department, JobTitle and Picture. Passing text causes a type error.

faqs.question: How do I clear a SharePoint person field from Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Patch the column with Blank(). In older apps, enable formula-level error management first, otherwise Blank() is ignored.

title: Patch a SharePoint choice field
shortDescription: Write choice values from Power Apps to SharePoint without schema errors.
fullDescription: Use the expected Value object when saving a single-choice SharePoint column from a dropdown or combo box.
problemStatement: Choice fields often fail when the app patches plain text instead of a SharePoint choice object.
whenNotToUse: Multi-choice fields without using a table of values
Columns stored as plain text
stepByStepInstructions: Bind the dropdown to Choices(Requests.Status).
Patch the selected value inside a Value object.
Refresh the item after saving if the screen depends on the new value.
commonMistakes: Using ddStatus.SelectedText.Value in modern controls.
Patching the whole selected record when only Value is expected.
Typing a value that is not one of the column's choices, which SharePoint rejects unless fill-in choices are allowed.
troubleshooting: If the formula errors, check whether the control returns Result, Value, or a custom field name.
If the error says a record was expected and text was supplied, wrap the text as { Value: "..." }.
If the saved value does not appear in the list, the text does not match a choice exactly, including case and spaces.
If the dropdown does not show the current value when editing, set its Default to the stored text value, or DefaultSelectedItems to a one-row table for a combo box.

faqs.question: What format does Patch need for a SharePoint choice column?
faqs.answer: A record with a Value property, for example { Value: "Approved" }. The Value must match one of the column's choices.

faqs.question: How do I populate a dropdown with a column's choices?
faqs.answer: Set Items to Choices(ListName.ColumnName). The dropdown's Selected record can then be passed straight to Patch.

faqs.question: Can I filter a SharePoint list by a choice column without a delegation warning?
faqs.answer: Yes. Compare the Value with equals, as in Filter(Requests, Status.Value = "Open"). That comparison is delegable.

title: Patch a SharePoint lookup field
shortDescription: Save a lookup selection with the Id and Value shape SharePoint expects.
fullDescription: A lookup patch pattern for connecting related SharePoint list records from a Power Apps form.
problemStatement: Lookup columns need both an Id and display Value; sending plain text will not connect the related record.
whenNotToUse: Large lookup lists where delegation needs special handling
Dataverse relationships
stepByStepInstructions: Load the lookup source into the combo box.
Confirm the selected record includes ID and Title.
Patch Id and Value together.
Test with a new item and an edit item.
commonMistakes: Using lowercase id instead of ID from SharePoint.
Patching the lookup display text only.
Patching one of the lookup's additional projected fields instead of the lookup column itself.
troubleshooting: If the lookup shows blank after save, verify the source item still exists and the ID is correct.
If the error mentions a read-only or unknown column, check the name. Additional lookup fields such as Department:Code cannot be written.
If the Patch succeeds but the list shows blank, the Id does not exist in the source list.
If a view with this column fails on a large list, the view contains more than 12 lookup, person and managed metadata columns.

faqs.question: What does Patch need for a SharePoint lookup column?
faqs.answer: A record with Id and Value, where Id is the ID of the item in the source list and Value is its display text.

faqs.question: Why is it ID in one place and Id in another?
faqs.answer: Items read from a SharePoint list expose their key as ID. The lookup record inside another item uses Id. Both hold the same number.

faqs.question: How do I show more fields from the looked-up item?
faqs.answer: Use LookUp against the source list with the lookup's Id, or add additional fields to the lookup column in SharePoint for read-only display.

title: Save gallery rows as JSON in a multiline text field
shortDescription: Store a lightweight editable table from Power Apps in one SharePoint item.
fullDescription: Use JSON serialization when a small child table does not justify a separate SharePoint list yet.
problemStatement: Small repeating sections can be cumbersome to save when the business wants one parent SharePoint item.
whenNotToUse: Rows that need permissions, workflows, or reporting
Large datasets
Child records with independent lifecycles
stepByStepInstructions: Keep the collection schema stable.
Serialize the collection with JSONFormat.Compact.
Save to a plain multiline text column.
Use ParseJSON to rehydrate the collection when editing.
commonMistakes: Using this pattern for data that should be relational.
Letting control-only columns leak into saved JSON.
Saving to a rich text column, which wraps the JSON in HTML and breaks parsing.
troubleshooting: If the JSON is too large, move child rows to a dedicated SharePoint list.
If JSON() reports an unsupported type, the collection holds an image, media or control reference. Use ShowColumns to keep simple columns, or add JSONFormat.IgnoreUnsupportedTypes.
If the saved text is cut off, the column is single line of text. Use multiple lines, plain text.
If you need to filter or report on the rows, JSON in a text column cannot be queried. Move the rows to a child list.

faqs.question: How much JSON can a SharePoint multiline text column hold?
faqs.answer: A plain multiple lines of text column holds about 63,999 characters by default. For anything close to that, use a child list instead.

faqs.question: When is saving rows as JSON a good idea?
faqs.answer: For small sets of rows that are only ever read back by the same app, such as a checklist. Data that needs filtering, reporting or editing elsewhere belongs in its own list.

faqs.question: Why use ShowColumns before JSON()?
faqs.answer: It removes columns added for the user interface and types that JSON() cannot serialise, which keeps the saved text small and stable.

title: Parse JSON from SharePoint back into a Power Apps collection
shortDescription: Rehydrate saved JSON rows into an editable collection.
fullDescription: Convert a multiline JSON field back into a typed Power Apps collection so users can continue editing rows.
problemStatement: ParseJSON returns untyped values, so apps need explicit conversion before collection rows behave predictably.
whenToUse: Loading draft checklist or deliverable rows
whenNotToUse: True relational child data
Large datasets
stepByStepInstructions: Check that the saved field is not blank.
Parse the JSON text.
Map each property into the expected type.
Bind the gallery to the rebuilt collection.
commonMistakes: Skipping Text(), Boolean(), or Value() conversions.
Assuming ParseJSON returns a typed table.
Calling ParseJSON on a blank value without a guard, which raises an error.
troubleshooting: If rows load with blank fields, compare the saved JSON property names to the parsing formula.
If every field is blank, the property names are case-sensitive. Title and title are different.
If ForAll reports that it expects a table, wrap the parsed value with Table() for a JSON object, or check the text really is an array.
If a number arrives as text in the JSON, convert it with Value(Text(...)).

faqs.question: Why do I need Text(), Value() and Boolean() after ParseJSON?
faqs.answer: ParseJSON returns untyped values. Each one must be converted to a Power Fx type before it can be used in a collection or control, unless you parse with a declared type.

faqs.question: How do I load a JSON array into a collection?
faqs.answer: Wrap ParseJSON in ForAll and build a typed record for each element, then pass the result to ClearCollect.

faqs.question: What happens if the saved JSON is invalid?
faqs.answer: ParseJSON raises an error. Wrap the call in IfError and fall back to an empty collection with a message to the user.

title: Submit multiple Power Apps forms together
shortDescription: Coordinate several edit forms and keep the user experience predictable.
fullDescription: A practical structure for validating and submitting multiple forms that write to related data sources.
problemStatement: Multiple forms can submit out of order or leave partial saves when validation and error handling are scattered.
whenToUse: Long request forms split into sections
whenNotToUse: Simple single-list forms
Transactions requiring guaranteed rollback
stepByStepInstructions: Validate all forms before submitting.
Use OnSuccess to chain dependent saves if one form needs the first record ID.
Use OnFailure to show clear feedback.
Disable the submit button while saving.
commonMistakes: Submitting child forms before the parent item exists.
Only checking one form's Valid property.
Calling SubmitForm twice on two forms that edit the same item, which causes a conflict error on the second save.
troubleshooting: If one form saves and another fails, move dependent saves into OnSuccess and add clear recovery messaging.
If the second form reports a conflict, both forms point at the same record. Combine their Updates in one Patch.
If Valid is false but nothing is highlighted, a required card is hidden or on another tab.
If the child saves without a parent ID, set the child's link field from the parent's LastSubmit in OnSuccess, not from the button.

faqs.question: Can I submit two forms with one button in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Yes. If they edit the same item, Patch once with both forms' Updates. If they edit different lists, submit the parent and submit the child from the parent's OnSuccess.

faqs.question: What does FormName.Updates return?
faqs.answer: A record of the values the form would save, taken from each data card's Update property. It can be passed to Patch.

faqs.question: Why does the second SubmitForm fail with a conflict?
faqs.answer: The first save changed the item, so the second form holds an outdated copy. Saving both forms' Updates in a single Patch avoids this.

title: Refresh selectedRequest after Patch
shortDescription: Keep the current record fresh after saving changes.
fullDescription: Refresh and reload the selected SharePoint item so calculated fields, status values, and related UI update correctly.
problemStatement: After Patch, the screen can keep showing old values because the selected variable was not updated.
whenNotToUse: Purely local collection-only screens
stepByStepInstructions: Store the Patch result.
Refresh the data source when SharePoint-calculated values matter.
Look up the saved item again by ID.
Rebind detail controls to the selected variable.
commonMistakes: Refreshing without updating the selected variable.
Looking up by title instead of ID.
Calling Refresh on a large list after every save, which reloads far more than the one record that changed.
troubleshooting: If the UI still shows old data, confirm controls reference selectedRequest rather than Gallery.Selected.
If a calculated or flow-updated column is still old, the value changes after the save. Re-read the item with LookUp a moment later.
If the variable becomes blank after a failed save, wrap the Patch in IfError so the old record is kept.
If a gallery does not show the change, it is bound to a collection. Patch the collection too.

faqs.question: Do I need Refresh after Patch in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Patch returns the updated record and data-bound galleries update automatically. Refresh is for changes made by other users or by flows.

faqs.question: How do I get the new ID of an item I just created?
faqs.answer: Store the result of Patch in a variable. The returned record includes the ID assigned by SharePoint.

faqs.question: Why does my screen still show old values after saving?
faqs.answer: The controls read from a variable that was set before the save. Assign the result of Patch back to that variable.

title: Default selected items for modern combo boxes
shortDescription: Set edit-form defaults for modern combo boxes without blank selections.
fullDescription: Modern combo boxes need default values that match their Items schema, especially for people, choice, and lookup fields.
problemStatement: Combo boxes appear blank in edit mode when DefaultSelectedItems does not match the Items record shape.
whenNotToUse: Classic dropdown controls with simple Default values
stepByStepInstructions: Inspect the Items schema.
Return a one-row table for single-select combo boxes.
Use Blank() when there is no saved value.
Keep the default shape aligned with the patched shape.
commonMistakes: Returning a record instead of a table.
Using email text as the default for a people picker object.
Changing DefaultSelectedItems and expecting the control to update without a Reset when the record variable changes.
troubleshooting: If the combo box remains blank, compare the selected record fields to the Items fields.
If the default shows for a moment and disappears, the field names in the default table do not match the Items table. Compare the DisplayFields.
If the previous record's selection stays, call Reset on the combo box after changing the record variable.
If Selected is blank although a default shows, the default row does not exist in Items. Use a row taken from the Items source.

faqs.question: Why does DefaultSelectedItems need a table?
faqs.answer: A combo box can hold several selections, so its default is always a table, even for one item. Wrap a single record in square brackets.

faqs.question: Why is my combo box blank when editing a record?
faqs.answer: The default record's fields do not match the fields of the Items source, or the default is a record instead of a table.

faqs.question: How do I default a people picker to the saved person?
faqs.answer: Build a one-row table whose column names match the picker's Items, such as DisplayName and Mail, using the saved person's values.

title: Role-based button visibility using a SharePoint security list
shortDescription: Control app actions from a simple SharePoint role list.
fullDescription: Use a SharePoint list to map users to roles, then drive button visibility from the current user's role.
problemStatement: Hard-coded email checks are brittle and require app edits whenever business roles change.
whenNotToUse: Highly sensitive security boundaries
Apps needing enterprise authorization policies
stepByStepInstructions: Create an AppSecurity list with Email and Role columns.
Load the current user's role on app start.
Use role checks for visibility and behavior.
Keep SharePoint item permissions aligned with the UI intent.
commonMistakes: Treating visibility as true security.
Forgetting users can still access data if list permissions allow it.
Calling the role lookup in every control's Visible property instead of once.
troubleshooting: If a valid user sees no buttons, normalize email casing and confirm their security list item is active.
If the lookup shows a delegation warning, remove Lower() from the column side and store emails in lower case.
If guests never match, their sign-in name differs from their email. Store the value returned by User().Email for them.
If a role change does not take effect, the role was read at start-up. Restart the app.

faqs.question: Is hiding a button in Power Apps real security?
faqs.answer: No. It only changes what the app shows. Anyone with access to the SharePoint list can still change the data there. Use list permissions for protection.

faqs.question: Where should I store app roles?
faqs.answer: A small SharePoint list of email and role works well. Give users read access so the app can look up their role, and restrict editing to administrators.

faqs.question: How do I check a role only once?
faqs.answer: Set a variable in App.OnStart or define a named formula in App.Formulas, then reference it from every control.

title: Avoid delegation warnings with SharePoint filters
shortDescription: Use SharePoint-friendly filters that keep large lists usable.
fullDescription: A practical filtering approach that avoids common non-delegable formulas and keeps results accurate as lists grow.
problemStatement: Non-delegable formulas can silently return incomplete results once a SharePoint list grows beyond the app limit.
whenNotToUse: Small one-off admin lists
Complex search requiring a real search service
stepByStepInstructions: Filter first by indexed columns where possible.
Use StartsWith for text search instead of in.
Avoid wrapping SharePoint columns in functions inside Filter.
Test with delegation warnings visible.
commonMistakes: Using Search() on SharePoint lists.
Using Lower(Column) inside the filter.
Ignoring yellow warning triangles.
Trusting results on a list under 500 items, where non-delegable formulas appear to work until the list grows.
troubleshooting: If results seem incomplete, simplify filters until warnings disappear, then add filters back one at a time.
If the warning is on a single part of the formula, hover the blue underline. It marks the exact function that is not delegable.
If a filter on a Yes/No column warns, compare explicitly with true or false.
If the list has more than 5,000 items and a delegable filter still fails, index the columns used in the filter.

faqs.question: What is the delegation limit in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: When a formula cannot be delegated, Power Apps processes only the first 500 rows by default, or up to 2,000 if you raise the data row limit. Rows beyond that are ignored without an error.

faqs.question: Is Search() delegable for SharePoint?
faqs.answer: No. Use StartsWith in a Filter, or run Search over a smaller set that a delegable filter has already returned.

faqs.question: How can I test for delegation problems?
faqs.answer: Set the data row limit to 1 in the app's settings while testing. Any formula that is not delegated will then return almost nothing.

title: Patch Request Status as a choice field
shortDescription: Save request lifecycle status updates cleanly from buttons.
fullDescription: A focused variant of choice patching for request workflows where status buttons move items through a lifecycle.
problemStatement: Status buttons often fail when they patch text to a SharePoint choice column.
whenNotToUse: Free-text status fields
Multi-status scenarios
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm the target status exists in SharePoint choices.
Patch the Value object from the action button.
Notify the user after save.
Refresh the selected record.
commonMistakes: Using a status label that does not exist in SharePoint.
Forgetting business validation before approval.
Hard-coding status text in many formulas, so a renamed choice breaks the app in several places.
troubleshooting: If the value does not save, compare the exact choice spelling in SharePoint.
If the status saves but a flow does not start, the flow's trigger condition is checking different text.
If two people change the status at once, the second Patch reports a conflict. Re-read the item and try again.
If the button should not be available, set its DisplayMode from the current status as well as checking in the formula.

faqs.question: How do I set a SharePoint choice column to a fixed value?
faqs.answer: Patch a record with the Value, for example { RequestStatus: { Value: "Approved" } }. The text must match one of the column's choices.

faqs.question: Should I save who approved and when in the same Patch?
faqs.answer: Yes. Writing the status, date and approver together keeps the record consistent if anything fails.

faqs.question: How do I stop a status being set from the wrong stage?
faqs.answer: Check the current status before the Patch and disable the button unless the item is at the expected stage.

title: Build a modal edit form
shortDescription: Open a focused edit panel without leaving the current screen.
fullDescription: Use variables and form modes to create a modal edit experience for quick request or checklist updates.
problemStatement: Users lose context when every small edit requires navigating to a separate screen.
whenNotToUse: Long multi-section forms
Processes requiring a guided wizard
stepByStepInstructions: Add a container overlay.
Drive its Visible property from varShowEditModal.
Set the form Item to varEditingRequest.
Close the modal on cancel or successful save.
commonMistakes: Not resetting the form when the modal closes.
Allowing the background gallery to change the selected item while editing.
Placing the modal below other controls in the tree view, so parts of the screen show through or stay clickable.
troubleshooting: If the wrong item opens, store ThisItem in a variable before showing the modal.
If the form is empty, check its Item is the variable and that EditForm was called after the variable was set.
If the modal will not close after saving, hide it in the form's OnSuccess, not in the button's OnSelect.
If controls behind the modal can still be tapped, the background rectangle does not cover the whole screen.

faqs.question: How do I make a popup form in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Put an edit form inside a container that covers the screen, and set the container's Visible property to a variable that a button turns on and off.

faqs.question: Why use a variable instead of Gallery.Selected for the form's Item?
faqs.answer: The gallery's selection can change while the modal is open. A variable keeps the form on the record the user chose.

faqs.question: Where should I close the modal after saving?
faqs.answer: In the form's OnSuccess. That runs only when the save worked, so the modal stays open if there is an error to fix.

title: Calculate totals from a gallery collection
shortDescription: Summarize editable gallery rows without waiting for a SharePoint save.
fullDescription: Calculate totals from local collection rows to give users immediate feedback in estimate, checklist, or budget screens.
problemStatement: Users need live totals while editing rows before those rows are saved to SharePoint.
whenNotToUse: Authoritative finance calculations needing server-side control
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm which gallery or filtered collection represents the records users can currently see.
Collect the visible rows into a local collection before calculating totals that drive labels or summary cards.
Use Sum, CountRows, and Filter against the local collection so the displayed totals match the screen state.
Test with no rows, one row, filtered rows, and records with blank numeric values.
commonMistakes: Summing text inputs without converting to numbers.
Calculating from gallery controls instead of the collection.
Using Sum directly on a large SharePoint list, which is not delegable and totals only the first rows.
troubleshooting: If totals do not update, confirm Patch(colEstimateRows, ThisItem, ...) fires on control change.
If the total grows as you scroll, the gallery loads rows in pages and AllItems reflects what is loaded. Total a collection instead.
If Sum returns blank, the column is text. Wrap it in Value().
If the total includes hidden rows, sum the same filtered source the gallery uses.

faqs.question: How do I show a total under a gallery in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Add a label with Sum(GalleryName.AllItems, ColumnName) and format it with Text(). It recalculates whenever the gallery changes.

faqs.question: Why is my gallery total wrong on a big list?
faqs.answer: Galleries load data in pages, and Sum on a SharePoint list is not delegable. Load the filtered rows into a collection and total that.

faqs.question: Can I sum values typed into text inputs in a gallery?
faqs.answer: Yes. Reference the control by name inside Sum over AllItems and convert its text with Value().

title: Patch a collection of checklist items
shortDescription: Save checklist rows from Power Apps to a SharePoint child list.
fullDescription: Use ForAll and Patch to save multiple checklist rows related to a parent request or project item.
problemStatement: Checklist galleries often need to save several edited rows while preserving their parent relationship.
whenNotToUse: Small temporary rows better stored as JSON
High-volume transactional updates
stepByStepInstructions: Keep the parent record ID available.
Track existing child row IDs when editing.
Patch existing rows or Defaults for new rows.
Reload the child list after save.
commonMistakes: Losing child IDs and creating duplicates.
Saving child rows before the parent request exists.
Running a LookUp inside ForAll for every row, which makes one extra call per item.
troubleshooting: If duplicate rows appear, inspect whether collection rows include the SharePoint ID.
If the bulk Patch reports a type mismatch, the records contain columns the list does not have. Build the record with only list columns.
If new rows are created again on the next save, the collection was not reloaded, so those rows still have no ID.
If RemoveIf shows a delegation warning, the list is being filtered locally. Index RequestId and keep each request's rows well under the row limit.

faqs.question: How do I save a whole collection to SharePoint in one go?
faqs.answer: Pass a table of records to Patch. Rows without an ID are created, and rows that include an ID update the matching item.

faqs.question: Is ForAll with Patch slow?
faqs.answer: One Patch per row makes one network call per row. A single Patch with a table of records is much faster for more than a few rows.

faqs.question: How do I avoid creating duplicate child rows?
faqs.answer: Keep the SharePoint ID on each collection row, update rows that have an ID, create only rows that do not, and reload the collection after saving.

title: Recalculate deliverable completion from checklist rows
shortDescription: Roll checklist completion into a parent deliverable percentage.
fullDescription: Calculate completion percentage from child checklist rows and save it back to the parent deliverable.
problemStatement: Parent deliverable status becomes unreliable when checklist progress is manually maintained.
whenNotToUse: Subjective status assessments without checklist criteria
stepByStepInstructions: Load checklist rows for the deliverable.
Count total and completed rows.
Guard against divide-by-zero.
Patch the calculated percentage to the parent.
commonMistakes: Calculating from stale rows.
Not handling empty checklists.
troubleshooting: If completion looks wrong, refresh child rows before recalculation.

title: Format a SharePoint hyperlink field in list JSON
shortDescription: Make hyperlink columns easier to scan and click in SharePoint lists.
fullDescription: Apply list column formatting to render a clean link label for URL fields in SharePoint.
problemStatement: Raw URLs make SharePoint lists noisy and hard for business users to scan.
whenNotToUse: Fields that need multiple links
Complex formatting better handled in a custom app
stepByStepInstructions: Open the SharePoint list view and choose Format current view or Format this column for the hyperlink field.
Paste the JSON formatting into the advanced mode editor and replace the field internal name if needed.
Test records with a valid URL, blank URL, and long display text so the view remains readable.
Save the formatting and document which column internal name the JSON depends on.
commonMistakes: Using JSON formatting to hide required data quality issues.
Forgetting target _blank for reference links.
Leaving the link visible when the field is empty, which shows a dead 'Open link' on every blank row.
troubleshooting: If the link does not open, confirm the field stores a valid URL.
If the description does not show, use @currentField.desc. @currentField alone returns the URL.
If nothing changes after saving, the JSON was applied to a different column or view. Formatting is saved per column.
If a referenced column such as [$TicketNumber] is blank in the link, add that column to the view.

faqs.question: How do I open a SharePoint hyperlink column in a new tab?
faqs.answer: Format the column with an a element and set the target attribute to _blank.

faqs.question: How do I show friendly text instead of the URL?
faqs.answer: Use @currentField.desc for the description stored with the link, or set txtContent to fixed text such as Open link.

faqs.question: Can I hide the link when the field is empty?
faqs.answer: Yes. Set the display style with an expression that returns none when @currentField is empty.

title: Send a Power Automate email with an HTML table
shortDescription: Turn selected SharePoint rows into a readable email table.
fullDescription: Use Create HTML table and a styled email body so status updates are readable outside SharePoint.
problemStatement: Plain item dumps in email are hard to read and often miss the business context.
whenNotToUse: Large reports better sent as attachments
Emails with sensitive data requiring special controls

stepByStepInstructions: Get the SharePoint items.
Select only the columns needed for the email.
Create an HTML table from the selected array.
Place the table inside a short HTML email body.
commonMistakes: Sending too many columns.
Not enabling HTML email body rendering.
Sending the email when the table is empty.
Passing Get items straight into Create HTML table, which outputs every internal column.
troubleshooting: If tags show as text, make sure the email action body is using HTML content.
If links show as text such as <a href, Create HTML table encodes HTML. Decode it with replace as in step 4.
If the table has no borders, email clients ignore style blocks. Put styles inline on the table, th and td tags.
If dates look like 2026-11-20T00:00:00Z, format them in the Select action.

faqs.question: How do I send a SharePoint list as a table in an email with Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use Get items, shape the columns with Select, pass the result to Create HTML table, and put its output in the body of Send an email (V2).

faqs.question: How do I style the HTML table?
faqs.answer: Use a Compose with replace() to add inline styles to the table, th and td tags. Most email clients ignore CSS in a style block.

faqs.question: Why do my links appear as raw HTML in the table?
faqs.answer: Create HTML table encodes angle brackets. Replace < and > with < and > after the table is built.

title: Attach SharePoint list attachments to an email in Power Automate
shortDescription: Collect list item attachments and send them in an email.
fullDescription: Use attachment metadata and content actions to build the array required by the email connector.
problemStatement: SharePoint attachment metadata alone does not include the file content needed by email actions.
whenNotToUse: Large files that should be linked instead
Highly sensitive files needing restricted sharing
stepByStepInstructions: Get attachments for the list item.
Loop through each attachment.
Get attachment content for each file.
Append Name and ContentBytes to an array.
Pass the array to the email Attachments field.
commonMistakes: Using attachment metadata instead of content.
Forgetting to initialize the attachment array.
Wrapping ContentBytes in quotes, which turns the file into text and corrupts it.
Turning on concurrency for the loop while appending to a variable.
troubleshooting: If attachments arrive corrupted, confirm ContentBytes is the raw output from Get attachment content.
If the email action only offers Name and Content boxes, use the toggle on the right of the Attachments field to enter the whole array.
If the email is rejected, the total size is over the mailbox limit, usually about 25 MB. Send links for large files.
If the wrong file content is attached, check File Identifier uses the Id of the current loop item.

faqs.question: How do I attach SharePoint list item attachments to an email in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use Get attachments, loop through them with Get attachment content, append each name and content to an array variable, and pass that array to the email action's Attachments field.

faqs.question: Why are my emailed attachments corrupted?
faqs.answer: ContentBytes was probably wrapped in quotes or built from metadata. It must be the unquoted output of Get attachment content.

faqs.question: What happens if the item has no attachments?
faqs.answer: The loop does not run and the email is sent without attachments. Add a condition on the count if an attachment is required.

title: Use OData filters correctly with SharePoint text fields
shortDescription: Filter SharePoint Get items actions with predictable OData expressions.
fullDescription: Use clear OData syntax for text matching in Power Automate SharePoint actions.
problemStatement: Small syntax issues in OData filters can return no rows or cause flow failures.
whenToUse: Find rows by title or key
whenNotToUse: Complex fuzzy searching
Queries needing joins across lists
formulaOrCode:
Power Automate OData filter examples for SharePoint text fields:

Exact match:
Title eq 'Contoso Request'

Status text column:
Status eq 'Active'

Starts with department code:
startswith(DepartmentCode,'FIN')

Escaped single quote in text:
Title eq 'Bob''s Request'

Recommended flow shape:
Get items -> Filter Query above -> Top Count 5000 -> Select only needed columns -> Apply to each result

More filters

Not equal:
Status ne 'Closed'

Combine with and / or (use brackets with or):
Status eq 'Active' and (Priority eq 'High' or Priority eq 'Critical')

Contains (works on single line of text):
substringof('urgent', Title)

Empty and not empty:
ProjectCode eq null
ProjectCode ne null

Choice column (use the column name, not Value):
Status eq 'Approved'

Person column by email:
AssignedTo/EMail eq 'megan@contoso.com'

Lookup column by ID or by text:
DepartmentId eq 12
Department/Title eq 'Finance'

Yes/No:
IsActive eq 1

Number and date:
Amount gt 1000
DueDate lt '2026-12-31'
Created ge '@{addDays(utcNow(), -7)}'

Dynamic value with an apostrophe escaped:
Title eq '@{replace(triggerBody()?['Title'], '''', '''''')}'

Internal names:
A column created as "Project Code" has the internal name Project_x0020_Code.
Find it in List settings > the column: the URL ends with Field=<internal name>.
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm the SharePoint internal column name before writing the OData filter.
Choose exact match, startswith, or another supported OData expression based on the search requirement.
Escape single quotes in text values and test the filter with one known matching record.
Limit returned columns and row count so the flow remains predictable.
commonMistakes: Using display names with spaces instead of internal names.
Forgetting quotes around text values.
Putting quotes around numbers or leaving them off text.
Using or without brackets, which changes what the filter means.
troubleshooting: If the action fails, copy the internal field name from list settings and retry.
If the error says the column does not exist, you used the display name. Use the internal name.
If the filter fails on a list over 5,000 items, the filtered column is not indexed.
If endswith is rejected, SharePoint does not support it. Use startswith or substringof, or filter afterwards with Filter array.

faqs.question: How do I filter Get items by a text column in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Write the internal column name, an operator and the value in single quotes, for example Title eq 'Contoso Request'.

faqs.question: How do I filter on a column with a space in its name?
faqs.answer: Use the internal name, where a space is encoded as _x0020_, for example Project_x0020_Code eq 'FIN-01'.

faqs.question: How do I handle an apostrophe in the value?
faqs.answer: Double it. In an expression use replace(value, '''', '''''') so O'Brien becomes O''Brien in the filter.

title: Build a PMO gate approval lifecycle
shortDescription: Model project intake gates with statuses, approvals, and clear ownership.
fullDescription: A practical SharePoint and Power Platform pattern for moving PMO requests through intake, review, approval, and launch readiness gates.
problemStatement: PMO intake processes become hard to manage when status, approval evidence, and decision ownership are not modeled explicitly.
whenNotToUse: Informal teams with no defined approval model
Regulated workflows needing formal records management design
formulaOrCode:
Suggested statuses:
Draft -> Submitted -> Intake Review -> More Info Needed -> Approved for Planning -> Rejected -> Launched
stepByStepInstructions: Define the status lifecycle before building screens.
Create explicit decision fields for approver, date, and comments.
Restrict status buttons by role.
Use Power Automate for notification and audit emails.
Report on aging requests by status.
commonMistakes: Letting users jump to any status from any state.
Mixing workflow status with project health status.
Skipping decision history.
troubleshooting: If the process feels confusing, separate intake status, approval decision, and project health into different fields.

title: Patch a SharePoint multi-choice field
shortDescription: Save several selected choices from a combo box into a SharePoint multi-choice column.
fullDescription: A Power Apps pattern for shaping selected combo box values into the table of Value records expected by SharePoint multi-choice fields.
problemStatement: Multi-choice columns fail or save blank when the app patches a comma-separated text string instead of a table of choice records.
whenNotToUse: High-volume tagging that should use a normalized child list
Plain text keyword storage
stepByStepInstructions: Bind the combo box to Choices(Requests.ImpactAreas).
Allow multiple selection on the control.
Patch a table of records with a Value property.
Reload the item after save to confirm SharePoint accepted the values.
commonMistakes: Joining selected values into one text string.
Using Result when the control returns Value.
Forgetting that multi-choice fields return a table.
Trying to filter the list by a multi-choice column and expecting delegation. It is evaluated locally.
troubleshooting: If only one value saves, check whether the combo box is configured for single select.
If values save blank, inspect the selected item property names.
If Patch reports that a table was expected, you passed a single record. Wrap it in Table() or use SelectedItems.
If clearing does not work with Blank(), pass an empty Table().
If a filter on the column shows a delegation warning, narrow the list with another delegable filter first.

faqs.question: What format does a SharePoint multi-choice column need in Patch?
faqs.answer: A table of records, each with a Value property, for example Table({ Value: "A" }, { Value: "B" }).

faqs.question: How do I show multi-choice values in a label?
faqs.answer: Use Concat(ThisItem.ColumnName, Value, ", ") to join the selected values into text.

faqs.question: How do I clear a multi-choice column?
faqs.answer: Patch it with an empty table, written as Table().

title: Patch a SharePoint multi-person field
shortDescription: Save multiple users from Power Apps into a SharePoint person column.
fullDescription: Use ForAll to build the expanded user records required for a SharePoint person column that allows multiple selections.
problemStatement: Multi-person SharePoint fields require a table of expanded user objects, not a list of emails or display names.
whenNotToUse: Security trimming that should be handled with Microsoft 365 groups
Large audience fields
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm the SharePoint person column allows multiple selections.
Use a user source that returns Mail and DisplayName.
Transform each selected user into an expanded user record.
Patch the resulting table to the person field.
commonMistakes: Reusing the single-person patch object without wrapping it in a table.
Using email addresses without claims.
Not clearing optional Department or JobTitle fields.
Filtering the list by a multi-person column and expecting it to be delegated.
troubleshooting: If SharePoint rejects the value, check that every selected user has a Mail value.
If defaults do not load, compare the saved table schema to the combo box Items schema.
If the error mentions that the user cannot be found, one selected account has no Mail value or is a guest with a different sign-in name.
If the column only keeps one person, 'Allow multiple selections' is off in the column settings.
If the default selection is empty when editing, the default table's field names must match the combo box Items, such as DisplayName and Mail.

faqs.question: How do I patch several people to a SharePoint person column?
faqs.answer: Build a table with ForAll over the combo box's SelectedItems, creating the same claims record for each person, and pass the table to Patch.

faqs.question: How do I clear a multi-person column?
faqs.answer: Patch the column with an empty table, written as Table().

faqs.question: Can I filter a list by a multi-person column?
faqs.answer: Not with delegation. Narrow the list with a delegable filter first, then test the person locally, or store the emails in a text column.

title: Create a SharePoint item and child tasks from one submit
shortDescription: Save a parent request, then create related task rows using the new parent ID.
fullDescription: A parent-child save pattern for apps that need one main SharePoint item plus several generated child records.
problemStatement: Child rows cannot be reliably created until the parent SharePoint item exists and the app has its new ID.
whenNotToUse: Simple single-list forms
Workflows needing transactional rollback
stepByStepInstructions: Patch the parent item and store the result.
Use the returned parent ID for child rows.
Loop through the task template collection.
Create each child task with the parent ID and starter status.
commonMistakes: Using LastSubmit from the wrong form.
Creating child rows before the parent item returns.
Saving parent title instead of parent ID.
No recovery path when the parent saves and the child rows fail.
troubleshooting: If child rows are orphaned, inspect the savedRequest variable immediately after parent Patch.
If duplicates appear, ensure the submit button is disabled during save.
If the bulk Patch fails with a type error, a field in the record does not match the list, often a choice column given plain text.
If tasks must exist even when the user closes the app mid-save, create them in a flow triggered by the new request.
If RequestId filters show a delegation warning, make it a Number column, not text.

faqs.question: How do I create a parent item and child items in one button press?
faqs.answer: Patch the parent first and store the returned record, then Patch the child rows using the parent's ID from that record.

faqs.question: How do I get the parent's ID for the child rows?
faqs.answer: Use the record returned by Patch, for example Set(savedRequest, Patch(...)), then savedRequest.ID.

faqs.question: Should the link to the parent be a lookup or a number column?
faqs.answer: A number column holding the parent's ID is easier to write in bulk and filters with delegation. A lookup adds SharePoint features but counts towards view limits.

title: Soft-delete SharePoint items from Power Apps
shortDescription: Hide records from users without removing the SharePoint item.
fullDescription: Use an IsArchived or DeletedOn field to preserve audit history while keeping active screens clean.
problemStatement: Hard deletes can remove useful audit context and make accidental deletion hard to recover from.
whenNotToUse: Data that must be purged for compliance
Temporary draft records with no audit value
stepByStepInstructions: Add archive fields to the SharePoint list.
Patch archive values instead of calling Remove.
Filter active galleries where IsArchived is not true.
Create an admin view for archived records.
commonMistakes: Calling Remove when the business expects recoverability.
Forgetting to filter archived records out of galleries.
Leaving archived rows in lookups, dropdowns and flows that read the list.
troubleshooting: If archived items still appear, check for blank IsArchived values and filter with IsArchived <> true.
If IsArchived = false misses old items, they hold blank. Set the column default to No and fill existing blanks once in grid view.
If the filter shows a delegation warning, write the comparison as IsArchived = false with the column on the left.
If the list grows very large, index IsArchived and filter on it first.

faqs.question: What is a soft delete in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Instead of removing the item, you set a flag such as IsArchived and hide flagged items from galleries. The data stays available to restore or audit.

faqs.question: How do I restore a soft-deleted item?
faqs.answer: Patch the flag back to false. Provide an admin screen filtered to archived items with a restore button.

faqs.question: Why not just use Remove and the recycle bin?
faqs.answer: The recycle bin keeps items for 93 days and needs someone with permission to restore them. A flag keeps control in the app and preserves history.

title: Handle Patch errors with IfError
shortDescription: Show useful save feedback when SharePoint rejects a Power Apps patch.
fullDescription: Wrap Patch calls with IfError so users see clear failure messages and the app can avoid pretending a save succeeded.
problemStatement: Apps often show success notifications even when SharePoint rejected the save due to validation or permissions.
whenNotToUse: Purely local collection edits
Simple forms already using OnFailure well
stepByStepInstructions: Wrap the Patch call in IfError.
Show a specific error notification.
Only show success in the success branch.
Consider logging error details for admin troubleshooting later.
commonMistakes: Putting Notify success after IfError so it always runs.
Hiding SharePoint required-field errors behind generic UI.
Chaining Navigate after the IfError, so the user leaves the screen even when the save failed.
troubleshooting: If the error branch never runs, confirm the expression inside IfError is the actual failing call.
If IfError is not recognised, turn on formula-level error management in Settings. It is on by default in newer apps.
If the success message shows after a failure, it is outside the IfError. Put it in the first argument after the Patch, or in the third argument.
If FirstError.Message is unhelpful, log FirstError.Kind and FirstError.Source with Trace and read them in Monitor.

faqs.question: How do I catch a Patch error in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Wrap the Patch in IfError. The second argument runs when the Patch fails, and FirstError.Message holds the reason.

faqs.question: What is the difference between IfError and Errors()?
faqs.answer: IfError handles the failure in the same formula. Errors(DataSource) is the older approach that you check after the call. IfError is clearer and works for any function.

faqs.question: How do I show the real SharePoint error to the user?
faqs.answer: Use FirstError.Message inside the error branch of IfError, usually after a short friendly sentence.

title: Build a delegation-safe SharePoint date range filter
shortDescription: Filter large SharePoint lists by date without losing records.
fullDescription: Use direct date comparisons against indexed SharePoint date columns to keep dashboard filters delegable.
problemStatement: Wrapping SharePoint date columns in DateValue or Text inside Filter can break delegation and return incomplete results.
whenNotToUse: Tiny lists where delegation is not a concern
Complex reporting better handled in Power BI
stepByStepInstructions: Use a real SharePoint date column.
Compare the column directly to date picker values.
Use an exclusive end boundary for full-day matching.
Index the date column in SharePoint for larger lists.
commonMistakes: Using Text(DueDate) in the filter.
Filtering with equals when times are stored with the date.
Forgetting the end date boundary.
Calling Year(), Month() or DateDiff() on the column inside the filter, which stops delegation.
troubleshooting: If expected records are missing, check whether DueDate includes time values and use a next-day exclusive end filter.
If the warning appears although the comparison is simple, the date value is calculated inside the Filter. Calculate it first in With or a variable.
If records on the end date are missing, the column stores a time. Use less than the following day.
If results are a day out for some users, the column is date-only and their time zone differs from the site's. Compare with a small margin or store the date as text for exact matching.

faqs.question: Are date filters delegable in SharePoint?
faqs.answer: Yes. Comparing a date column with =, <, >, <= or >= is delegable, provided the value on the other side is calculated outside the filter.

faqs.question: Why does my end date exclude records from that day?
faqs.answer: Date and time columns store a time. Filter with less than the day after the end date so the whole final day is included.

faqs.question: How do I filter by month without a delegation warning?
faqs.answer: Work out the first day of the month and the first day of the next month, then filter with >= and <. Do not use Month() on the column.

title: Design SharePoint columns with stable internal names
shortDescription: Avoid painful internal-name surprises before building apps and flows.
fullDescription: Create SharePoint columns with clean internal names first, then rename display labels for business readability.
problemStatement: Columns created with spaces or temporary names can leave awkward internal names that make formulas and flow filters harder to maintain.
whenNotToUse: Existing mature lists where renaming would break integrations
formulaOrCode:
Recommended creation order:
1. Create column as ProjectCode
2. Save the column
3. Rename display label to Project Code

What the internal name becomes
  Created as            Internal name
  ProjectCode           ProjectCode
  Project Code          Project_x0020_Code
  Cost (USD)            Cost_x0020__x0028_USD_x0029_
  Approved?             Approved_x003f_
  2026 Budget           _x0032_026_x0020_Budget
  Imported from Excel   field_1, field_2, ...
  Names are cut at 32 characters, and each encoded character uses seven.

Find a column's internal name
  List settings > click the column > the page URL ends with  &Field=Project_x0020_Code
  REST: /_api/web/lists/getbytitle('Requests')/fields?$select=Title,InternalName&$filter=Hidden eq false

Where each name is used
  Display name   : SharePoint forms and views; Power Apps formulas (shown), 'Project Code'
  Internal name  : Power Automate filter queries and dynamic content keys, REST, JSON formatting [$Project_x0020_Code],
                   calculated column references after a rename, PnP scripts

Naming rules
  PascalCase, letters and digits only, start with a letter, under 32 characters.
  Yes/No starts with Is or Has. Dates end with Date or On.
  Do not reuse built-in names such as Title, Created, Modified, Author or Editor.

Already created with spaces?
  The internal name cannot be changed. For a list that is not yet in use, delete and recreate the column.
  For a live list, keep it and document the internal name.
stepByStepInstructions: Create columns with simple internal names.
Avoid spaces, punctuation, and temporary labels during creation.
Rename display labels after saving.
Document internal names for app and flow builders.
commonMistakes: Creating a column as Project Code and later discovering Project_x0020_Code.
Renaming a display name and assuming the internal name changed.
Creating lists by importing a spreadsheet, which produces internal names like field_1 that nobody can read.
troubleshooting: If an OData filter fails, verify the internal name from list settings rather than the display label.
If Power Automate cannot find the column in a filter, use the internal name with _x0020_ in place of each space.
If JSON formatting shows nothing for a column reference, write it as [$InternalName] and add the column to the view.
If two columns seem to have the same name, one was renamed. Check their internal names in the column settings URL.

faqs.question: What is a SharePoint internal column name?
faqs.answer: It is the permanent name SharePoint gives a column when it is created. The display name can change later, but the internal name never does.

faqs.question: Can I change a column's internal name?
faqs.answer: No. The only way is to delete the column and create it again, which loses its data and breaks anything that referenced it.

faqs.question: Why does my column name contain _x0020_?
faqs.answer: The column was created with a space in its name. SharePoint encodes the space as _x0020_ in the internal name.

title: SharePoint list schema for project intake
shortDescription: Start a project intake list with fields that support workflow, reporting, and governance.
fullDescription: A practical starter schema for project request intake that works with Power Apps, approvals, and PMO reporting.
problemStatement: Project intake lists become messy when request details, status, decision history, and prioritization are not separated clearly.
whenNotToUse: Full enterprise portfolio management replacement
Highly regulated intake requiring formal records design
formulaOrCode:
Core columns:
ProjectCode, RequestTitle, BusinessOwner, Sponsor, IntakeStatus, Priority, RequestedStartDate, TargetFinishDate, Decision, DecisionDate, DecisionComments

Column details
  Internal name        Type                 Notes
  ProjectCode          Single line          unique values, indexed. Set by a flow, e.g. PRJ-2026-014
  RequestTitle         (use Title)          rename the Title column's display name
  BusinessProblem      Multiple lines       plain text, required at submission
  ExpectedBenefit      Multiple lines       plain text
  BusinessOwner        Person               single, required
  Sponsor              Person               single
  Department           Choice               indexed
  IntakeStatus         Choice               Draft | Submitted | In review | More info needed | Approved | Rejected | On hold   (default Draft, indexed)
  Priority             Choice               Low | Medium | High
  EstimatedCost        Currency
  EstimatedEffortDays  Number
  RequestedStartDate   Date only
  TargetFinishDate     Date only
  StrategicAlignment   Choice               Growth | Efficiency | Compliance | Customer | Risk reduction
  Decision             Choice               Approve | Reject | Defer
  DecisionDate         Date only
  DecisionBy           Person
  DecisionComments     Multiple lines       plain text

Validation (list settings > Validation settings)
  =IF(ISBLANK([TargetFinishDate]), TRUE, [TargetFinishDate]>=[RequestedStartDate])
  Message: "Target finish cannot be before the requested start."

Views
  My requests        : Created By = [Me]
  Awaiting review    : IntakeStatus = Submitted, sort Created ascending
  Review board       : IntakeStatus = In review, group by Department, with EstimatedCost totals
  Decisions this year: Decision is not empty, sort DecisionDate descending

Settings
  Versioning on (50 versions). Attachments on for a business case document.
  Index IntakeStatus, Department and ProjectCode before the list grows.
stepByStepInstructions: Separate intake status from delivery health.
Use choice columns for lifecycle values.
Create people fields for owner, sponsor, and reviewer.
Add decision fields for audit context.
Index status and owner fields for dashboards.
commonMistakes: Using one Status field for both approval lifecycle and project health.
Skipping decision comments.
Making every field required before the draft stage.
troubleshooting: If reports are hard to build, check whether lifecycle, priority, and ownership are stored as structured columns.
If drafts cannot be saved, a column needed only at submission is marked required. Enforce it in the form or list validation by status.
If the review board view has no totals, set them under the view's Totals section for the cost column.
If project codes collide, generate them from the item ID in a flow and enforce unique values on the column.

faqs.question: What columns does a project intake list need?
faqs.answer: A title, the business problem and benefit, an owner and sponsor, a status, priority, dates, an estimate, and decision fields for the outcome, date, decision maker and comments.

faqs.question: Should intake status and project health be one column?
faqs.answer: No. Intake status tracks the approval lifecycle. Project health belongs on the project record after approval. Mixing them makes both hard to report.

faqs.question: How do I generate a project code automatically?
faqs.answer: Use a flow on item creation that builds the code from a prefix, the year and the item ID, and writes it to an indexed, unique text column.

title: Document library metadata pattern for project files
shortDescription: Use metadata and views so PMO documents do not depend only on folders.
fullDescription: Design project document libraries with a small set of metadata fields that support views, filtering, and lifecycle management.
problemStatement: Folder-only libraries make it difficult to find files by document type, project phase, owner, or approval status.
whenNotToUse: Simple team file drops with no reporting need
Formal records repositories needing retention design
formulaOrCode:
Suggested metadata:
DocumentType, ProjectPhase, DocumentOwner, ApprovalStatus, EffectiveDate, RelatedProjectCode

Column details
  DocumentType        Choice     Plan | Status report | Change request | Minutes | Specification | Contract | Other   (required)
  ProjectPhase        Choice     Initiate | Plan | Deliver | Close
  DocumentOwner       Person     single
  ApprovalStatus      Choice     Draft | In review | Approved | Superseded   (default Draft)
  EffectiveDate       Date only
  RelatedProjectCode  Single line, indexed. Or a lookup to the Projects list.
  ReviewDate          Date only  when the document should next be checked

Fill metadata automatically
  Library settings > Column default value settings: set RelatedProjectCode and ProjectPhase per folder.
  Each project's folder then tags every file dropped into it.

Views
  By document type   : group by DocumentType
  Approved documents : ApprovalStatus = Approved        (link this view from the project site's home page)
  My drafts          : DocumentOwner = [Me] AND ApprovalStatus = Draft
  Review due         : ReviewDate <= [Today]+30
  Missing metadata   : DocumentType is empty

Folders or metadata?
  Use a shallow folder level for things that never change, such as the project.
  Use metadata for everything users filter by: type, phase, status.
  Keep total path length under 400 characters.

Library settings
  Versioning: major versions, keep 100. Add minor versions if drafts need to stay hidden from readers.
  Require check out: off, so co-authoring works.

Power Automate and Power Apps
  Trigger "When a file is created or modified (properties only)", then read triggerBody()?['DocumentType']?['Value'].
  In Power Apps, filter a library like a list: Filter(ProjectDocuments, RelatedProjectCode = varProject.ProjectCode)
stepByStepInstructions: Define a short metadata set before migration.
Use choice fields for document type and phase.
Create views by phase, owner, and approval status.
Keep folder structure shallow if folders are still needed.
commonMistakes: Adding too many required metadata fields.
Using free-text document types.
Creating deep folder trees that hide useful metadata.
troubleshooting: If users resist metadata, reduce required fields and prefill values from the project context where possible.
If files uploaded by drag and drop have no metadata, set folder defaults or make only one or two columns required.
If a view filter on RelatedProjectCode fails on a big library, index that column.
If people cannot find approved versions, give them a link to the Approved documents view instead of the library root.

faqs.question: Is metadata better than folders in SharePoint?
faqs.answer: Metadata is better for anything people filter or group by, because a file can only live in one folder but can have several properties. A shallow folder level is still useful for separating projects.

faqs.question: How many metadata columns should be required?
faqs.answer: As few as possible, usually one or two. Fill the rest with default values per folder so users do not have to type them.

faqs.question: How do I set metadata automatically for uploaded files?
faqs.answer: Use Column default value settings in the library settings to assign values per folder. Files added to that folder receive them.

title: SharePoint permissions pattern for request lists
shortDescription: Balance broad collaboration with controlled approval actions.
fullDescription: Use list permissions, views, and app-level role checks together so users can collaborate without accidentally approving or editing restricted fields.
problemStatement: Power Apps visibility rules do not replace SharePoint permissions, but SharePoint permissions alone may not create the right workflow experience.
whenToUse: Lists with contributor and approver roles
whenNotToUse: Highly confidential data requiring item-level security architecture
Apps with external guest access not yet governed
formulaOrCode:
Recommended layers:
1. SharePoint controls who can read and edit the list
2. Power Apps controls which actions are visible
3. Power Automate records approval decisions and notifications

Groups and permission levels
  Group                    Level on the request list       Who
  Request Visitors         Read                            people who only view outcomes
  Request Members          Contribute                      requesters (add and edit items, no list design)
  Request Approvers        Contribute                      approvers
  Request Owners           Full Control                    two or three named administrators
  Flow service account     Contribute or Edit              runs the approval flows

  Use Contribute for members. The Edit level also lets people add, change and delete columns and views.

Item-level permissions (List settings > Advanced settings)
  Read access            : Read items that were created by the user
  Create and Edit access : Create items and edit items that were created by the user
  Requesters then see only their own requests. People with Manage Lists rights (owners) see everything.
  Approvers need another route to see all items: a flow that grants access, or a separate approver view
  on a list without this restriction.

Protect decision fields
  SharePoint has no column-level permissions. Choose one:
  1. Keep decision columns out of the requester's form and write them only from a flow.
  2. Store decisions in a second list that requesters can read but not edit.
  3. Add a flow that reverts decision columns changed by anyone outside the approver group.

Lock an item after submission (in the approval flow)
  Stop sharing an item or a file       (breaks inheritance and removes existing access)
  Grant access to an item or a folder  (give the requester Can view, approvers Can edit)
  Use only where needed. Many items with unique permissions slow a list.

Check as a real user
  List settings > Permissions for this list > Check Permissions > enter a requester's name.
  Then sign in as a test requester and try grid edit and the default form, not only the app.
stepByStepInstructions: Define data access separately from button visibility.
Keep approver-only fields protected through process design.
Use role lists for app behavior.
Use SharePoint groups for actual list access.
Review inherited permissions before launch.
commonMistakes: Treating hidden buttons as security.
Giving everyone edit rights to sensitive decision fields.
Breaking inheritance without documenting why.
troubleshooting: If users can still edit fields outside the app, review list forms, grid edit permissions, and SharePoint group membership.
If requesters can see other people's items, item-level permissions are not set, or they belong to a group with Manage Lists rights.
If approvers cannot see requests after item-level permissions are turned on, add them through a flow or give them a level that includes Manage Lists.
If a flow fails with access denied, its connection account is missing from the list's permissions.

faqs.question: Can SharePoint restrict users to seeing only their own list items?
faqs.answer: Yes. In the list's advanced settings, set item-level permissions so users read and edit only the items they created.

faqs.question: Does SharePoint have column-level security?
faqs.answer: No. To protect specific fields, write them only from a flow, keep them in a separate list, or revert unauthorised changes.

faqs.question: Is hiding fields in a Power App enough to secure them?
faqs.answer: No. Users with edit rights can still change those fields in the SharePoint list. Security has to be set on the list itself.

title: Power Automate approval with SharePoint status sync
shortDescription: Keep approval outcomes and request status aligned in SharePoint.
fullDescription: A flow pattern for starting an approval, recording the decision, and updating a SharePoint choice status consistently.
problemStatement: Approval flows become confusing when the approval outcome and SharePoint request status drift apart.
whenNotToUse: Complex multi-stage approval engines
Approvals needing custom delegation rules
formulaOrCode:
Power Automate approval flow implementation:
1. Trigger: When an item is created or modified.
2. Condition: Status is equal to Submitted.
3. Start and wait for an approval with AssignedTo = ApproverEmail.
4. If Outcome is Approve, update SharePoint Status = Approved, DecisionDate = utcNow(), DecisionBy = responder email.
5. If Outcome is Reject, update Status = Rejected and store DecisionComments.
6. Add a Catch scope to update ProcessingStatus = Failed and notify the support owner.

Flow detail

Trigger: When an item is created or modified
  Settings > Trigger conditions:
    @equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Submitted')

Scope "Try"
  Update item                      Status: In approval          (stops the flow starting twice)

  Start and wait for an approval   Type: Approve/Reject - First to respond
    Title       : Approve: @{triggerBody()?['Title']}
    Assigned to : @{triggerBody()?['Approver']?['Email']}
    Details     : requester, amount and reason
    Item link   : @{triggerBody()?['{Link}']}

  Condition: outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/outcome'] is equal to Approve
    If yes -> Update item
        Status           : Approved
        DecisionDate     : @{utcNow()}
        DecisionBy       : @{first(outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/responses'])?['responder']?['email']}
        DecisionComments : @{first(outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/responses'])?['comments']}
    If no  -> Update item
        Status           : Rejected
        DecisionDate, DecisionBy, DecisionComments as above

  Send an email (V2) to the requester with the outcome and comments

Scope "Catch"   (Configure run after: has failed, has timed out)
  Update item   ProcessingStatus: Failed
  Send an email to the support owner with the item link and:
    https://make.powerautomate.com/environments/@{workflow()?['tags']?['environmentName']}/flows/@{workflow()?['name']}/runs/@{workflow()?['run']?['name']}

Outcome values
  Approve/Reject types return exactly "Approve" or "Reject".
  "Everyone must approve" returns "Approve" only when all approvers approve.
stepByStepInstructions: Start the approval from the SharePoint item context.
Use outcome conditions for Approved and Rejected.
Update both lifecycle status and decision fields.
Send a confirmation email with the decision summary.
commonMistakes: Updating status before the approval completes.
Not storing approver comments.
Using email notification as the only audit trail.
troubleshooting: If status does not update, inspect the approval outcome value and branch condition casing.
If the flow starts again after it updates the item, the trigger condition is missing or the flow sets the status back to Submitted.
If the run times out after 30 days, flows cannot wait longer. Add a reminder and an escalation before that.
If DecisionBy is empty, read the responder from the responses array as shown, not from the trigger.

faqs.question: How do I update a SharePoint status after an approval in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Add a condition on the approval's outcome after Start and wait for an approval, then use Update item in each branch to set the status, decision date, approver and comments.

faqs.question: What does the approval outcome return?
faqs.answer: For Approve/Reject approvals it returns the text Approve or Reject. Compare with those exact values.

faqs.question: How do I stop the approval flow from triggering itself?
faqs.answer: Use a trigger condition so the flow starts only when the status is Submitted, and change the status to something else as the first action.

title: Parse JSON sent from Power Apps in Power Automate
shortDescription: Send structured rows from Power Apps to a flow and parse them safely.
fullDescription: Use JSON from Power Apps for lightweight row arrays, then parse and loop through the payload in Power Automate.
problemStatement: Flows that receive collection data as text need a schema before they can loop through rows predictably.
whenToUse: Email table generation from app data
whenNotToUse: Large payloads better saved directly to a data source
Data requiring complex validation before submission
stepByStepInstructions: Serialize the Power Apps collection.
Pass the JSON text into the flow.
Use Parse JSON with a sample payload schema.
Loop through parsed rows and create or update records.
commonMistakes: Changing the app collection schema without updating Parse JSON.
Passing display-only control values instead of clean data fields.
Marking every property as required in the schema, so one missing value fails the whole run.
troubleshooting: If Parse JSON fails, capture the exact payload from a flow run and regenerate the schema from that sample.
If the error is 'Invalid type. Expected String but got Null', allow null for that property with "type": ["string", "null"].
If the flow receives an empty array, the collection was empty or JSON() ran before it was filled.
If the payload is cut off, very large text inputs can hit request size limits. Send fewer columns or split the rows into batches.

faqs.question: How do I pass a collection from Power Apps to Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Convert it to text with JSON() and pass it as a text input. In the flow, use Parse JSON to turn it back into an array.

faqs.question: How do I create the Parse JSON schema?
faqs.answer: Run the flow once, copy the payload from the trigger's outputs, and use Generate from sample in the Parse JSON action. Then allow nulls where values can be empty.

faqs.question: Why does Parse JSON fail on null values?
faqs.answer: The generated schema lists a single type for each property. Change the type to an array that includes null, such as ["string", "null"].

title: Format dates in Power Automate with Compose
shortDescription: Create reusable formatted date values before email or SharePoint updates.
fullDescription: Use Compose actions to make date formatting explicit and easier to reuse across flow steps.
problemStatement: Date expressions scattered directly inside emails and updates are hard to troubleshoot and easy to format inconsistently.
whenNotToUse: Dates that should remain raw ISO values for downstream systems
formulaOrCode:
Power Automate date formatting expressions:

Format today for display:
formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'MMMM d, yyyy')

Format a SharePoint due date:
formatDateTime(triggerBody()?['DueDate'], 'yyyy-MM-dd')

Convert from UTC before formatting:
formatDateTime(convertTimeZone(triggerBody()?['DueDate'], 'UTC', 'Pacific Standard Time'), 'MMM d, yyyy h:mm tt')

Safe fallback when date is blank:
if(empty(triggerBody()?['DueDate']), 'No due date', formatDateTime(triggerBody()?['DueDate'], 'yyyy-MM-dd'))

More formats
  'yyyy-MM-dd'                 2026-11-20              for filters and file names
  'dd/MM/yyyy'                 20/11/2026
  'M/d/yyyy'                   11/20/2026
  'dddd, d MMMM yyyy'          Friday, 20 November 2026
  'MMM d'                      Nov 20
  'HH:mm'                      14:05                   24-hour
  'h:mm tt'                    2:05 PM
  'yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ'       2026-11-20T14:05:00Z    ISO 8601 for APIs
  'yyyyMMdd-HHmmss'            20261120-140500         unique file names
  Case matters: MM is month, mm is minutes. HH is 24-hour, hh is 12-hour.

In another language
  formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'dddd d MMMM yyyy', 'fr-FR')

Time zones
  convertFromUtc(utcNow(), 'GMT Standard Time', 'dd MMM yyyy HH:mm')
  convertTimeZone(triggerBody()?['Start'], 'UTC', 'W. Europe Standard Time', 'HH:mm')
  Use Windows time zone names. Daylight saving is applied for you.

Date arithmetic
  addDays(utcNow(), 7, 'yyyy-MM-dd')
  addToTime(utcNow(), 1, 'Month', 'yyyy-MM-dd')
  startOfMonth(utcNow(), 'yyyy-MM-dd')
  dayOfWeek(utcNow())                              0 = Sunday
  Days between two dates:
  div(sub(ticks(triggerBody()?['DueDate']), ticks(utcNow())), 864000000000)

Text that is not ISO format (for example 20/11/2026 from a form)
  parseDateTime('20/11/2026', 'en-GB', 'dd/MM/yyyy')

Excel serial dates (a number such as 46346)
  addDays('1899-12-30', int(item()?['Date']), 'yyyy-MM-dd')
stepByStepInstructions: Add a Compose action immediately after the trigger or Get item action.
Use formatDateTime for display-only values and convertTimeZone when the audience expects local time.
Add an empty check before formatting optional date fields.
Use the Compose output in email, Teams, approval, or audit text instead of repeating the expression.
commonMistakes: Formatting dates before checking for blanks.
Using local-looking formats for system integrations.
Writing mm for month or MM for minutes. The case decides which one you get.
troubleshooting: If the flow fails on blank dates, wrap the expression in an if empty check.
If the error says the datetime string must match ISO 8601 format, the input is text in another format. Convert it with parseDateTime first.
If the time is hours out, the value is UTC. Convert with convertFromUtc before formatting.
If an Excel date arrives as a number, either set the Excel action's DateTime Format to ISO 8601 or convert the serial number with addDays.

faqs.question: How do I format a date in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use formatDateTime(value, 'format'), for example formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'dd MMM yyyy').

faqs.question: How do I convert UTC to my local time in a flow?
faqs.answer: Use convertFromUtc(value, 'your Windows time zone name', 'format'), or the Convert time zone action.

faqs.question: Why does formatDateTime fail on an empty date?
faqs.answer: It cannot format null. Wrap it in if(empty(value), '', formatDateTime(value, 'format')).

title: Update SharePoint items without overwriting important fields
shortDescription: Reduce accidental data loss when a flow updates SharePoint items.
fullDescription: Use focused update steps and read-before-write discipline so flows do not overwrite fields that users or apps changed.
problemStatement: SharePoint Update item actions can unintentionally write stale or blank values if required fields are not handled carefully.
whenNotToUse: Simple single-field updates available through a purpose-built action or API pattern
formulaOrCode:
Flow discipline:
Get item -> calculate only changed fields -> Update item with existing values preserved for required fields

Three ways to update without overwriting other fields

1. Update item, with current values re-read first
   Get item (Id from the trigger)                      current values, not the trigger's snapshot
   Update item
     Title           : @{body('Get_item')?['Title']}   every required column must be supplied
     Status          : Approved                        the fields you mean to change
     (leave optional fields empty: Update item keeps their existing values when left blank,
      but required fields must always be filled)

2. Change only the fields you name: Send an HTTP request to SharePoint
   Method  : POST
   Uri     : _api/web/lists/getbytitle('Requests')/items(@{triggerBody()?['ID']})/validateUpdateListItem
   Headers : Accept: application/json;odata=nometadata
             Content-Type: application/json;odata=nometadata
   Body    :
   {
     "formValues": [
       { "FieldName": "Status", "FieldValue": "Approved" },
       { "FieldName": "DecisionDate", "FieldValue": "@{formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'M/d/yyyy')}" }
     ],
     "bNewDocumentUpdate": false
   }
   Nothing else on the item is touched. Set bNewDocumentUpdate to true to avoid creating a new version.

3. Fail instead of overwriting when someone else has edited the item (optimistic concurrency)
   Method  : POST
   Uri     : _api/web/lists/getbytitle('Requests')/items(@{body('Get_item')?['ID']})
   Headers : Accept: application/json;odata=nometadata
             Content-Type: application/json;odata=nometadata
             IF-MATCH: @{body('Get_item')?['{ETag}']}
             X-HTTP-Method: MERGE
   Body    : { "Status": "Approved" }
   If the item changed after Get item, SharePoint returns 412 Precondition Failed.
