   Handle it with a run-after branch: Get item again, re-apply the change, retry.

After a long wait (for example an approval), always Get item again before updating.
stepByStepInstructions: Get the current item before updating.
Only change fields the flow owns.
Pass existing required field values when the connector requires them.
Avoid updating broad records from stale trigger data.
commonMistakes: Leaving required fields blank in Update item.
Assuming trigger data is still current after approval waits.
Letting one flow own too many unrelated fields.
troubleshooting: If fields revert unexpectedly, compare the flow run inputs to the item version history.
If Update item fails asking for a required field, supply every required column, using values from Get item.
If the HTTP update returns 412, the ETag no longer matches because the item changed. Re-read and retry.
If validateUpdateListItem returns success but nothing changes, check the response body. Each field reports its own error message, often a date or person format problem.

faqs.question: Does Update item in Power Automate overwrite fields I leave blank?
faqs.answer: Optional fields left empty keep their current values. Required fields must be supplied on every update, so read them with Get item first.

faqs.question: How do I update a single SharePoint field in a flow?
faqs.answer: Use Send an HTTP request to SharePoint with validateUpdateListItem, or a MERGE request, and include only the fields you want to change.

faqs.question: What is an ETag in SharePoint?
faqs.answer: It is a version marker returned with each item. Sending it in an IF-MATCH header makes the update fail if someone else has changed the item since you read it.

title: Use Try/Catch scopes for Power Automate error handling
shortDescription: Group flow actions into success and failure paths that are easier to support.
fullDescription: Organize Power Automate flows with Try, Catch, and Finally scopes so failures produce clear notifications and cleanup behavior.
problemStatement: Flows with long linear action chains are difficult to troubleshoot when one middle step fails.
whenNotToUse: Tiny personal productivity flows where overhead is not worth it
formulaOrCode:
Pattern:
Scope - Try
Scope - Catch: run after Try has failed, timed out, or skipped
Scope - Finally: run after Try and Catch complete

Detail

Scope "Try"
  All the actions of the business operation.

Scope "Catch"
  Configure run after (on the scope's menu): tick "has failed" and "has timed out". Untick "is successful".

  Filter array "Failed actions"
    From      : @{result('Try')}
    Condition : @equals(item()?['status'], 'Failed')

  Compose "Error message"
    @{coalesce(
        first(body('Failed_actions'))?['error']?['message'],
        first(body('Failed_actions'))?['outputs']?['body']?['error']?['message'],
        first(body('Failed_actions'))?['outputs']?['body']?['message'],
        'Unknown error'
    )}

  Compose "Run link"
    https://make.powerautomate.com/environments/@{workflow()?['tags']?['environmentName']}/flows/@{workflow()?['name']}/runs/@{workflow()?['run']?['name']}

  Update item          ProcessingStatus: Failed, ErrorMessage: @{outputs('Error_message')}
  Send an email (V2)   Subject: Flow failed: @{workflow()?['tags']?['flowDisplayName']}
                       Body: failed action @{first(body('Failed_actions'))?['name']}, the error message,
                             the item link and the run link

  Terminate            Status: Failed, Message: @{outputs('Error_message')}
                       (keeps the run marked as failed in run history)

Scope "Finally"
  Configure run after Catch: is successful, has failed, is skipped, has timed out.
  Clean-up that must always happen, such as releasing a lock column.
  Place it before the Terminate if the Catch ends the run.

Retry before failing
  Each action > Settings > Retry policy: Exponential interval, count 4, interval PT10S.
stepByStepInstructions: Put main work inside a Try scope.
Configure Catch to run after Try failure.
Send a support-friendly failure notification.
Use Finally for cleanup or run logging.
commonMistakes: Only handling one failed action instead of the whole business operation.
Sending failure emails without the item link or flow run link.
Leaving the run marked as succeeded after an error was caught, so failures never show in run history.
troubleshooting: If Catch never runs, inspect the run-after settings on the Catch scope.
If result('Try') is rejected, use the scope's name with spaces replaced by underscores.
If the error message is empty, the failing action reports its error in outputs.body. The coalesce above checks the common locations.
If Finally is skipped, its run-after settings need every state ticked.

faqs.question: How do I add try and catch to a Power Automate flow?
faqs.answer: Put the main actions in a scope, add a second scope after it, and set the second scope's Configure run after to has failed and has timed out.

faqs.question: How do I get the error message from a failed action?
faqs.answer: Use result('ScopeName') to list the actions in the Try scope, filter for status Failed and read the error message from the first match.

faqs.question: Why does my flow show as succeeded even though it failed?
faqs.answer: The Catch scope handled the error, so the run completed. End the Catch with a Terminate action set to Failed.

title: PMO status report health rollup
shortDescription: Turn scope, schedule, budget, and risk ratings into a clear overall status.
fullDescription: A practical rollup pattern for project status reporting that keeps yellow and red signals visible instead of averaged away.
problemStatement: Overall project status loses credibility when serious schedule or budget risks are buried under a green average.
whenNotToUse: Projects without agreed health definitions
Teams using fully qualitative narratives only
formulaOrCode:
Rollup rule:
If any dimension is Red, overall cannot be Green.
If two or more dimensions are Yellow, overall should be Yellow unless leadership accepts the risk.
stepByStepInstructions: Define health dimensions.
Document what Green, Yellow, and Red mean.
Apply conservative rollup rules.
Require narrative explanation for any Yellow or Red dimension.
commonMistakes: Averaging colors numerically.
Letting teams mark overall green while schedule is red.
Skipping explanation for yellow status.
troubleshooting: If status debates repeat, publish explicit criteria for each color and dimension.

title: Risk, issue, and action log schema
shortDescription: Separate risks, issues, actions, and decisions without making PMs maintain four disconnected tools.
fullDescription: A PMO-friendly schema pattern for tracking risks, issues, actions, and decisions with enough structure for reporting.
problemStatement: Teams blur risks, issues, actions, and decisions together, making executive reporting and follow-up unclear.
whenNotToUse: Very small projects with no formal governance
Enterprise tools already enforcing RAID structure
formulaOrCode:
Core fields:
Type, Title, Description, Owner, DueDate, Impact, Probability, Severity, Status, EscalationNeeded, RelatedProject
stepByStepInstructions: Use a Type field for Risk, Issue, Action, or Decision.
Require owner and status.
Use due dates for actions and decisions.
Use impact and probability only where they make sense.
Create views by project and escalation need.
commonMistakes: Making risk probability required for action items.
Tracking decisions without decision date or decision maker.
Letting every item sit in Open status.
troubleshooting: If reports are noisy, split views by Type and show only fields relevant to that type.

title: Convert rough project notes into an executive summary
shortDescription: Structure messy status notes into a short leadership-ready update.
fullDescription: A reusable writing pattern for turning accomplishments, next steps, risks, and decisions into a concise executive summary.
problemStatement: Status updates often bury the real message in task-level notes that executives do not have time to parse.
whenNotToUse: Detailed project team work logs
Formal incident postmortems
formulaOrCode:
Summary structure:
1. Current status and reason
2. Meaningful progress this period
3. Risks or decisions needing attention
4. Next checkpoint
stepByStepInstructions: Start with the overall status.
Mention only business-relevant progress.
Call out yellow or red risks directly.
End with the next decision or checkpoint.
commonMistakes: Listing every task completed.
Using vague phrases like on track without evidence.
Hiding decisions needed at the bottom.
troubleshooting: If the summary feels too long, remove details that do not change a leader's decision or awareness.

title: Decision log pattern for SharePoint
shortDescription: Capture who decided what, when, and why so decisions do not disappear into meeting notes.
fullDescription: A simple SharePoint decision log pattern that supports PMO reporting and future audit questions without creating heavy process.
problemStatement: Important project decisions are often buried in meeting notes and become hard to trace later.
whenNotToUse: Informal team notes where no formal decision record is needed
formulaOrCode:
Suggested fields:
DecisionTitle, DecisionDescription, DecisionMaker, DecisionDate, Context, Impact, RelatedProject, FollowUpAction
stepByStepInstructions: Create a dedicated decision log list.
Capture decision maker and date as structured fields.
Link decisions to projects or requests.
Review open follow-up actions weekly.
commonMistakes: Writing decisions only as meeting note paragraphs.
Forgetting the decision maker.
Not linking follow-up actions.
troubleshooting: If users avoid the log, add decisions during meeting closeout instead of after the fact.

title: Control Power Apps form mode for new, edit, and view screens
shortDescription: Make form behavior predictable across create, edit, and read-only experiences.
fullDescription: Use NewForm, EditForm, ViewForm, and screen variables deliberately so users do not accidentally edit or overwrite records.
problemStatement: Forms can open in the wrong mode when navigation, selected records, and reset behavior are not handled consistently.
whenNotToUse: Fully custom patch screens without EditForm controls
stepByStepInstructions: Set the selected record before navigating for edit or view.
Call the correct form mode function.
Reset forms after successful save or cancel.
Use DisplayMode to keep view-only controls read-only.
commonMistakes: Using EditForm for new records.
Navigating before selectedRequest is set.
Forgetting ResetForm on cancel.
troubleshooting: If the wrong record opens, check whether the form Item property points to selectedRequest or Gallery.Selected.
If a new form shows the last record's values, call ResetForm before NewForm.
If the form is blank in edit mode, its Item is empty. Set the variable before calling EditForm.
If the form reports 'No item to display', it is in edit or view mode with a blank Item. Call NewForm, or set the record first.

faqs.question: What is the difference between NewForm, EditForm and ViewForm?
faqs.answer: NewForm prepares the form to create an item, EditForm lets the user change the item in the form's Item property, and ViewForm shows it read-only.

faqs.question: Can one screen handle new, edit and view?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use one form and call NewForm, EditForm or ViewForm before navigating to the screen. Drive headings and buttons from the form's Mode property.

faqs.question: How do I return to view mode after saving?
faqs.answer: In the form's OnSuccess, store LastSubmit in the record variable and call ViewForm.

title: Save draft and submit later in Power Apps
shortDescription: Let users save incomplete requests without triggering the formal workflow.
fullDescription: Use separate Draft and Submitted statuses so business users can save work in progress before routing a request for review.
problemStatement: Users often need to save partial forms, but workflows should not start until the request is intentionally submitted.
whenNotToUse: Very short forms with all required information available immediately
stepByStepInstructions: Add Draft and Submitted choices to the status column.
Use a save draft button that relaxes business validation.
Use a submit button that enforces required fields.
Trigger flows only when status changes to Submitted.
commonMistakes: Starting approval flows on every item creation.
Making all final required fields mandatory for draft saves.
Creating a new item on each draft save because the saved record was not kept in a variable.
troubleshooting: If draft items start routing, check the flow trigger condition and status value.
If a draft cannot be saved, a column is marked required in SharePoint. Make it optional and enforce it at submit.
If each save creates another draft, store the result of Patch in the variable used by Coalesce.
If old drafts pile up, add a scheduled flow that reminds owners or deletes drafts older than a set number of days.

faqs.question: How do I add a save as draft button in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Patch the item with a Draft status and only light validation, and store the returned record so later saves update the same item.

faqs.question: How do I stop a flow from running on drafts?
faqs.answer: Add a trigger condition so the flow starts only when the status equals Submitted.

faqs.question: Can SharePoint required columns work with drafts?
faqs.answer: Not well. A required column blocks the draft save. Make the columns optional in SharePoint and enforce them in the app at submission.

title: Disable submit buttons while saving
shortDescription: Prevent duplicate SharePoint items from double-clicked submit buttons.
fullDescription: Use a saving variable to block duplicate submits while Patch or SubmitForm is in progress.
problemStatement: Fast double-clicks can create duplicate records or run approval logic twice.
whenNotToUse: Read-only actions
Pure navigation buttons
stepByStepInstructions: Set varSaving before the save begins.
Disable the button when varSaving is true.
Reset varSaving after success or failure.
Show clear feedback so users know the save is running.
commonMistakes: Resetting varSaving only in the success path.
Leaving the button enabled while a flow call runs.
Relying on the disabled state alone, without making the save safe to run twice.
troubleshooting: If duplicates still appear, confirm every submit path checks the same saving variable.
If the button stays disabled, an error skipped the line that resets the flag. Reset it after the IfError, and in the form's OnFailure.
If a double tap still gets through, check the flag at the start of OnSelect as well as in DisplayMode.
If the screen opens with the button disabled, reset the flag in the screen's OnVisible.

faqs.question: How do I stop users clicking Submit twice in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Set a variable to true at the start of the save, set the button's DisplayMode to Disabled while it is true, and set it back to false when the save ends.

faqs.question: Where do I reset the saving flag when I use SubmitForm?
faqs.answer: In both the form's OnSuccess and OnFailure, because SubmitForm finishes after the button's formula has ended.

faqs.question: Why did I still get duplicate records?
faqs.answer: The flag only protects one screen. Keep the saved record in a variable and patch that record, so a repeated save updates it instead of creating another.

title: Inline edit and save gallery rows
shortDescription: Let users edit small row fields directly in a gallery and save changes predictably.
fullDescription: Use a local collection for edited gallery rows, then patch only changed values back to SharePoint.
problemStatement: Editing directly against gallery controls can become unreliable when users change several rows before saving.
whenNotToUse: Large editable grids
Financial data requiring strict validation
stepByStepInstructions: Load rows into an editable collection.
Patch the collection as users change controls.
Mark changed rows with IsDirty.
Patch only dirty rows back to SharePoint.
commonMistakes: Reading values directly from gallery controls during ForAll.
Saving every row even when only one changed.
Letting the user leave the screen with unsaved rows and no warning.
troubleshooting: If changes save to the wrong row, confirm every collection row includes the SharePoint ID.
If typing loses focus after each character, the collection is being patched on every keystroke. Use OnChange, which fires when the user leaves the field, or set DelayOutput to true.
If the bulk Patch creates new rows instead of updating, the records are missing the ID.
If a row's inputs reset while scrolling, bind each input's Default to the collection as shown.

faqs.question: How do I edit rows directly in a Power Apps gallery?
faqs.answer: Bind the gallery to a collection, put input controls in the row, and patch the collection from each control's OnChange. Save the changed rows to the data source with one button.

faqs.question: How do I save only the rows that changed?
faqs.answer: Add an IsDirty column to the collection, set it to true when a row is edited, and patch only the rows where it is true.

faqs.question: Why not patch SharePoint on every change?
faqs.answer: It works for a few edits, but each change is a separate network call. Collecting the edits and saving once is faster and lets the user discard changes.

title: Bulk update selected gallery items
shortDescription: Apply the same status or owner update to several selected SharePoint rows.
fullDescription: Track selected rows in a collection and loop through them when the user confirms a bulk action.
problemStatement: Users waste time opening records one at a time when a shared update applies to several items.
whenNotToUse: Updates requiring unique validation per row
Large batches better handled by Power Automate
stepByStepInstructions: Add a checkbox to each gallery row.
Collect or remove rows as users check items.
Preview the selected count.
Patch selected rows after confirmation.
commonMistakes: Bulk updating without a confirmation step.
Not clearing selected rows after the action completes.
Updating hundreds of rows from the app, where a flow would be more reliable and would not depend on the user keeping the app open.
troubleshooting: If some rows fail, add IfError around each Patch and collect failed IDs.
If the bulk Patch changes nothing, each record needs the ID so Patch can find the row.
If checkboxes lose their state while scrolling, bind Default to the selection collection.
If UpdateIf shows a delegation warning, it only changes rows within the data row limit. Use a flow for larger sets.

faqs.question: How do I update multiple selected items in a Power Apps gallery?
faqs.answer: Collect the selected rows with a checkbox, then call Patch once with a table that contains each row's ID and the new values.

faqs.question: Is ForAll with Patch or a single Patch faster?
faqs.answer: A single Patch with a table of records is faster because it batches the work. Use ForAll with IfError when you need to know exactly which rows failed.

faqs.question: How many rows can I bulk update from Power Apps?
faqs.answer: A few hundred is practical. For larger updates, pass the IDs to a flow so the work continues if the user closes the app.

title: Search SharePoint with multiple fields in Power Apps
shortDescription: Build a practical multi-field search while staying honest about delegation limits.
fullDescription: Combine delegable StartsWith filters for key fields and avoid non-delegable broad text scans on large SharePoint lists.
problemStatement: Users expect search across several fields, but SharePoint delegation limits make broad contains searches risky.
whenNotToUse: True full-text search requirements
Very large data sets needing Microsoft Search or Dataverse
stepByStepInstructions: Choose a small number of searchable fields.
Prefer StartsWith over in for SharePoint.
Index high-use columns.
Tell users which fields search covers.
commonMistakes: Using Search() against a large SharePoint list.
Searching every column with non-delegable formulas.
Expecting StartsWith to find text in the middle of a value. It matches the beginning only.
troubleshooting: If results are incomplete, simplify the formula until delegation warnings disappear.
If typing is slow, turn on DelayOutput so the gallery does not query on every keystroke.
If the person column cannot be searched, StartsWith on a person's DisplayName is not delegable. Save the name to a text column and search that.
If capital letters seem to matter, SharePoint's StartsWith ignores case, but a collection search with the in operator is also case-insensitive while exactin is not.

faqs.question: How do I search several SharePoint columns in Power Apps without a delegation warning?
faqs.answer: Use Filter with StartsWith on each column, joined with ||. StartsWith is delegable for SharePoint text columns.

faqs.question: Can I do a contains search on a SharePoint list?
faqs.answer: Not with delegation. Narrow the list with a delegable filter and run Search on the result, or search a collection for small lists.

faqs.question: Why does my search miss items in a large list?
faqs.answer: The formula is not delegable, so only the first 500 to 2,000 rows are searched. Replace Search or in with StartsWith.

title: Cascading dropdowns from SharePoint lists
shortDescription: Filter child dropdown options based on a parent selection.
fullDescription: Use parent-child SharePoint reference data to guide users through valid dropdown combinations.
problemStatement: Users can pick invalid combinations when every dropdown shows all possible values.
whenNotToUse: Small flat option sets
Reference data that changes constantly without governance
stepByStepInstructions: Load the child reference list into a local collection during App.OnStart or screen OnVisible.
Bind the parent dropdown to the parent choice or reference source.
Filter the child dropdown Items by the selected parent value and active flag.
Reset the child dropdown whenever the parent dropdown changes so stale selections are not saved.
commonMistakes: Not resetting the child dropdown when parent changes.
Filtering on display names instead of stable IDs.
Loading the child list from SharePoint on every parent change instead of filtering a cached collection.
troubleshooting: If child options do not appear, inspect whether the parent selected record has ID or Id.
If the child shows every option, the filter compares different types, such as a lookup record with text. Compare Id with ID, or Value with Value.
If the child keeps its old selection after the parent changes, call Reset on the child in the parent's OnChange.
If the saved child value does not show when editing, the child's Items are filtered by a parent that has not been set yet. Set the parent's default first.

faqs.question: How do I create dependent dropdowns in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Filter the child dropdown's Items by the parent's selected value, and reset the child in the parent's OnChange.

faqs.question: Where should the dropdown options come from?
faqs.answer: Keep child options in a SharePoint list with a column that points to the parent. Load it into a collection once and filter that.

faqs.question: Do cascading dropdowns work inside an edit form?
faqs.answer: Yes. Filter the child card's combo box Items by the parent card's selected value and reset the child control when the parent changes.

title: Cache the current user's profile in Power Apps
shortDescription: Load user profile details once and reuse them across the app.
fullDescription: Store the current user's profile and role context in variables to reduce repeated connector calls and simplify formulas.
problemStatement: Repeated profile lookups make formulas noisy and can slow screens that use the same user details in many places.
whenToUse: Request forms that default requester fields
whenNotToUse: Apps that do not use profile data
Scenarios requiring real-time manager lookup on every action
stepByStepInstructions: Set current user variables when the app starts.
Normalize email casing.
Reuse the variables in filters and defaults.
Refresh only when the user explicitly needs updated profile data.
commonMistakes: Calling Office365Users.MyProfileV2 in many control properties.
Comparing mixed-case email strings.
Calling ManagerV2 without IfError, which raises an error for users who have no manager.
troubleshooting: If role lookups fail, compare Lower(User().Email) to the stored email in the security list.
If the app shows an error at start for some users, they have no manager or no mailbox. Wrap the calls in IfError.
If guests get no profile, the Office 365 Users connector cannot read them in some tenants. Fall back to User().
If the department is blank, the directory holds no value for that user. Show a fallback and let them choose.

faqs.question: How do I get the current user's details in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: User() returns the email, full name and image. For department, job title, manager and more, call Office365Users.MyProfileV2() once and store the result.

faqs.question: Why should I cache the user profile?
faqs.answer: Each connector call takes time and counts towards API limits. Reading the profile once into a variable or named formula keeps screens fast.

faqs.question: How do I get the user's manager?
faqs.answer: Call Office365Users.ManagerV2(User().Email) and wrap it in IfError, because it fails for users without a manager.

title: Show a useful empty state for galleries
shortDescription: Give users clear feedback when filters return no rows.
fullDescription: Use a visible empty-state container to explain whether a gallery has no records, no matches, or needs a filter change.
problemStatement: Blank gallery screens make users wonder whether the app is broken, loading, or simply has no matching records.
whenNotToUse: Screens where empty content is impossible by design
stepByStepInstructions: Place an empty-state container in the same area as the gallery.
Set the container Visible property to CountRows(gallery.AllItems) = 0.
Write different empty-state copy for no data, filtered data, and searched data scenarios.
Test with zero records, filtered-out records, and records that appear after clearing search.
commonMistakes: Showing a generic no data message while data is still loading.
Not distinguishing no records from no search matches.
An empty state with no action, leaving the user with nowhere to go.
troubleshooting: If the empty state flickers, add a loading variable and hide the empty state while data loads.
If the empty state shows briefly on every visit, it is visible while data loads. Add the loading flag.
If the empty state never shows, it is behind the gallery. Hide the gallery when it has no rows or bring the container forward.
If the message is wrong after clearing the search, check the order of the conditions in the If.

faqs.question: How do I show a message when a Power Apps gallery is empty?
faqs.answer: Add a label or container and set its Visible property to IsEmpty(GalleryName.AllItems).

faqs.question: How do I stop the empty message flashing while data loads?
faqs.answer: Set a loading variable to true before loading and false afterwards, and show the empty state only when it is false.

faqs.question: What should an empty state say?
faqs.answer: Explain why nothing is shown and offer the next step: create the first item, clear the search or change the filter.

title: Optimistically update a local collection after Patch
shortDescription: Make saved changes appear immediately while SharePoint refresh catches up.
fullDescription: Patch SharePoint and the local collection together so dashboards feel responsive without waiting for a full refresh.
problemStatement: Refreshing a large SharePoint list after every save can make apps feel slow and disrupt the current screen.
whenNotToUse: High-conflict records requiring fresh server state
Complex calculated SharePoint fields
stepByStepInstructions: Store the result of Patch.
Patch the matching row in the local collection.
Refresh in the background only when needed.
Fall back to a full reload after errors.
commonMistakes: Updating the collection before confirming Patch succeeded.
Forgetting SharePoint calculated fields may need a refresh.
Building the collection with ShowColumns or AddColumns and then patching a full record into it, which fails on mismatched columns.
troubleshooting: If the collection shows stale calculated values, reload the saved item by ID after Patch.
If Patch on the collection reports incompatible types, the collection's columns differ from the list's. Load the collection straight from the list.
If the row jumps position after updating, the gallery is sorted by Modified. Sort by a column the update does not change.
If changes by other users never appear, the collection is a snapshot. Offer a refresh that reloads it.

faqs.question: What is an optimistic update in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: The app changes the local collection straight away so the screen responds instantly, then saves to the data source and undoes the local change if the save fails.

faqs.question: How do I update one row in a collection after Patch?
faqs.answer: Patch the collection using LookUp on the ID, and pass the record returned by the data source Patch.

faqs.question: Why not just Refresh the data source?
faqs.answer: Refresh reloads data from the server, which is slower and can reset gallery scroll position. Updating one row in a collection is immediate.

title: Index SharePoint columns for large list views
shortDescription: Design list views and filters that keep working past the list view threshold.
fullDescription: Index high-use columns and align views with the way Power Apps, Power Automate, and business users filter the list.
problemStatement: Lists that work during testing can become unreliable when item counts grow and filters are not supported by indexes.
whenNotToUse: Small lookup lists with only a few dozen rows
formulaOrCode:
Good index candidates:
Status, AssignedTo, ProjectCode, DueDate, IsArchived, Created

How to add an index
  List settings > Indexed columns > Create a new index > choose the column > Create
  Up to 20 indexes per list. Add them before the list reaches 5,000 items.
  Above 5,000 items SharePoint may refuse to create an index; above 20,000 it cannot be created at all.

Can be indexed
  Single line of text, Number, Currency, Date and time, Choice (single), Yes/No,
  Person or Group (single), Lookup (single), Managed metadata (single)
Cannot be indexed
  Multiple lines of text, Choice (multiple), Person (multiple), Calculated, Hyperlink, Image

Make a view work past 5,000 items
  1. The FIRST filter condition must be on an indexed column.
  2. That condition alone must return fewer than 5,000 items.
  3. Join further conditions with AND. An OR on the first condition defeats the index.
  4. Sort and group by indexed columns, or not at all.
  5. Turn totals off, and keep lookup, person and managed metadata columns to 12 or fewer in the view.

  Works : IsArchived = No  AND  Status = Open  AND  AssignedTo = [Me]
  Fails : Status = Open  OR  Priority = High          (first condition uses OR)
  Fails : Title contains 'server'                     (contains cannot use an index)

Compound index
  Indexed columns > Create a new index > pick a primary and a secondary column (for example Status + DueDate).
  Helps views that always filter on both.

The same rules apply to
  Power Automate Get items : Filter Query on an indexed column, with Top Count and pagination
  Power Apps               : delegable Filter on an indexed column
  REST and Graph           : $filter on an indexed column

Automatic indexing
  SharePoint adds indexes for you on lists under 20,000 items when views need them.
  Do not rely on it for columns used only by flows and apps.

Signs you need an index
  "The attempted operation is prohibited because it exceeds the list view threshold."
  A flow's Get items returns nothing or fails on a large list.
stepByStepInstructions: Identify common filters before launch.
Index status, owner, date, and archive fields.
Create views that filter on indexed columns first.
Avoid broad unfiltered all-items views for large lists.
commonMistakes: Waiting until after threshold problems appear.
Indexing many unused columns instead of the key filters.
Using OR in the first filter condition, which stops SharePoint using the index.
troubleshooting: If a view fails, simplify it to one indexed filter first, then add secondary conditions.
If creating an index fails, the list is already too large. Reduce it by archiving or deleting, create the index, then restore.
If an indexed view still fails, its first condition returns more than 5,000 items. Add a narrower first condition, such as a date range.
If a flow fails on the list, add an indexed column to its Filter Query and turn on pagination.

faqs.question: What is the SharePoint list view threshold?
faqs.answer: A view, query or flow cannot process more than 5,000 items in one operation unless it filters on an indexed column that brings the result under that number.

faqs.question: Which columns should I index?
faqs.answer: The columns your views, apps and flows filter on first: usually status, assigned to, a date, and an archive flag.

faqs.question: Can I add an index to a list that already has more than 5,000 items?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, up to 20,000 items, but it can fail. It is safest to add indexes while the list is small.

title: Govern SharePoint choice values before apps depend on them
shortDescription: Keep choice columns stable enough for formulas, filters, and reporting.
fullDescription: Treat high-value SharePoint choices as governed reference data so app logic and reporting do not break when labels change.
problemStatement: Uncontrolled choice edits can break formulas, flow conditions, dashboard filters, and historical reporting.
whenNotToUse: Ad hoc notes
Fields intentionally meant for open-ended text
formulaOrCode:
Governed choices example:
Draft, Submitted, Intake Review, More Info Needed, Approved, Rejected, Closed

Choice register (one row per governed column)
  List       Column          Values (exact text)                                                        Owner            Used by
  Requests   RequestStatus   Draft | Submitted | Intake Review | More Info Needed | Approved | Rejected | Closed   Process owner    Request app, Approval flow, Status report
  Requests   Priority        Low | Medium | High                                                        Process owner    Request app, Reminder flow

Rules
  1. Values are business terms, in sentence case, with no trailing spaces.
  2. "Can add values manually" (fill-in choices) is off for any column that drives logic.
  3. Nobody renames a value in list settings. A rename is a change request.
  4. Retired values are removed from the column only after no item uses them.

Renaming a value safely
  1. Add the new value alongside the old one.
  2. Update every formula, trigger condition, flow condition, view filter and report that tests the old text.
  3. Move existing items to the new value (grid edit or a flow). Renaming in settings does not update saved items.
  4. Remove the old value from the column.

Where the text is hard-coded
  Power Apps      : Status.Value = "Approved", Switch(...), dropdown defaults
  Power Automate  : trigger conditions, Condition and Switch actions, Filter Query (Status eq 'Approved')
  SharePoint      : view filters, JSON formatting, validation formulas, calculated columns
  Power BI        : measures, slicers, conditional formatting

Reduce the risk
  Keep the labels in one place in each app, for example a named formula:
    nfStatus = { Draft: "Draft", Submitted: "Submitted", Approved: "Approved", Rejected: "Rejected" };
    Filter(Requests, RequestStatus.Value = nfStatus.Approved)
  For values that change often or need an owner or active flag, use a lookup to a reference list.
stepByStepInstructions: Define choices before building automations.
Document which choices drive business logic.
Restrict who can edit list settings.
Use migration steps when labels must change.
commonMistakes: Letting makers rename status choices casually.
Using different labels for the same lifecycle across lists.
Leaving fill-in choices on for a status column, so users can invent values no flow handles.
troubleshooting: If a flow branch stops working, compare the exact current choice label to the condition value.
If old items still show the previous label after a rename, saved items keep their text. Update them in grid view or with a flow.
If a filter returns nothing after a change, check for a trailing space or different capitalisation in the choice text.
If nobody knows what depends on a value, search flows and app formulas for the exact text before changing it.

faqs.question: What happens when I rename a SharePoint choice value?
faqs.answer: New items use the new text, but existing items keep the old value, and any flow, formula or view that tests the old text stops matching.

faqs.question: Should status be a choice column or a lookup?
faqs.answer: A choice column suits a short, stable list. Use a lookup to a reference list when values change often or need an owner, an order or an active flag.

faqs.question: How do I stop users adding their own choice values?
faqs.answer: Edit the column and turn off the option that allows values to be added manually.

title: Format SharePoint status values as color-coded pills
shortDescription: Make status columns easier to scan in SharePoint lists.
fullDescription: Use column formatting JSON to show request or project statuses as compact color-coded labels.
problemStatement: Plain text status columns make busy SharePoint views harder to scan.
whenNotToUse: Lists where color meaning has not been agreed
Accessibility-sensitive views without text labels
stepByStepInstructions: Open the SharePoint list and select the Status column formatting option.
Paste the JSON status pill formatting and replace status values with the exact choices from the list.
Assign a readable color and label for each supported status value.
Test all status choices, including blank or unexpected values, before publishing the view.
commonMistakes: Using color without the status text.
Formatting labels that do not match the actual choice values.
Hard-coding light background colours that become unreadable on a dark site theme.
troubleshooting: If colors do not apply, compare the current field text to the condition labels.
If the Save button rejects the JSON, check for a missing comma or bracket. The editor underlines the position.
If a reference to another column shows nothing, write it as [$InternalName] and add that column to the view.
If the icon is missing, the iconName is not a Fluent UI icon name. Names are case sensitive.

faqs.question: How do I colour-code a status column in SharePoint?
faqs.answer: Open Format this column from the column settings. Use the built-in Choice pills option, or paste JSON in advanced mode to set colours by value.

faqs.question: Does column formatting change the data?
faqs.answer: No. Formatting only changes how the value is displayed in the view. Filters, flows and apps still see the original value.

faqs.question: Can the pill colour depend on a different column?
faqs.answer: Yes. Reference the other column as [$InternalName] in the expression and make sure it is included in the view.

title: Choose between SharePoint calculated columns and Power Apps formulas
shortDescription: Decide where calculations should live before users depend on the output.
fullDescription: Use SharePoint calculated columns for simple list-visible calculations and Power Apps formulas for interactive screen behavior.
problemStatement: Putting calculations in the wrong layer can create stale values, confusing views, or formulas that are hard to maintain.
whenNotToUse: Complex business rules
Values requiring external data
Interactive calculations before save
formulaOrCode:
Rule of thumb:
SharePoint calculated column: simple saved display logic
Power Apps formula: interactive UI logic
Power Automate: cross-record or process-driven updates

Comparison
                               Calculated column        Power Apps formula       Power Automate
  Recalculates                 when the item is saved   whenever inputs change   when the flow runs
  Uses other rows or lists     no                       yes                      yes
  Uses the current user        no                       yes                      limited (trigger user)
  Uses today's date            only as of the last save yes                      yes (scheduled)
  Visible in views and exports yes                      no                       yes (writes a real column)
  Can be indexed               no                       n/a                      yes (normal column)
  Delegable filter in apps     no                       n/a                      yes
  Editable by users            no                       n/a                      yes, unless protected

Calculated column examples (list settings > Create column > Calculated)
  Days open        =DATEDIF([Created],[ClosedDate],"d")
  Fiscal year      ="FY"&TEXT(IF(MONTH([Created])>=7,YEAR([Created])+1,YEAR([Created])),"0000")
  Request label    =[ProjectCode]&" - "&[Title]
  Cost band        =IF([EstimatedCost]>=50000,"Large",IF([EstimatedCost]>=10000,"Medium","Small"))

Power Apps examples
  Days remaining (always current)    DateDiff(Today(), ThisItem.DueDate, TimeUnit.Days)
  Overdue flag                       ThisItem.DueDate < Today() && ThisItem.Status.Value <> "Closed"
  Total of child rows                Sum(Filter(RequestLines, RequestId = ThisItem.ID), Amount)

Use Power Automate when the value must be stored and filtered
  On create or change, calculate the value and write it to a normal indexed column.
  A daily scheduled flow keeps date-based flags such as IsOverdue current.

Common traps
  [Today] and [Me] cannot be used in a calculated column formula.
  A calculated column that uses a date does not update overnight. It changes only when the item is saved.
  Calculated columns cannot reference lookup, person or multi-select choice columns.
  In Power Apps a calculated column arrives as text, so wrap numbers in Value() and dates in DateValue().
stepByStepInstructions: Decide who needs the calculated value and where.
Use SharePoint for simple persisted display values.
Use Power Apps for live screen calculations.
Use flow when the value depends on process events.
commonMistakes: Using calculated columns for business rules that need approvals.
Expecting SharePoint calculations to behave like app variables.
Using a calculated column for 'days until due', which is only correct on the day the item was last saved.
troubleshooting: If a calculated value appears stale in Power Apps, refresh and reload the saved record by ID.
If a calculated number will not add up in Power Apps, it is arriving as text. Convert it with Value().
If filtering on a calculated column gives a delegation warning, store the value in a normal column from a flow.
If the formula is rejected, check the column names in square brackets and whether your region uses semicolons instead of commas.

faqs.question: When should I use a SharePoint calculated column?
faqs.answer: Use it for simple values derived from other columns in the same item that should appear in views and exports, such as a label, a band or a fiscal year.

faqs.question: Can a calculated column use today's date?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. It is calculated when the item is saved and does not update each day. Calculate it in Power Apps or update a column with a daily flow.

faqs.question: Can I filter a Power Apps gallery on a calculated column?
faqs.answer: Only without delegation. For large lists, write the value to a normal column with a flow and filter on that.

title: Choose lookup columns vs choice columns
shortDescription: Pick the right SharePoint field type for stable app and reporting behavior.
fullDescription: Use choice columns for small governed value sets and lookup columns when values need their own metadata or lifecycle.
problemStatement: Choosing a field type casually can make future filtering, reporting, and maintenance harder.
whenNotToUse: Free text descriptions
High-volume many-to-many relationships
formulaOrCode:
Use Choice when values are few and simple.
Use Lookup when values need owners, active flags, descriptions, or reporting metadata.

Comparison
                               Choice                         Lookup
  Values are managed in        column settings (site owner)   a list (business owner can edit)
  Extra attributes per value   none                           any columns: owner, active flag, order, description
  Retire a value               remove it; old items keep text IsActive = No; old items still resolve
  Rename a value               old items keep the old text    every item shows the new text
  Cascading dropdowns          needs a separate mapping list  natural (child list points at parent)
  Power Apps filter            Status.Value = "Open"          Department.Id = 4 or Department.Value = "Finance"
  Power Automate filter query  Status eq 'Open'               DepartmentId eq 4   or   Department/Title eq 'Finance'
  View threshold               no effect                      counts towards the 12 lookup-type columns per view
  Delete behaviour             n/a                            optional: restrict or cascade delete

Choose Choice for
  Status, Priority, Yes/No/Maybe style answers. Fewer than about 15 values that rarely change.

Choose Lookup for
  Departments, cost centres, locations, categories with owners, anything another list also uses,
  anything the business wants to maintain without a site owner.

Reference list design
  Title (the value shown), IsActive (Yes/No, default Yes), SortOrder (Number), Owner (Person), Description
  Lookup column: Get information from the reference list, column Title. Index it.
  Show only active values in Power Apps:
    Sort(Filter(Departments, IsActive), SortOrder)

Patch each type from Power Apps
  Choice : { Priority: { Value: "High" } }
  Lookup : { Department: { Id: ddDepartment.Selected.ID, Value: ddDepartment.Selected.Title } }

Alternative: store the reference list ID in a Number column
  Fully delegable, no lookup column limits, but SharePoint views show a number instead of the name.
stepByStepInstructions: List the values and how often they change.
Check whether each value needs extra fields.
Use choice for simple stable lists.
Use lookup for governed reference records.
commonMistakes: Using choices for complex reference data.
Using lookups where a simple choice would be easier for makers.
Adding more than 12 lookup, person and managed metadata columns to one view, which makes it fail.
troubleshooting: If formulas are becoming complex around a choice value, consider moving that concept to a reference list.
If a view fails with a lookup column threshold message, remove some lookup, person or managed metadata columns from that view.
If a Power Automate filter on the lookup fails, filter on the Id with ColumnNameId eq 4, or on ColumnName/Title.
If retired values still appear in the dropdown, filter the reference list by its active flag in the app.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a choice and a lookup column in SharePoint?
faqs.answer: A choice column stores text from a fixed set defined on the column. A lookup column points to an item in another list, so the values can have their own attributes and be maintained as data.

faqs.question: Are lookup columns bad for performance?
faqs.answer: A few are fine. A view can include up to 12 lookup-type columns, counting person and managed metadata columns, so avoid using them for everything.

faqs.question: How do I convert a choice column to a lookup?
faqs.answer: You cannot convert it. Create the reference list and a new lookup column, copy the values across with a flow or grid edit, then remove the old column.

title: SharePoint site navigation for business apps
shortDescription: Organize list, page, and app links so users can find the working surface quickly.
fullDescription: A lightweight navigation pattern for SharePoint sites that host Power Apps, lists, dashboards, and guidance pages.
problemStatement: Business app sites become confusing when users see raw list links, old pages, and admin-only assets in the same navigation.
whenNotToUse: Single-purpose list pages with only one audience
formulaOrCode:
Suggested navigation:
Home, Submit Request, My Requests, Team Dashboard, Reports, Help

Map each link to a task and a destination
  Label            Goes to                                                     Audience
  Home             site home page                                              everyone
  Submit request   the app, or the list's new form                             everyone
  My requests      list view filtered to Created By = [Me]                     everyone
  Team dashboard   list view grouped by status, or a Power BI report page      managers
  Reports          page with the embedded report                               managers
  Help             page with how-to steps, contact and FAQs                    everyone
  Admin (optional) reference lists and settings links                          owners only

Link formats
  Canvas app               https://apps.powerapps.com/play/e/<environment-id>/a/<app-id>?tenantId=<tenant-id>
  App with a deep link     ...&screen=MyRequests            (read it with Param("screen") in the app)
  List view                https://<tenant>.sharepoint.com/sites/<site>/Lists/Requests/MyRequests.aspx
  New item form            https://<tenant>.sharepoint.com/sites/<site>/Lists/Requests/NewForm.aspx
  Filtered view by URL     .../Lists/Requests/AllItems.aspx?FilterField1=Status&FilterValue1=Open

Set it up
  Team site       : left navigation > Edit
  Communication   : top navigation > Edit
  Add link > paste the address > give it the task name > Save
  Audience targeting: Edit navigation > turn on "Enable site navigation audience targeting", then set
  a Microsoft 365 or security group on the Admin and manager links.
  Targeting hides the link only. It does not secure the destination.

Home page
  Add a Quick links web part (Button or Tiles layout) with the same three or four main tasks,
  and a Call to action web part for "Submit request".

Keep it short
  Five to seven links. Lists that only apps and flows use should not appear in navigation.
  List settings > List name, description and navigation > Display this list on the Quick Launch: No.
stepByStepInstructions: Start navigation with user tasks, not backend lists.
Group admin links away from daily user links.
Use clear labels that match the business process.
Review navigation after launch based on support questions.
commonMistakes: Putting every list in top navigation.
Using maker names instead of business task names.
Hiding a link with audience targeting and assuming the page or list behind it is now secure.
troubleshooting: If users bookmark list views directly, add clearer task links on the site home page.
If a manager cannot see a targeted link, check they are a member of the target group. Changes can take a few hours to show.
If the app link asks for permission or shows an error, the app has not been shared with that user.
If a list reappears in navigation, turn off Quick Launch display in the list's settings.

faqs.question: How do I add a Power App to SharePoint navigation?
faqs.answer: Copy the app's web link from its Details page in Power Apps, then edit the site navigation and add a link with that address.

faqs.question: Can I show a navigation link only to certain people?
faqs.answer: Yes. Turn on audience targeting for the site navigation and assign a group to the link. It hides the link but does not change permissions.

faqs.question: How many navigation links should a business app site have?
faqs.answer: Five to seven task-based links are enough. Put less common destinations on a Help or Admin page.

title: SharePoint list release checklist
shortDescription: Review schema, views, permissions, and app dependencies before launch.
fullDescription: A practical checklist for releasing SharePoint-backed apps without missing common governance and support details.
problemStatement: Small SharePoint solutions often launch before permissions, indexes, views, and ownership are ready.
whenNotToUse: Personal prototype lists that are not yet shared
formulaOrCode:
Release checks:
Schema reviewed, internal names documented, permissions verified, indexes added, views tested, flows owned by service account or team owner, support owner assigned

Release checklist in detail

Schema
  [ ] Internal names recorded for every column apps and flows use
  [ ] Required columns limited to what every entry route can supply
  [ ] Choice values final and fill-in turned off on logic columns
  [ ] Defaults set (status = Draft, flags = No)
  [ ] Validation formulas tested with good and bad values

Scale
  [ ] Indexes on status, owner, date and archive flag
  [ ] Each view's first filter is on an indexed column
  [ ] Lookup-type columns per view: 12 or fewer
  [ ] Archive or retention approach agreed

Permissions
  [ ] Tested as a requester, an approver and a read-only user, not as an owner
  [ ] Item-level permissions set if people should see only their own items
  [ ] Flow service account has Contribute or Edit
  [ ] Sharing settings reviewed (who may share, external access)

Views
  [ ] Default view is useful and filtered, not All Items
  [ ] My items, Awaiting action and Closed views exist
  [ ] Grid edit turned off if a status must change only through the app
      (List settings > Advanced settings > Quick property editing: No)

Automation
  [ ] Flows are in a solution, owned by a service account or with at least two owners
  [ ] Trigger conditions in place; no flow retriggers itself
  [ ] Failure notifications go to a monitored mailbox
  [ ] Connection references use the service account

Operations
  [ ] Versioning on, with a limit (50 is typical)
  [ ] Support owner and backup named on the site's Help page
  [ ] Test items removed, ID gaps accepted
  [ ] Short user guide linked from navigation

Copy the list to another site
  List > Export > Export to CSV for data only.
  New list > From existing list for structure, views and formatting (no data).
  PnP PowerShell:  Get-PnPSiteTemplate -Out requests.xml -ListsToExtract "Requests" -Handlers Lists
                   Invoke-PnPSiteTemplate -Path requests.xml      (run against the target site)
stepByStepInstructions: Review field names and required settings.
Verify permissions with a non-owner test user.
Check indexed filters and default views.
Confirm flow ownership and failure notifications.
Document support contacts.
commonMistakes: Testing only as site owner.
Forgetting flow ownership transfer.
Launching with all-items views only.
troubleshooting: If users report missing data, test the exact SharePoint group membership and view filters they have.
If a user cannot add items after release, check their group's permission level and any required column the form does not show.
If a flow stops when its maker leaves, add co-owners or move it to a service account and update its connections.
If a view breaks months later, the list passed 5,000 items and the view's first filter is not on an indexed column.

faqs.question: What should I check before releasing a SharePoint list to users?
faqs.answer: Column names and required fields, indexes, permissions tested as real users, useful default views, flow ownership and failure alerts, versioning, and a named support owner.

faqs.question: How do I copy a SharePoint list to another site?
faqs.answer: Use New list > From existing list for structure, or a PnP site template for lists with lookups, views and formatting.

faqs.question: Who should own the flows behind a list?
faqs.answer: A service account, or at least two named owners. A flow owned by one person stops when their account is disabled.

title: Run a flow only when status changes
shortDescription: Use trigger conditions so flows do not run on every SharePoint edit.
fullDescription: Reduce noisy flow runs by checking status and previous values before starting approval or notification logic.
problemStatement: Flows that trigger on every item update can send duplicate emails, start repeated approvals, or waste run capacity.
whenNotToUse: Flows that intentionally audit every item change
formulaOrCode:
Trigger: When an item is created or modified (SharePoint)
Trigger > Settings > Trigger conditions

Run only when the status is a specific value
@equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Approved')

Run only when the status differs from the last value the flow handled
1. Add a PreviousStatus single line of text column to the list.
2. Trigger condition:
   @not(equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], coalesce(triggerBody()?['PreviousStatus'], '')))
3. Run the flow's actions.
4. As the last action, Update item and set PreviousStatus to triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'].
   The update retriggers the flow check, but the two values now match, so no new run starts.

Both together: status has just changed to Approved
@and(
  equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Approved'),
  not(equals(coalesce(triggerBody()?['PreviousStatus'], ''), 'Approved'))
)

Other condition shapes
  Any of several values
    @or(equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Approved'), equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Rejected'))
  Text column instead of a choice column
    @equals(triggerBody()?['StatusText'], 'Approved')
  Yes/No column
    @equals(triggerBody()?['IsUrgent'], true)
  Not the flow's own account (extra loop protection)
    @not(equals(triggerBody()?['Editor']?['Email'], 'svc-flow@contoso.com'))

  Each condition is a separate line in the settings. All lines must be true for the flow to run.

Without an extra column: compare versions inside the flow
  Trigger: When an item or a file is modified
  Action : Get changes for an item or a file (properties only)
             Id    : @{triggerBody()?['ID']}
             Since : @{triggerOutputs()?['body/{TriggerWindowStartToken}']}
  Condition: body('Get_changes_for_an_item_or_a_file_(properties_only)')?['ColumnHasChanged']?['Status'] is equal to true
  Needs versioning turned on. The flow still starts on every edit, so each edit uses a run.

Build the expression faster
  Add a Filter array action, set the condition with the designer, switch to advanced mode,
  copy the expression into the trigger condition, replace item() with triggerBody(), then delete the action.
stepByStepInstructions: Add a PreviousStatus tracking column when SharePoint version comparison is not enough.
Configure the trigger condition so the flow only runs when Status differs from PreviousStatus.
Run the approval, notification, or update logic only after the trigger condition passes.
Update PreviousStatus at the end of the flow to prevent duplicate runs.
commonMistakes: Putting the condition after the trigger, which still consumes a run.
Using the display label incorrectly for choice fields.
Leaving the leading @ off the trigger condition, or wrapping it in quotes.
troubleshooting: If the flow never starts, inspect the trigger payload and confirm the choice value path.
If the flow starts on every edit, the condition is on an action inside the flow. Move it to the trigger's settings.
If the flow never starts after adding PreviousStatus, the column is empty on old items. The coalesce in the condition handles that.
If the flow runs twice for one change, the final Update item changed the status as well as PreviousStatus. Update only PreviousStatus.

faqs.question: How do I trigger a flow only when a SharePoint column changes?
faqs.answer: Store the last handled value in a second column and add a trigger condition that runs the flow only when the two differ. Or use Get changes for an item or a file inside the flow.

faqs.question: Where do I add a trigger condition in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Open the trigger's settings and add the expression under Trigger conditions. It must start with @.

faqs.question: Does a trigger condition save flow runs?
faqs.answer: Yes. When the condition is false the flow does not start, so nothing appears in run history and no run is counted.

title: Start an approval from a Power Apps button
shortDescription: Let users intentionally launch an approval flow from inside the app.
fullDescription: Call a Power Automate flow from Power Apps after validating the record and passing the SharePoint item ID.
problemStatement: Approval flows need a reliable item ID and should start only after users intentionally submit a valid request.
whenNotToUse: Simple auto-notifications
Processes that should start from every list item creation
stepByStepInstructions: Patch and validate the SharePoint item first.
Store the saved item result.
Call the flow with the saved item ID.
Have the flow get the item by ID before starting approval.
commonMistakes: Calling the flow before the item save completes.
Passing title instead of item ID.
Starting approval without locking the request status.
troubleshooting: If the flow cannot find the item, log the ID passed from Power Apps and compare it to SharePoint.
If the app shows a timeout while the approval is pending, the flow responds after the approval. Move the Respond action before it.
If users get a connection or permission prompt, the flow runs with their connections. They need access to the list and to Approvals, or set run-only users to use a fixed connection.
If the flow is missing from the app after editing its inputs, remove and re-add it in the Power Automate pane.

faqs.question: How do I start an approval from a Power Apps button?
faqs.answer: Save the item, then call a flow with the item's ID. In the flow, get the item, respond to the app, and then run Start and wait for an approval.

faqs.question: Why does my app time out waiting for the approval flow?
faqs.answer: The app only waits about two minutes. Respond to the app before the approval action, and update the item's status when the approver decides.

faqs.question: Should the app call the flow or should SharePoint trigger it?
faqs.answer: Either works. A SharePoint trigger with a status condition is simpler to secure and also runs when the item is changed outside the app.

title: Add a button-style link to Power Automate emails
shortDescription: Send clean action emails with a clear link back to the SharePoint item or app.
fullDescription: Use simple HTML in email bodies to create a visually clear call-to-action button for reviewers and stakeholders.
problemStatement: Plain URLs in workflow emails are easy to miss and make action requests feel less polished.
whenNotToUse: Environments where email clients strip HTML heavily
formulaOrCode:
Open request Works in Outlook desktop too (table-based, sometimes called a bulletproof button)
Open request

If the button does not work, copy this link: @{outputs('Item_link')}

Outlook desktop ignores padding on a bare link, which is why the plain version can look like underlined text there. The table cell carries the colour and shape. Where the link comes from (Compose "Item link") The SharePoint item @{triggerBody()?['{Link}']} Display form by ID https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Requests/Lists/Requests/DispForm.aspx?ID=@{triggerBody()?['ID']} A canvas app screen https://apps.powerapps.com/play/e//a/?tenantId=&requestId=@{triggerBody()?['ID']} A file in a library @{triggerBody()?['{Link}']} Two buttons side by side
Open request All requests
In the Send an email (V2) action Switch the body to code view (the button) before pasting, or the editor escapes the tags. Use inline styles only. Email clients remove style blocks and classes.
stepByStepInstructions: Build or retrieve the item link.
Add a short instruction sentence.
Place the styled anchor after the summary.
Test the email in Outlook desktop and web.
commonMistakes: Sending a button with no plain text context.
Using dark text on dark button backgrounds.
Pasting the HTML into the rich text editor instead of code view, so the tags show as text.
troubleshooting: If the button does not render, confirm the email body is HTML and not plain text.
If Outlook shows a plain underlined link, use the table-based version. Outlook desktop ignores padding and border-radius on links.
If the tags appear as text in the email, the HTML was pasted in rich text mode. Switch the body to code view and paste again.
If the link opens a not found page, URL-encode values in the query string with encodeUriComponent().

faqs.question: How do I add a button to a Power Automate email?
faqs.answer: Use an HTML link styled as a button inside a table cell, and paste it into the email body in code view.

faqs.question: Why does my email button look wrong in Outlook?
faqs.answer: Outlook desktop uses Word to render HTML and ignores padding on links. Put the colour on a table cell around the link.

faqs.question: Can the button run an action, such as approve?
faqs.answer: A link can only open an address. For decisions inside the email, use an approval action or Send email with options.

title: Route approval to a user's manager
shortDescription: Use Microsoft 365 profile data to send approval requests to the requester's manager.
fullDescription: Look up the requester's manager in Power Automate and use that person as the approval assignee.
problemStatement: Manual approver selection creates routing mistakes when approval should follow the organizational reporting line.
whenNotToUse: Matrix organizations where manager is not the correct approver
Processes with delegated approval rules
stepByStepInstructions: Store requester email in SharePoint.
Use Get manager V2 with that email.
Handle cases where no manager is returned.
Start the approval assigned to the manager's mail.
commonMistakes: Assuming every user has a manager in the directory.
Using display name instead of mail for approval assignment.
Letting the flow fail when Get manager returns 404, instead of configuring run after and a fallback.
troubleshooting: If manager lookup fails, test the same user in the Office 365 Users connector and add a fallback approver.
If the action fails with 'No manager found for the specified user', the directory has no manager for that person. Use the run-after fallback.
If the approval goes to nobody, the manager has no mailbox. Fall back from mail to userPrincipalName.
If guest users fail the lookup, they have no manager in your directory. Route them to the backup approver.

faqs.question: How do I get a user's manager in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use the Office 365 Users action Get manager (V2) with the user's email or UPN. It returns the manager's mail, display name and other profile fields.

faqs.question: What happens if the user has no manager?
faqs.answer: The action fails with a 404 error. Set the next action to run after failure as well and use a backup approver.

faqs.question: Where does the manager information come from?
faqs.answer: From the Manager attribute in Microsoft Entra ID. If it is wrong in the flow, it needs correcting in the directory or HR system.

title: Send reminders before a SharePoint due date
shortDescription: Notify owners about upcoming due dates without sending reminders for closed items.
fullDescription: Use a scheduled flow with an OData filter to find open items due soon and send targeted reminders.
problemStatement: Manual follow-up is unreliable when task owners need reminders before due dates.
whenNotToUse: High-volume reminder systems needing notification preferences and throttling
formulaOrCode:
Status ne 'Closed' and DueDate le '@{formatDateTime(addDays(utcNow(), 3), 'yyyy-MM-dd')}'

Flow detail

Trigger: Recurrence
  Frequency: Day, Interval: 1, At these hours: 8, Time zone: your local zone

Get items (SharePoint)
  Filter Query (items due within the next 3 days, not yet reminded):
    Status ne 'Closed' and DueDate ge '@{formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'yyyy-MM-dd')}' and DueDate le '@{formatDateTime(addDays(utcNow(), 3), 'yyyy-MM-dd')}' and ReminderSentOn eq null
  Top Count: 500        Settings > Pagination: On

  Exactly 3 days before, once only:
    DueDate ge '@{formatDateTime(addDays(utcNow(), 3), 'yyyy-MM-dd')}' and DueDate lt '@{formatDateTime(addDays(utcNow(), 4), 'yyyy-MM-dd')}'

  Overdue:
    Status ne 'Closed' and DueDate lt '@{formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'yyyy-MM-dd')}'

Apply to each: value
  Send an email (V2)
    To      : @{items('Apply_to_each')?['AssignedTo']?['Email']}
    Subject : Due @{formatDateTime(items('Apply_to_each')?['DueDate'], 'dd MMM')}: @{items('Apply_to_each')?['Title']}
    Body    : link @{items('Apply_to_each')?['{Link}']}
  Update item
    ReminderSentOn : @{utcNow()}

One email per person instead of one per item
  Select    : From value, Map the AssignedTo email
  Compose   : union(body('Select'), body('Select'))               distinct owners
  Apply to each owner:
    Filter array : value where AssignedTo Email equals the current owner
    Create HTML table from the filtered items (Title, DueDate, link)
    Send one email with the table

Columns needed
  DueDate (Date), Status (Choice), AssignedTo (Person), ReminderSentOn (Date and time, empty by default).
  Index DueDate and Status on large lists.
stepByStepInstructions: Create a scheduled flow.
Get open items due within the reminder window.
Send one concise email per owner or item.
Mark reminder sent only if duplicate prevention is needed.
commonMistakes: Sending reminders for closed items.
Using local date formats inside OData filters.
Sending the same reminder every day because nothing records that it was sent.
troubleshooting: If no items return, inspect the generated filter string and internal date column name.
If the filter fails with a message about the column, use the internal name, and for choice columns compare the text directly: Status ne 'Closed'.
If reminders arrive a day early or late, utcNow() is UTC. Use convertFromUtc(utcNow(), 'your time zone', 'yyyy-MM-dd') in the filter.
If only 100 items are checked, set Top Count and turn on pagination.

faqs.question: How do I send a reminder email before a due date in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Run a scheduled flow each day, use Get items with a filter on the due date, and send an email for each item returned.

faqs.question: How do I stop the reminder being sent every day?
faqs.answer: Filter for the exact day, or write the date sent to a column and exclude items where it is filled.

faqs.question: How do I write a date filter in Get items?
faqs.answer: Compare the column to a date in yyyy-MM-dd format inside single quotes, built with formatDateTime and addDays.

title: Create a Planner task from a SharePoint item
shortDescription: Turn approved requests or action items into Planner tasks.
fullDescription: Use a flow to create Planner tasks from SharePoint rows while preserving the source item link.
problemStatement: Teams often approve or capture work in SharePoint but need execution tracked in Planner.
whenNotToUse: Complex project schedules better handled in Project or Jira
stepByStepInstructions: Trigger from approved SharePoint items.
Create a Planner task with title, due date, and owner.
Add the SharePoint item link to task notes.
Write the Planner task ID back to SharePoint.
commonMistakes: Creating duplicate Planner tasks on every edit.
Not storing the Planner task ID for traceability.
Assigning the task to someone who is not a member of the plan's Microsoft 365 group, which makes the action fail.
troubleshooting: If duplicates appear, check for an existing PlannerTaskId before creating a new task.
If Create a task fails with a 403 error, the flow's connection account is not a member of the group that owns the plan.
If the description is missing, it is set by Update task details, not by Create a task.
If the completion flow finds no item, index PlannerTaskId and check the stored ID matches exactly.

faqs.question: How do I create a Planner task from a SharePoint list item?
faqs.answer: Use a flow triggered by the item, add the Planner action Create a task with the group, plan, bucket, title and assignee, then save the task ID back to the item.

faqs.question: How do I stop duplicate Planner tasks?
faqs.answer: Store the task ID on the item and add a trigger condition that runs the flow only when that column is empty.

faqs.question: Can completing the Planner task update SharePoint?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use a second flow with the trigger When a task is completed and find the item by the stored task ID.

title: Document a Power Automate flow inventory
shortDescription: Capture the essential maintenance details for each production flow.
fullDescription: Use a simple inventory structure to track flow purpose, owner, trigger, dependencies, and support notes.
problemStatement: Production flows become risky when nobody knows what they do, who owns them, or what breaks if they stop.
whenNotToUse: Personal experiments that will be deleted soon
formulaOrCode:
Inventory fields:
FlowName, BusinessPurpose, Owner, TriggerType, ConnectedLists, Criticality, FailureNotification, LastReviewedDate, SupportNotes

Inventory list columns
  Title (FlowName)       Single line
  FlowId                 Single line, unique, indexed        the GUID from the flow's address
  Environment            Choice                              Dev | Test | Prod
  SolutionName           Single line
  BusinessPurpose        Multiple lines                      what breaks for the business if it stops
  BusinessOwner          Person
  TechnicalOwner         Person
  BackupOwner            Person
  TriggerType            Choice                              Automated | Scheduled | Instant | Power Apps
  TriggerDetail          Single line                         for example "Requests list, item modified, Status = Submitted"
  ConnectedLists         Multiple lines                      site and list addresses
  Connectors             Choice (multi)                      SharePoint | Outlook | Approvals | Teams | Dataverse | HTTP | Other
  UsesPremium            Yes/No
  ConnectionAccount      Single line                         the service account, never a password
  Criticality            Choice                              High | Medium | Low
  FailureNotification    Single line                         mailbox or channel that receives failures
  State                  Choice                              On | Off | Suspended | Retired
  LastReviewedDate       Date
  NextReviewDate         Date
  SupportNotes           Multiple lines                      known issues, how to rerun, who to tell
  FlowLink               Hyperlink

Views
  Critical flows       : Criticality = High, sort by Title
  Review due           : NextReviewDate <= [Today]+30
  No backup owner      : BackupOwner is empty
  By list              : group by TriggerDetail

Fill it automatically (scheduled flow, weekly)
  Power Automate Management > List flows as admin (environment) 
  Apply to each flow:
    Get items where FlowId eq '@{items('Apply_to_each')?['name']}'
    If none  -> Create item with FlowName @{items('Apply_to_each')?['properties']?['displayName']}, State, created time
    If found -> Update item State and last modified time
  The connector supplies names, state, creator and dates. Purpose, owners and criticality are filled by people.

With PowerShell
  Get-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName <environment-id> | Select DisplayName, FlowName, Enabled, CreatedBy, LastModifiedTime

For a whole tenant, the Center of Excellence Starter Kit builds this inventory in Dataverse.
stepByStepInstructions: Create a flow inventory list.
Document each production flow's trigger and purpose.
Capture ownership and support routing.
Review the inventory quarterly.
commonMistakes: Documenting only the technical trigger.
Skipping ownership and failure notification details.
Recording passwords or secrets in the inventory instead of the name of the connection account.
troubleshooting: If support cannot triage failures, add source list links and business process notes to the inventory.
If List flows as admin returns nothing, the connection needs a Power Platform administrator or environment admin role.
If the inventory goes stale, add the Review due view to the owners' monthly routine and send reminders from NextReviewDate.
If a flow is missing from the list, it may be in another environment. Run the collection flow once per environment.

faqs.question: What should a Power Automate flow inventory include?
faqs.answer: For each flow: its purpose, business and technical owners, a backup, the trigger, the lists and connectors it uses, its criticality, where failures are sent and when it was last reviewed.

faqs.question: How do I list all flows in an environment?
faqs.answer: Use the Power Automate Management connector's List flows as admin action, the Get-AdminFlow PowerShell cmdlet, or the Center of Excellence Starter Kit.

faqs.question: Why keep an inventory if the admin center lists flows?
faqs.answer: The admin center shows technical facts. It does not record why a flow exists, who to call when it fails or how critical it is.

title: Avoid infinite update loops in SharePoint flows
shortDescription: Stop a flow from retriggering itself after it updates the same item.
fullDescription: Use trigger conditions, status fields, or flow-owned flags to prevent SharePoint update loops.
problemStatement: A flow that updates the item that triggered it can run repeatedly unless the trigger is constrained.
whenNotToUse: Flows that do not update their trigger item
formulaOrCode:
Loop prevention options:
- Trigger only when Status equals Submitted
- Set ProcessedByFlow to true
- Exit when Modified By is the flow owner account

Why it loops
  A flow triggered by "When an item is created or modified" that updates the same item
  creates a new modification, which starts the flow again.

Option 1: trigger condition on a state the flow then changes (best)
  Trigger > Settings > Trigger conditions:
    @equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Submitted')
  First action: Update item, Status = In review.
  The update fires the trigger check again, the condition is false, and no run starts.

Option 2: a processed flag
  Trigger condition:
    @not(equals(triggerBody()?['ProcessedByFlow'], true))
  Last action: Update item, ProcessedByFlow = Yes.
  Reset the flag (in the app, or with another rule) when the item should be processed again.

Option 3: ignore edits made by the flow's own account
  Trigger condition:
    @not(equals(triggerBody()?['Editor']?['Email'], 'svc-flow@contoso.com'))
  Only works when the flow uses a dedicated service account. If it runs under a person's
  connection, that person's own edits would be ignored too.

Option 4: update without triggering
  Send an HTTP request to SharePoint
    Method : POST
    Uri    : _api/web/lists/getbytitle('Requests')/items(@{triggerBody()?['ID']})/validateUpdateListItem
    Body   :
    {
      "formValues": [ { "FieldName": "ProcessingNote", "FieldValue": "Checked by flow" } ],
      "bNewDocumentUpdate": true
    }
  With bNewDocumentUpdate set to true the change is saved as a system update: no new version
  and the Modified date stays the same. Flows still receive the change event in some cases,
