problemStatement: Without a policy, any maker can build a flow that copies SharePoint or Dataverse records to a personal Dropbox or a social network, and nobody is alerted.
whenToUse: Any tenant where users can make apps and flows
Before premium connectors are widely licensed
When a new environment is created for a team
whenNotToUse: As the only control over sensitive data. DLP limits connector combinations, not what a permitted connector can read.
Blocking connectors that existing business flows rely on, without a migration plan
formulaOrCode:
Tenant baseline policy (all environments except those excluded)

Business
  SharePoint, OneDrive for Business, Office 365 Outlook,
  Office 365 Users, Microsoft Teams, Approvals, Excel Online (Business),
  Planner, Microsoft Forms, Notifications, Dataverse

Non-business (default group for new connectors)
  Everything not listed elsewhere, such as MSN Weather and RSS

Blocked
  Consumer storage and social connectors (Dropbox, Google Drive,
  X, Facebook), HTTP, HTTP with Microsoft Entra ID, custom connectors
  not on the approved list

Team environment policy (scoped to <Team> Dev, Test and Prod)
  Business adds : SQL Server, HTTP, the team's approved custom connectors
  Endpoint rules: HTTP allowed only to https://api.contoso.com/*

Roll-out
  [ ] List connectors in use with the admin PowerShell module
  [ ] Tell owners of affected apps and flows the date and the reason
  [ ] Apply to one pilot environment first
  [ ] Set the default group for new connectors to Non-business or Blocked
  [ ] Review the policy every quarter
stepByStepInstructions: In the Power Platform admin center, open Policies, Data policies, and choose New policy.
Move the Microsoft 365 connectors your organization uses into Business.
Move connectors you never want used into Blocked. Some Microsoft connectors cannot be blocked.
Set the default group for new connectors so future connectors do not land in Business.
Scope the policy to all environments, then create a second policy for environments that need more.
Before saving, check which existing apps and flows would be affected and contact their owners.
commonMistakes: Putting every connector in Business, which permits every combination.
Leaving the default group as Business, so new connectors are trusted automatically.
Applying several overlapping policies without knowing that the most restrictive combination wins.
Forgetting custom connectors and HTTP, which can reach any endpoint.
troubleshooting: If a flow is suspended after the change, its connectors are now in different groups or blocked. Open the flow to see which.
If a maker sees a policy error when saving an app, compare the app's connectors with the policy groups for that environment.
If a connector cannot be moved to Blocked, it is one of the non-blockable Microsoft connectors. Classify it as Business or Non-business instead.
If two policies seem to conflict, remember both apply. A connector blocked in either is blocked.
seoTitle: Power Platform DLP policy: business, non-business, blocked
seoDescription: How to design a Power Platform DLP policy with business, non-business and blocked connector groups, plus a roll-out checklist that avoids breaking flows.

faqs.question: What happens when business and non-business connectors are mixed?
faqs.answer: The app cannot be saved or run, and a flow is suspended. Connectors in the same group can be combined freely.

faqs.question: What happens when more than one DLP policy applies?
faqs.answer: All of them apply. The result is the most restrictive combination, so a connector blocked by any policy is blocked.

faqs.question: Will a new DLP policy break existing flows?
faqs.answer: It can. Flows that violate the policy are suspended. Check usage and warn owners before turning a policy on.

title: Export an inventory of apps and flows with PowerShell
shortDescription: List every canvas app and cloud flow in the tenant, with owner and environment, into CSV files.
fullDescription: A short script using the Power Apps administration module that produces two CSV files: one for apps and one for flows. It is a quick way to see what exists before setting policy, and a lighter option than installing the full CoE Starter Kit.
problemStatement: Admins are asked how many apps exist, who owns them and which environments they live in, and the admin center only answers one environment at a time.
whenToUse: Before writing a DLP policy or environment strategy
A quick audit without installing extra solutions
Scheduled exports for a simple report
whenNotToUse: Ongoing governance at scale, where the CoE Starter Kit or the admin center's inventory views are a better fit
When you are not a Power Platform or Dynamics 365 administrator
formulaOrCode:
# Run once
Install-Module -Name Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser

# Sign in as a Power Platform administrator
Add-PowerAppsAccount

# Environments, for readable names
$envs = @{}
Get-AdminPowerAppEnvironment | ForEach-Object { $envs[$_.EnvironmentName] = $_.DisplayName }

# Canvas apps
Get-AdminPowerApp |
    Select-Object DisplayName,
        AppName,
        @{ n = 'Environment'; e = { $envs[$_.EnvironmentName] } },
        @{ n = 'Owner';       e = { $_.Owner.displayName } },
        @{ n = 'OwnerEmail';  e = { $_.Owner.email } },
        CreatedTime,
        LastModifiedTime |
    Export-Csv -Path .\apps.csv -NoTypeInformation

# Cloud flows
Get-AdminFlow |
    Select-Object DisplayName,
        FlowName,
        Enabled,
        @{ n = 'Environment'; e = { $envs[$_.EnvironmentName] } },
        @{ n = 'CreatorId';   e = { $_.CreatedBy.userId } },
        CreatedTime,
        LastModifiedTime |
    Export-Csv -Path .\flows.csv -NoTypeInformation
stepByStepInstructions: Open PowerShell and install the administration module.
Run Add-PowerAppsAccount and sign in with an admin account.
Run the script. Large tenants can take several minutes.
Open apps.csv and flows.csv in Excel and add a pivot by environment and by owner.
Match the flow CreatorId values to people with Microsoft Graph or the Entra admin center if you need names.
Save the script and re-run it on a schedule if you want a trend.
commonMistakes: Running the maker cmdlets such as Get-PowerApp, which only return what the signed-in user can see.
Running without an admin role and concluding the tenant is nearly empty.
Treating last modified as last used. The script does not report usage.
Sharing the CSV widely. It contains names and email addresses.
troubleshooting: If the cmdlets are not recognized, the module did not install. Run Install-Module again and restart PowerShell.
If sign-in fails in PowerShell 7, try Windows PowerShell 5.1, which the module supports most reliably.
If the owner column is empty, the app's owner account has been deleted. Those are your orphaned apps.
If the export stops part-way in a very large tenant, loop over environments and pass -EnvironmentName to each call.
seoTitle: PowerShell: export all Power Apps and flows to CSV
seoDescription: Use Get-AdminPowerApp and Get-AdminFlow to export a tenant-wide inventory of canvas apps and cloud flows with owner and environment to CSV.
secondaryKeywords: list all Power Apps in tenant

faqs.question: Which role do I need to run this?
faqs.answer: Power Platform administrator or Dynamics 365 administrator. Without it, the admin cmdlets return little or nothing.

faqs.question: Does this show how often an app is used?
faqs.answer: No. It lists what exists and who owns it. Usage comes from the admin center analytics or the CoE Starter Kit.

faqs.question: Does it include model-driven apps?
faqs.answer: No. Get-AdminPowerApp returns canvas apps. Model-driven apps are listed per environment in Dataverse.

title: Find and reassign orphaned apps and flows
shortDescription: Identify apps and flows whose owner has left, then give them a new owner with PowerShell.
fullDescription: When a maker leaves, their apps keep running but nobody can edit them, and their flows eventually fail when connections expire. This pattern finds those items and reassigns them before that happens.
problemStatement: A business process stops weeks after someone leaves, because the flow that ran it was owned by their account and its connections have expired.
whenToUse: As part of the leaver process
A periodic clean-up of the default environment
Before deleting user accounts in bulk
whenNotToUse: Solution-aware flows in managed environments, which should be owned by a service account from the start
Reassigning items without telling the new owner what they do
formulaOrCode:
Add-PowerAppsAccount

# 1. Canvas apps with no resolvable owner
$orphanApps = Get-AdminPowerApp | Where-Object { -not $_.Owner.displayName }
$orphanApps | Select-Object DisplayName, AppName, EnvironmentName

# 2. Everything owned by one leaver (use their Entra object ID)
$leaverId = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000'
$apps  = Get-AdminPowerApp -Owner $leaverId
$flows = Get-AdminFlow -CreatedBy $leaverId

# 3. Give each app a new owner
$newOwnerId = '11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111'
foreach ($app in $apps) {
    Set-AdminPowerAppOwner -AppName $app.AppName -EnvironmentName $app.EnvironmentName -AppOwner $newOwnerId
}

# 4. Add the new person as a co-owner of each flow
foreach ($flow in $flows) {
    Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole -EnvironmentName $flow.EnvironmentName -FlowName $flow.FlowName -RoleName CanEdit -PrincipalType User -PrincipalObjectId $newOwnerId
}
stepByStepInstructions: Get the leaver's object ID from the Entra admin center before the account is deleted.
Run steps 1 and 2 to list what they own, and export the list for the manager.
Agree a new owner for each item.
Run step 3 to change app ownership and step 4 to add a flow co-owner.
Ask the new owner to open each flow and replace the connections with their own or a service account's.
Delete items nobody claims after a notice period.
commonMistakes: Waiting until the account is deleted, which makes ownership harder to trace.
Adding a flow co-owner and stopping there. The flow still runs on the leaver's connections until someone replaces them.
Reassigning everything to one admin, who then owns hundreds of items they do not understand.
Forgetting flows that the leaver co-owned but did not create.
troubleshooting: If Set-AdminPowerAppOwner fails, check that the new owner has a licence and access to the environment.
If a flow still fails after reassignment, open it and fix connections. Ownership and connections are separate.
If a solution-aware flow does not change owner, change the owner in the flow's details page in the maker portal or through Dataverse instead.
If Get-AdminFlow -CreatedBy returns nothing, confirm you passed the object ID and not the email address.
seoTitle: Find orphaned Power Apps and flows and change the owner
seoDescription: PowerShell to find orphaned canvas apps and flows, change an app owner with Set-AdminPowerAppOwner, and add a flow co-owner with Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole.

faqs.question: What happens to a flow when its owner leaves?
faqs.answer: It keeps running until its connections expire or the account is deleted, and then it fails. Until it is reassigned, nobody else can edit it.

faqs.question: Can I change the owner of a canvas app?
faqs.answer: Yes. An administrator can run Set-AdminPowerAppOwner, or set a new owner from the admin center.

faqs.question: Does adding a co-owner fix the flow's connections?
faqs.answer: No. The new owner must open the flow and switch each action to a valid connection.

title: Secure Power Pages data with table permissions and web roles
shortDescription: Give site visitors access to exactly the Dataverse rows they should see, and no more.
fullDescription: On a Power Pages site, a user sees a row only when a table permission linked to one of their web roles allows it. This pattern explains the access types, shows a typical setup for a request portal, and lists the checks to run before launch.
problemStatement: Lists and forms show "You don't have permission to view these records", or worse, a permission set to global access exposes every row to every visitor.
whenToUse: Any list, form or Liquid query that reads Dataverse data on a site
Portals where users should see only their own or their company's rows
whenNotToUse: Static content pages with no Dataverse data
As a replacement for Dataverse security roles, which still govern internal users
formulaOrCode:
Request portal: table permissions

Table        Access type  Relationship           Privileges            Web role
-----------  -----------  ---------------------  --------------------  -------------------
Request      Contact      Request -> Contact     Read, Create, Write   Authenticated Users
Request      Account      Request -> Account     Read                  Account Managers
Comment      Parent       Request -> Comment     Read, Create, Append  (inherits from Request)
Category     Global       -                      Read                  Authenticated Users,
                                                                        Anonymous Users
Request      Global       -                      Read, Write, Delete   Portal Staff

Access types
  Global  : every row of the table
  Contact : rows linked to the signed-in contact
  Account : rows linked to the contact's parent account
  Self    : the signed-in user's own contact row
  Parent  : rows related to a row the user can already access

Pre-launch checks
  [ ] No Global permission with Write or Delete on the Anonymous Users role
  [ ] Every list and form has "Enable table permissions" on
  [ ] Lookup targets used on forms have at least Read
  [ ] Tested as anonymous, as a normal user, and as a user from another account
stepByStepInstructions: In the Power Pages design studio, open Security, Table permissions, and choose New permission.
Pick the table and the narrowest access type that works. For Contact and Account access, choose the relationship that links the row to the user.
Tick only the privileges needed and assign the web role.
Add child permissions with Parent access for related tables such as comments or attachments.
Add Read on tables used by lookups and dropdowns on your forms.
Sign in as test users in different roles and confirm each sees only what they should.
commonMistakes: Using Global access because it makes the error go away.
Turning off table permissions on a list or form to fix an access error.
Forgetting Append and Append To when a form sets a lookup or adds a child row.
Assigning permissions to a custom role but forgetting that signed-in users only get Authenticated Users by default.
troubleshooting: If a list shows a permission error, check that a permission exists for that table, has Read, and is linked to a web role the user holds.
If a form saves but a lookup stays empty, add Append on the child table and Append To on the lookup's target table.
If changes do not show, clear the site cache from the design studio's preview options or wait for it to refresh.
If a user sees too much, look for a Global permission on a role they hold. Permissions add together.
seoTitle: Power Pages table permissions and web roles explained
seoDescription: How Power Pages table permissions and web roles work: global, contact, account, self and parent access, a sample request portal setup, and launch checks.
secondaryKeywords: you don't have permission to view these records

faqs.question: Why does my list say I don't have permission to view these records?
faqs.answer: No table permission grants Read on that table to a web role the current user has. Add one with the right access type.

faqs.question: What is the difference between contact and account access?
faqs.answer: Contact access returns rows linked to the signed-in contact. Account access returns rows linked to that contact's parent account, so colleagues see each other's rows.

faqs.question: Do anonymous visitors need table permissions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Give the Anonymous Users role a Read permission only on the tables that are safe to show publicly.

title: Query Dataverse with FetchXML in Power Pages Liquid
shortDescription: Render a custom list of Dataverse rows on a page with the Liquid fetchxml tag.
fullDescription: When the built-in list component is not flexible enough, Liquid can run a FetchXML query and loop over the results to produce any HTML. This pattern shows a filtered, sorted query with a link to a detail page and an empty state.
problemStatement: The list component cannot produce cards, grouped layouts or custom markup, and makers are unsure how to read Dataverse rows directly in a page.
whenToUse: Custom layouts such as cards, tiles or grouped lists
Showing rows filtered by the signed-in user
Small result sets rendered on the server
whenNotToUse: Large tables that need paging, sorting and search. Use the list component or the Web API.
Data that changes after the page loads without a refresh
formulaOrCode:
{% fetchxml requests %} {% endfetchxml %} {% assign rows = requests.results.entities %} {% if rows.size > 0 %}
    {% for row in rows %}
  • {{ row.bv_name | escape }} {{ row.bv_status.label }} {{ row.createdon | date: "d MMM yyyy" }}
    • {% endfor %}
{% else %}

You have no open requests.

{% endif %}
stepByStepInstructions: Build and test the query in Dataverse first, for example with a view's Download FetchXML option.
Create a web template in the Portal Management app and paste the code above, changing table and column names.
Add a table permission that gives the user's web role Read on the table. Liquid queries respect table permissions.
Include the web template in a page with {% include 'Template Name' %} or use it as the source of a page template.
Open the page signed in as a test user and confirm only their rows appear.
Escape any text column you print with the escape filter.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the table permission, so the query returns no rows and shows no error.
Printing user-entered text without the escape filter.
Using display names instead of logical names in the FetchXML.
Running a large query on every page load, which slows the page.
troubleshooting: If the list is empty, test as a user with a Global Read permission. If rows appear, the query is right and the permission is the problem.
If the page shows a Liquid error, check that every tag is closed and that the FetchXML is valid XML.
If a choice column prints a number, use .label. For a lookup, use .name and .id.
If results look stale, the server cache has not refreshed. Clear the cache from the design studio preview options or the site's admin tools.
seoTitle: Power Pages Liquid fetchxml example: custom Dataverse list
seoDescription: A Power Pages Liquid fetchxml example that lists the signed-in user's Dataverse rows with sorting, an empty state, and links to a detail page.

faqs.question: Does Liquid fetchxml respect table permissions?
faqs.answer: Yes. The query returns only rows the current user's web roles allow, so a missing permission looks like an empty result.

faqs.question: How do I read a choice or lookup value in Liquid?
faqs.answer: Use row.column.label for a choice, and row.column.name or row.column.id for a lookup.

faqs.question: How many rows can a Liquid fetchxml query return?
faqs.answer: Keep it small. Set top or count in the query and use the list component or Web API when you need paging.

title: Create a Dataverse row from Power Pages with the Web API
shortDescription: Enable the portal Web API for a table and post a new row from JavaScript.
fullDescription: The Power Pages Web API lets page scripts create, update and delete Dataverse rows without a form component. This pattern covers the site settings that switch it on, the token wrapper every request needs, and a create call with a lookup.
problemStatement: Custom interfaces such as inline editing or multi-step wizards need to write to Dataverse from script, and requests fail with 403 or 404 until three separate settings line up.
whenToUse: Custom forms or wizards that the form component cannot produce
Inline updates without a page reload
Saving several related rows from one screen
whenNotToUse: Simple create or edit pages, where a basic form is quicker and safer
Anonymous writes to sensitive tables
stepByStepInstructions: Add the two site settings for the table. List only the columns the script needs instead of using *.
Create a table permission with the privileges the script uses and link it to a web role.
Add the wrapper function to the page or to a shared web file.
Call the API with the entity set name in the URL and logical column names in the body.
Set lookups with the navigation property name followed by @odata.bind.
Test signed in as a normal user and read the response text when a call fails.
commonMistakes: Using the table's logical name in the URL instead of the plural entity set name.
Setting the fields site setting to * on a table with sensitive columns.
Calling $.ajax directly without the token wrapper.
Using the lookup's logical name in @odata.bind. It needs the navigation property name, which is case-sensitive.
troubleshooting: A 404 usually means the enabled site setting is missing or the entity set name is wrong.
A 403 means the user's web role has no table permission with the needed privilege.
"Attribute X is not enabled for Web Api" means the column is missing from the fields site setting.
If nothing changes after adding site settings, clear the site cache and reload.
seoTitle: Power Pages Web API: create a Dataverse record with JavaScript
seoDescription: Enable the Power Pages Web API with site settings and table permissions, then create a Dataverse row from JavaScript using the safeAjax wrapper.
primaryKeyword: Power Pages Web API create record

faqs.question: Which site settings turn on the Web API?
faqs.answer: Webapi/<table logical name>/enabled set to true, and Webapi/<table logical name>/fields set to a comma-separated list of column logical names.

faqs.question: Why do I need the safeAjax wrapper?
faqs.answer: Every write request must carry the site's anti-forgery token. The wrapper fetches the token and adds it to the request header.

faqs.question: Can anonymous visitors use the Web API?
faqs.answer: Only if the Anonymous Users role has a table permission for it. Grant that with great care, and never for sensitive tables.

title: Show Power Pages content by sign-in state and web role
shortDescription: Use Liquid to show different content to anonymous visitors, signed-in users and specific roles.
fullDescription: Liquid exposes the current user and their web roles on every page. This pattern shows the common checks and explains where they are enough and where page permissions or table permissions are needed instead.
problemStatement: A page needs a staff-only panel or a different message for signed-in users, and makers are unsure how to test the user's role in a template.
whenToUse: Showing or hiding sections of a page by role
Showing a sign-in prompt to anonymous visitors
whenNotToUse: Protecting a whole page. Use page permissions.
Protecting data. Use table permissions. Hidden HTML is not security.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the web roles in the design studio under Security, and assign them to contacts.
Open the page's code or a web template and add the Liquid above.
Match role names exactly, including capitals and spaces.
Move role-specific sections into their own web templates and include them, so the logic stays readable.
Add a page permission if anonymous users should not reach the page at all.
Test in a private browser window as anonymous, then as a user in each role.
commonMistakes: Relying on hidden content to protect data that a list or Web API call would still return.
Misspelling the role name, which fails silently.
Forgetting that every signed-in user has the Authenticated Users role.
Putting role checks in content snippets that are cached and shared between users.
troubleshooting: If a role check never passes, print {{ user.roles | join: ', ' }} temporarily to see the exact names.
If user is empty for a signed-in person, check that the page is not being served from an output cache for anonymous users.
If the sign-in link returns to the home page, check that returnUrl is URL-encoded.
If the content shows for the wrong people, check for the role being inherited through another assignment.
seoTitle: Power Pages Liquid: check user web role and sign-in state
seoDescription: Liquid examples for Power Pages that check whether a user is signed in and which web roles they have, with notes on what this does and does not secure.

faqs.question: How do I check if a user is signed in with Liquid?
faqs.answer: Use {% if user %}. The user object is empty for anonymous visitors.

faqs.question: Is hiding content with Liquid secure?
faqs.answer: The hidden HTML is not sent to the browser, but any data it would have shown is only protected if table permissions also restrict it.

faqs.question: How do I restrict a whole page to a role?
faqs.answer: Use page permissions in the design studio and choose which web roles can see the page.

title: Post an adaptive card in Teams and wait for a response
shortDescription: Send a card with inputs and buttons from a flow, then branch on what the person chose.
fullDescription: The Teams action Post adaptive card and wait for a response pauses a flow until someone submits the card. This pattern provides a card with a comment box and two buttons, and the expressions that read the answer.
problemStatement: The standard Approvals action cannot collect custom fields or use custom button labels, and makers are unsure how to read the values a card returns.
whenToUse: Decisions that need extra input such as a reason, a date or a choice
Quick responses inside a Teams chat or channel
Custom button labels beyond Approve and Reject
whenNotToUse: Formal approvals that need the Approvals history, reassignment or mobile approval centre
Responses expected to take longer than 30 days, which is the flow run limit
stepByStepInstructions: Add the Microsoft Teams action Post adaptive card and wait for a response.
Set Post as to Flow bot and Post in to Chat with Flow bot or Channel, then choose the recipient.
Paste the card JSON into the Message field and replace the dynamic values with your own.
Fill in Update message so the card changes to a confirmation after it is submitted.
Add a Condition or Switch on the decision expression.
In the action's settings, set a timeout such as P7D, and add a parallel branch that runs after the action has timed out.
commonMistakes: Using a card schema version newer than Teams supports, which makes the card fail to render.
Giving two inputs the same id, so one value overwrites the other.
Leaving no timeout, so runs wait for 30 days and then fail.
Posting to a channel and expecting only one named person to be able to respond. Anyone in the channel can submit.
troubleshooting: If the card does not appear, validate the JSON in the Adaptive Cards designer with the host set to Microsoft Teams.
If an expression returns null, open the run history and read the action's raw output to see the exact property names.
If the flow never continues, check that the card uses Action.Submit. Action.OpenUrl and Action.Execute do not resume this action.
If the recipient reports "something went wrong" on submit, the flow run has already timed out or been cancelled.
seoTitle: Power Automate: post adaptive card and wait for a response
seoDescription: Adaptive card JSON with inputs and buttons for the Teams wait-for-response action, plus the expressions that read the decision, comments and responder.
primaryKeyword: post adaptive card and wait for a response

faqs.question: How do I read the values from the card?
faqs.answer: Use body('Post_adaptive_card_and_wait_for_a_response')?['data']?['<input id>'], replacing the action name with yours if you renamed it.

faqs.question: How long will the flow wait?
faqs.answer: Up to the flow run limit of 30 days, or the timeout you set on the action. Add a branch for the timed-out case.

faqs.question: Which adaptive card version should I use?
faqs.answer: Use 1.4 for flow-posted cards in Teams unless you have confirmed a newer version renders for your users.

title: Mention a user in a Teams message or adaptive card from a flow
shortDescription: Add an @mention that notifies the person, in both plain messages and adaptive cards.
fullDescription: A mention needs more than the person's name in the text. Plain messages use a mention token, and adaptive cards need an at tag in the text plus a matching entry in the card's msteams entities. This pattern shows both.
problemStatement: A flow posts "@Jane Doe" as plain text, the name is not highlighted, and Jane never gets a notification.
whenToUse: Channel posts where one person needs to act
Cards that assign work to a named owner
Escalations that must trigger a Teams notification
whenNotToUse: Messages sent to a one-to-one chat with the Flow bot, where the recipient is already notified
Mentioning large numbers of people in one message
stepByStepInstructions: For a plain message, add Get an @mention token for a user and pass the person's email address.
Insert the token's dynamic value into the message body.
For a card, write the name inside an at tag in a TextBlock.
Add an msteams entities entry whose text matches the at tag exactly, character for character.
Set mentioned.id to the user's UPN or Entra object ID and mentioned.name to their display name.
Post to a test channel and confirm the name is highlighted and the person gets a notification.
commonMistakes: Typing @Name as text and expecting Teams to resolve it.
A mismatch between the at tag text and the entity text, including extra spaces.
Using an external email address for a guest instead of their UPN or object ID.
Putting the mention in a card element that does not support it. Use a TextBlock.
troubleshooting: If the name shows as plain text in a card, compare the two at tag strings. They must be identical.
If the token action fails with user not found, check that the address is the person's UPN and that they are a member of the tenant.
If the mention renders but nobody is notified, the person may have muted the channel or turned off mention notifications.
To mention several people, add one at tag and one entity per person.
seoTitle: Power Automate: mention a user in Teams and adaptive cards
seoDescription: How to @mention a user from Power Automate in a Teams message with a mention token, and in an adaptive card with at tags and msteams entities.
secondaryKeywords: Get an @mention token for a user

faqs.question: Why is my mention plain text in an adaptive card?
faqs.answer: The text inside the at tag and the text in the msteams entity must match exactly. Any difference stops Teams from linking them.

faqs.question: Can I mention a channel or team from a flow?
faqs.answer: Plain messages can use the tag mention token action for tags. Channel and team mentions are more limited, so test in your tenant before relying on them.

faqs.question: What goes in mentioned.id?
faqs.answer: The user's UPN or their Entra object ID.

title: Build an adaptive card list from SharePoint items
shortDescription: Turn a set of SharePoint items into rows on a single Teams card with the Select action.
fullDescription: Instead of posting one message per item, this pattern shapes Get items results into card elements with Select and places them in one adaptive card. It works for daily digests, overdue lists and queue summaries.
problemStatement: A flow inside Apply to each posts a separate Teams message for every item, flooding the channel and hitting connector limits.
whenToUse: Daily or weekly summaries of open items
Posting up to a few dozen rows in one card
Replacing an Apply to each that posts messages
whenNotToUse: Hundreds of rows. Link to a view instead.
Rows that each need their own buttons and response
stepByStepInstructions: Add Get items with a filter query and a Top Count so the card stays a readable size.
Add a Select action. Switch Map to text mode with the small icon on the right, then paste the element JSON.
Add a Condition that checks the Select output is not empty.
Add Post card in a chat or channel and paste the card JSON. Insert the Select output as shown, without quotes around it.
Run the flow and open the Post card input in run history to check the JSON is valid.
Add a link to the full SharePoint view at the bottom of the card.
commonMistakes: Wrapping the Select output in quotes, which turns the array into a string and breaks the card.
Using Map in key-value mode, which cannot produce nested card elements.
Posting without a row limit, so the card exceeds the size Teams accepts.
Forgetting the empty case and posting a card with no rows.
troubleshooting: If the card fails to post, copy the action input from run history into the Adaptive Cards designer to find the invalid part.
If a title containing quotes or line breaks breaks the JSON, wrap the value in replace() to escape quotes or use a Compose with string handling first.
If dates show as raw text, the column is empty for some items. Wrap formatDateTime in an if(empty(...)) check.
If the message is rejected as too large, lower Top Count. Teams limits card payloads to roughly 28 KB.
seoTitle: Adaptive card from SharePoint list items with Select
seoDescription: Build one Teams adaptive card listing many SharePoint items in Power Automate, using Get items, Select in text mode, and a container bound to the output.

faqs.question: Can an adaptive card loop over an array in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Build the repeated elements with a Select action and insert the resulting array into the card's body.

faqs.question: How many items can one card show?
faqs.answer: Keep it to a few dozen. Teams limits the card payload to roughly 28 KB, and long cards are hard to read.

faqs.question: Why use Select instead of Apply to each?
faqs.answer: Select transforms the whole array in one action, runs much faster, and avoids posting a message per item.

title: Send a Teams notification that opens a Power Apps record
shortDescription: Post a message with a button that launches a canvas app directly on the right record.
fullDescription: A notification is more useful when one click takes the reader to the item. This pattern builds a link to a canvas app with a record ID parameter, reads that parameter when the app starts, and posts the link in a Teams card.
problemStatement: People receive a Teams notification, open the app, and then have to search for the record the message was about.
whenToUse: Apps that already have a detail screen for one record
Links shared in email as well as Teams
whenNotToUse: Apps embedded as a Teams tab, which use a Teams deep link format instead
Records the reader may not have permission to open
stepByStepInstructions: Copy the app's web link from its Details page in the maker portal.
In the flow, build the link in a Compose action and append your own parameter with the record ID.
Add the link to an Action.OpenUrl button in the card.
In the app, set App.StartScreen to choose the detail screen when the parameter is present.
Load the record with LookUp and Param, converting the value with Value() for a numeric ID.
Test the link in a browser first, then from Teams on desktop and mobile.
commonMistakes: Navigating in App.OnStart instead of using App.StartScreen.
Forgetting that Param always returns text, so a numeric ID comparison finds nothing.
Hard-coding the app link per environment instead of storing it in an environment variable.
Not handling a record that no longer exists or that the user cannot see.
troubleshooting: If the app opens on the home screen, check the parameter name. Names are case-sensitive.
If the detail screen is blank, the lookup returned nothing. Show a message when nfDeepLinkRequest is blank and offer a way back.
If the link opens the browser instead of the Teams app, that is expected for web links. Use a Teams deep link if the app is pinned as a tab.
If the link works for you but not for others, share the app and the data source with them.
seoTitle: Deep link from Teams to a Power Apps record with Param
seoDescription: Send a Teams adaptive card with a button that opens a canvas app on a specific record, using a URL parameter, Param() and App.StartScreen.
secondaryKeywords: open Power Apps record from Teams

faqs.question: How do I pass a record ID to a canvas app?
faqs.answer: Add a query parameter to the app's web link, such as &requestId=42, and read it in the app with Param("requestId").

faqs.question: Where should the app decide which screen to open?
faqs.answer: In App.StartScreen. It replaces Navigate in OnStart and lets the app load faster.

faqs.question: Does the link work on mobile?
faqs.answer: Yes. On a phone with the Power Apps app installed, the link opens the app and passes the parameter.

title: Patch multiple records at once with ForAll and Patch
shortDescription: Save many rows in one call by passing a table to Patch, and know when ForAll is still needed.
fullDescription: Looping over a collection with ForAll and calling Patch for each row works, but it sends one request per row. Passing two tables to Patch updates all rows in a single call. This pattern shows both forms, for creating and for updating.
problemStatement: Saving an editable gallery or a checklist takes many seconds because the app patches rows one at a time, and a failure half-way leaves the data partly saved with no message.
whenToUse: Saving edits from a gallery or a collection
Creating many rows from a template
Bulk status changes on selected items
whenNotToUse: Changing the same column to the same value on rows matching a condition. UpdateIf is shorter.
Thousands of rows, which belong in a flow
stepByStepInstructions: Keep gallery edits in a collection, with an IsDirty column you set to true in each control's OnChange.
On Save, filter the collection to dirty rows.
Call Patch with the data source, a table of record identifiers, and a table of changes in the same order.
Wrap the call in IfError and clear the dirty flags only on success.
Use the ForAll form only when rows need different handling, such as a mix of new and existing rows.
commonMistakes: Calling Patch inside ForAll for hundreds of rows, which sends hundreds of requests.
Passing two tables with different row counts or order to Patch.
Using ThisRecord or column names that clash between the collection and the data source. Name the loop record with As.
Assuming ForAll runs in order. It may run in parallel, so do not rely on one iteration seeing another's result.
troubleshooting: "The specified column is read-only" means the change table includes a column such as ID, Created or a calculated column. Remove it from the change record.
If only some rows save, check Errors(Tasks) after the call to see which rows failed and why.
If new rows are created instead of updated, the first table does not contain the primary key. Include ID, or the Dataverse primary key column.
If the save is still slow, check for a formula inside ForAll that calls LookUp against the data source for every row.
seoTitle: Power Apps ForAll Patch: update multiple records at once
seoDescription: Patch multiple records in Power Apps with a single Patch call using two tables, or with ForAll, including error handling and the common read-only column error.

faqs.question: Is Patch with a table faster than ForAll with Patch?
faqs.answer: Yes, usually much faster. Patch with tables batches the work, while ForAll with Patch sends a separate request for each row.

faqs.question: Can I create and update rows in the same Patch call?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. Split the collection into new rows and existing rows and make one call for each.

faqs.question: How do I know which rows failed?
faqs.answer: Wrap the call in IfError for the first error, and read Errors(DataSource) afterwards for row-level detail.

title: Change or delete many rows with UpdateIf and RemoveIf
shortDescription: Apply one change to every row that matches a condition, in a collection or a data source.
fullDescription: UpdateIf and RemoveIf act on all rows that meet a condition, without a loop. They are ideal for collections and for small data sources, with one important limit: against a data source they are not delegable.
problemStatement: Makers write ForAll loops to tick every row, clear a flag or remove completed items, when one function call would do it faster and more clearly.
whenToUse: Select all and clear all in a gallery backed by a collection
Marking every matching row with the same value
Removing rows from a collection or a small list
whenNotToUse: Data sources with more rows than the data row limit. Only the first 500 to 2,000 rows are considered.
Rows that each need a different value. Use Patch with a table.
stepByStepInstructions: Identify the condition that picks the rows and the change they all share.
Call UpdateIf with the table, the condition and a record of changes.
Use the row's own column names inside the change record to build on current values.
Use RemoveIf with the same kind of condition to delete rows.
For a data source, confirm the table is small, or load the matching rows into a collection first and Patch them.
commonMistakes: Using UpdateIf or RemoveIf on a large SharePoint list and assuming every matching row was processed.
Passing the gallery's AllItems instead of the underlying collection.
Using a context variable with the same name as a column, so the condition compares the column with itself.
Forgetting that RemoveIf on a data source deletes permanently.
troubleshooting: If nothing changes, test the condition alone with CountRows(Filter(table, condition)).
If only some rows change in a data source, you have hit the data row limit. Filter into a collection and Patch instead.
If you see a delegation warning, that is the same limit being reported. Treat it as an error for these functions.
If the gallery does not refresh, make sure its Items is the collection you updated.
seoTitle: Power Apps UpdateIf and RemoveIf with examples
seoDescription: Use UpdateIf and RemoveIf in Power Apps to change or delete all rows matching a condition, with select-all examples and the delegation limit explained.

faqs.question: Is UpdateIf delegable?
faqs.answer: No. Against a data source it only processes rows within the app's data row limit, which is 500 by default and 2,000 at most.

faqs.question: What is the difference between UpdateIf and Patch?
faqs.answer: UpdateIf applies one change to every row that matches a condition. Patch changes specific records, each with its own values.

faqs.question: How do I update every row in a collection?
faqs.answer: Use true as the condition: UpdateIf(colItems, true, { Column: value }).

title: Use With to make long Power Fx formulas readable
shortDescription: Name intermediate values inside a formula instead of repeating the same lookup or calculation.
fullDescription: The With function evaluates a record of named values once and makes them available to the rest of the formula. It removes repeated LookUp calls, shortens nested expressions and avoids creating variables that exist only for one calculation.
problemStatement: A label or a Patch formula repeats the same LookUp three times, runs slower than it should, and is hard to change without missing one copy.
whenToUse: The same sub-expression appears more than once in a formula
Multi-step calculations such as totals with tax and discount
Non-behaviour properties such as Text or Items, where Set is not allowed
whenNotToUse: Values needed across several controls. Use a named formula or a variable.
Simple formulas where naming a value adds nothing
stepByStepInstructions: Find a sub-expression that is repeated or hard to read.
Wrap the formula in With and move the sub-expression into the first argument as a named field.
Replace each repeat with the name.
Nest a second With when a value depends on an earlier one. Fields in the same record cannot refer to each other.
Check the result is unchanged, then format the formula so each named value is on its own line.
commonMistakes: Referring to one field from another in the same With record, which is not allowed.
Giving a With name the same name as a column in scope, which makes the formula ambiguous.
Expecting a With value to exist outside the formula. It is scoped to that one call.
Using Set or UpdateContext for throwaway values, which leaves stale variables around the app.
troubleshooting: "Name isn't valid" on a With field means you used it outside the With call or inside the same record that defines it.
If the wrong value appears inside a gallery or ForAll, a column has the same name. Rename the With field.
If performance did not improve, the expensive call is elsewhere. Use Monitor to see which requests repeat.
If delegation warnings appear after the change, keep the data source call directly inside Filter or LookUp and name only its result.
seoTitle: Power Apps With function: examples and when to use it
seoDescription: Power Fx With function examples that replace repeated LookUp calls, chain calculations and capture a Patch result, plus the scoping rules that trip people up.

faqs.question: What is the difference between With and Set?
faqs.answer: With names a value for one formula only and works in any property. Set creates a global variable and only works in behaviour formulas such as OnSelect.

faqs.question: Can one With value use another?
faqs.answer: Not inside the same record. Nest a second With to build on an earlier value.

faqs.question: Does With improve performance?
faqs.answer: It can. A repeated LookUp or calculation is evaluated once instead of several times.

title: Group rows and show totals with GroupBy and AddColumns
shortDescription: Summarize a table by category with counts and sums, ready for a gallery or chart.
fullDescription: GroupBy collects rows that share a value into a nested table. AddColumns then calculates a count or a total for each group. This pattern produces a summary table and a gallery with expandable detail rows.
problemStatement: A dashboard needs totals by status or by owner, and makers end up writing one CountRows formula per label that has to be edited whenever a new status is added.
whenToUse: Totals by status, owner, month or category
Grouped galleries with a header row per group
whenNotToUse: Very large lists. GroupBy is not delegable, so summarize on the server with a view, a flow or Power BI.
A single total, where Sum or CountRows alone is enough
stepByStepInstructions: Load the rows to summarize into a collection with a delegable filter, so the set is small and known.
Add a text column for any choice, lookup or person field you want to group by.
Call GroupBy with the column to group on and a name for the nested table.
Use AddColumns to calculate CountRows, Sum, Min or Max over the nested table.
Bind a gallery or chart to the result, and use a nested gallery for the detail rows.
commonMistakes: Grouping directly on a choice or lookup column. Group on a text value instead.
Running GroupBy directly against a large data source and trusting the totals.
Using the older syntax with column names in quotes. Current versions take column names without quotes.
Recalculating the summary in a gallery's Items on every change instead of storing it once.
troubleshooting: If GroupBy shows a type error, the group column is a record. Add a text column from its Value or DisplayName and group on that.
If totals look low, the source was cut off at the data row limit. Filter the source first so fewer rows are loaded.
If a group for blank values appears, replace blanks with a label using Coalesce in the AddColumns step.
If the nested gallery is empty, check that its Items uses the name you gave the nested table.
seoTitle: Power Apps GroupBy with Sum and Count: gallery example
seoDescription: Use GroupBy and AddColumns in Power Apps to count and sum rows by category, group on a choice column, and show the result in a nested gallery or chart.

faqs.question: Is GroupBy delegable?
faqs.answer: No. It runs in the app on the rows already loaded, so filter the source first or summarize on the server for large lists.

faqs.question: How do I group by a SharePoint choice column?
faqs.answer: Add a text column with AddColumns that holds the choice's Value, then group by that column.

faqs.question: How do I get a total for each group?
faqs.answer: Wrap GroupBy in AddColumns and use Sum, CountRows, Min or Max over the nested table.

title: Make a canvas app work offline with SaveData and LoadData
shortDescription: Cache reference data on the device, queue new records while offline, and sync when the connection returns.
fullDescription: SaveData and LoadData store collections on the device. With the Connection signal, an app can keep working without a network, hold new records in a queue, and send them when it is back online. This pattern gives the three formulas that make that work.
problemStatement: Field staff lose their entries when signal drops, because the app tries to Patch straight to the data source and fails.
whenToUse: Inspections, site visits and field data capture on phones or tablets
Simple create-only scenarios with small reference lists
SharePoint-backed apps, which have no built-in offline mode
whenNotToUse: Dataverse apps that can use the built-in offline profile feature instead
Scenarios where several people edit the same record offline and conflicts must be merged
Large data sets. Device storage for SaveData is limited.
stepByStepInstructions: List the reference data the app needs offline and keep it small.
Add the OnStart formula to cache reference data when online and read the cache when offline.
Change the Save button to queue the record when offline, saving the queue to the device after every change.
Add a timer that sends queued records when the connection returns and removes each one after it succeeds.
Show the number of unsent records on screen so users know nothing is lost.
Test on a real phone in airplane mode. SaveData behaves differently in the browser.
commonMistakes: Testing only in the browser or Studio, where storage limits and behaviour differ from the mobile player.
Forgetting the third argument of LoadData, so the first run fails when no file exists.
Not saving the queue after each change, so a closed app loses unsent records.
Caching whole lists with attachments or images, which exceeds device storage.
troubleshooting: If LoadData errors on first run, pass true as the third argument to ignore a missing file.
If queued records are sent twice, remove each record from the queue only after its Patch succeeds, and store a LocalId column to detect duplicates.
If the app will not open offline at all, it must have been opened online once on that device so the app itself is cached.
If Connection.Connected is true but saves fail, the device has a network without internet. The IfError branch queues the record.
seoTitle: Power Apps offline mode with SaveData and LoadData
seoDescription: Build an offline-capable canvas app: cache data with SaveData and LoadData, queue new records with Connection.Connected, and sync with a timer.

faqs.question: Does SaveData work in a web browser?
faqs.answer: It works with much smaller limits than on the mobile players. Offline apps should be tested and used in the Power Apps mobile app.

faqs.question: How much data can SaveData store?
faqs.answer: It depends on the device's free memory and storage. Keep cached collections to what the app needs, and avoid images.

faqs.question: Do I need this with Dataverse?
faqs.answer: Not usually. Dataverse canvas apps can use the built-in offline feature with an offline profile, which handles sync for you.

title: Save a photo from Power Apps to a SharePoint document library
shortDescription: Send an image from the camera or Add picture control to a flow that creates the file.
fullDescription: Power Apps cannot write to a document library directly. The reliable route is a small flow with a file input that the app calls. This pattern covers the flow, the formula that passes the image, and how to tag the file with the related record.
problemStatement: Photos saved to a list's attachments are hard to find and reuse, and makers struggle to pass an image to a flow in a form that produces a working file.
whenToUse: Inspection or evidence photos that belong in a library with metadata
Images that other tools need to reach by URL
whenNotToUse: A single small image that can live in a SharePoint image column
When list attachments through an Edit form are good enough
stepByStepInstructions: Create the flow with the Power Apps (V2) trigger and add a File input plus any text or number inputs.
Add Create file and map File Content to the file input's contentBytes.
Add Update file properties to set metadata such as the related request ID.
Add Respond to a Power App or flow so the app knows when the upload has finished.
Add the flow to the app from the Power Automate pane.
Call the flow with a record containing name and contentBytes, as shown.
commonMistakes: Using the older Power Apps trigger, which has no file input type.
Passing the image as text built with JSON(), which adds a data URI prefix that corrupts the file.
Reusing the same file name, so each upload overwrites the last.
Uploading full-resolution photos on mobile data. Reduce the Add picture control's image size where possible.
troubleshooting: If the file is created but will not open, the content was sent as text. Use a File input and pass the image directly as contentBytes.
If the flow fails with file already exists, add a timestamp to the name.
If the app shows a timeout on large photos, upload one photo per call and show a spinner while varUploading is true.
If Update file properties fails, use the ItemId output of Create file, not the file identifier.
seoTitle: Power Apps: upload a photo to a SharePoint document library
seoDescription: Save a camera or Add picture image from Power Apps to a SharePoint document library using a Power Apps (V2) flow with a file input and metadata.
primaryKeyword: Power Apps upload image to SharePoint document library

faqs.question: Can Power Apps save a file to a document library without a flow?
faqs.answer: Not directly. The SharePoint connector in canvas apps works with lists. A flow with Create file is the standard approach.

faqs.question: How do I pass an image to a flow?
faqs.answer: Use the Power Apps (V2) trigger with a File input, and pass a record with name and contentBytes set to the control's image.

faqs.question: How do I link the photo to a list item?
faqs.answer: Add a column to the library for the item's ID and set it with Update file properties after the file is created.

title: Scan a barcode and look up a record in Power Apps
shortDescription: Use the barcode reader control to find an item, with a clear message when nothing matches.
fullDescription: The barcode reader control scans barcodes and QR codes on phones and tablets. This pattern reads the scanned value, finds the matching record with a delegable lookup, and handles the not-found and multiple-scan cases.
problemStatement: Typing asset tags or product codes on a phone is slow and error-prone, and makers are unsure how to read the value the scanner returns.
whenToUse: Opening a record from a QR code on a label
whenNotToUse: Apps used only in a desktop browser, where the control is not supported
Continuous high-volume scanning, which suits a dedicated scanner device
stepByStepInstructions: Insert the Barcode reader control from the Media group.
Set the scanning mode. Automatic is fastest for one code at a time.
In OnScan, read the first barcode's Value and look up the record on an indexed text column.
Show a warning when no record matches, and navigate to the detail screen when one does.
Add a text input and button as a manual fallback.
Test on a real device. The control does not scan in the browser.
commonMistakes: Reading BarcodeReader1.Value from older examples. The current control returns a Barcodes table.
Looking up on a number column when the barcode value is text.
Not trimming the value, so codes with trailing spaces or line breaks fail to match.
Forgetting a manual entry option for damaged labels.
troubleshooting: If nothing happens on scan, check that the app has camera permission on the device.
If the lookup finds nothing, show varScanned in a label and compare it with the stored value. Leading zeros and check digits often differ.
If the wrong code is read when several are visible, switch to Select to scan so the user taps the right one.
If the lookup shows a delegation warning, compare with = on a text column instead of using in or a function on the column.
seoTitle: Power Apps barcode scanner: scan and look up a record
seoDescription: Use the Power Apps barcode reader control to scan a barcode or QR code and look up a record, with OnScan formulas for single and multiple scans.

faqs.question: Does the barcode reader work in a browser?
faqs.answer: No. It works in the Power Apps mobile app on iOS and Android. Provide a manual entry option for desktop users.

faqs.question: How do I read the scanned value?
faqs.answer: Use First(BarcodeReader1.Barcodes).Value in the control's OnScan property.

faqs.question: Can it scan QR codes?
faqs.answer: Yes. With the barcode type set to Auto it reads QR codes and the common 1D barcode formats.

title: Export a Power Apps collection or gallery to CSV
shortDescription: Send the rows on screen to a flow that builds a CSV file and returns a download link.
fullDescription: Canvas apps have no built-in export button. This pattern passes the filtered rows as JSON to a flow, which creates a CSV file in SharePoint and returns a link that the app opens.
problemStatement: Users want the filtered list they see in the app as a file for Excel, and screenshots or copying from a gallery is not acceptable.
whenToUse: Up to a few thousand rows
Users who need the data in Excel
whenNotToUse: Full list exports, where SharePoint's own Export to Excel is simpler
Very large data sets, which should be generated by the flow from the source directly
stepByStepInstructions: Shape the rows with ForAll so the export has plain text and number columns with friendly names.
Convert the table to text with JSON and pass it to the flow.
In the flow, convert the text back with json() and feed it to Create CSV table.
Create the file with a byte order mark in front, so Excel reads accented characters correctly.
Create a sharing link and return it with Respond to a Power App or flow.
Open the link in the app with Launch.
commonMistakes: Passing records with choice, person or lookup columns, which export as nested JSON instead of text.
Exporting galRequests.AllItems when the gallery has only loaded the first 100 rows. Use the underlying filtered collection for a complete export.
Leaving out the byte order mark, so Excel shows garbled characters.
Returning the file path instead of a link the user is allowed to open.
troubleshooting: If the CSV has a single column of JSON, the flow skipped the json() step and treated the input as text.
If the flow fails on a large export, the text input is too big. Send filter values to the flow and let it query the source itself.
If dates shift by a day, format them as text in the app before sending.
If Launch does nothing on mobile, the link type is blocked for the user. Use an organization view link.
seoTitle: Power Apps export to CSV or Excel from a gallery
seoDescription: Export a Power Apps collection or gallery to a CSV file: pass JSON to a Power Automate flow, create the CSV in SharePoint and return a download link.
secondaryKeywords: Power Apps export gallery to Excel

faqs.question: Can Power Apps export to Excel without a flow?
faqs.answer: Not as a file. Canvas apps need a flow, or you can send users to the SharePoint list's own Export to Excel option.

faqs.question: Why does Excel show strange characters in my CSV?
faqs.answer: The file has no byte order mark. Add one in front of the content when the flow creates the file.

faqs.question: Why are some rows missing from the export?
faqs.answer: A gallery loads rows as you scroll, so AllItems may be incomplete. Export from the collection or filter that feeds the gallery.

title: Sort a gallery by clicking column headers
shortDescription: Let users sort by any column and reverse the order with a second click, without breaking delegation.
fullDescription: Two variables hold the sort column and direction. Header labels update them, and the gallery's Items formula uses SortByColumns so the sort is delegated to the data source.
problemStatement: Table-style galleries feel unfinished without sortable headers, and a Switch full of separate Sort formulas quickly becomes hard to maintain.
whenToUse: Galleries laid out as a table
Lists where users look for the newest, oldest or largest item
Any gallery that already uses Filter
whenNotToUse: Sorting by a choice, lookup or person column in SharePoint, which cannot be delegated
Small fixed lists where one default order is enough
stepByStepInstructions: Set default sort values in the screen's OnVisible.
Add a label above each gallery column and set its OnSelect to the formula above with that column's internal name.
Add a small icon to each header that shows the direction and is visible only for the active column.
Wrap the gallery's existing Items formula in SortByColumns.
Test each header twice to confirm the direction flips.
commonMistakes: Using display names with spaces. SortByColumns needs the internal column name as text.
Offering a sortable header on a choice or person column and getting a delegation warning.
Putting the sort inside the filter instead of around it.
Using a global variable, so two screens fight over the same sort state.
troubleshooting: If a header does nothing, the column name does not match the internal name. Check it in the list's column settings URL.
If you see a delegation warning, that column type cannot be sorted on the server. Sort on a text or date column, or add a text copy of the value.
If the direction never flips, check the order of fields in UpdateContext. The direction must be calculated from the old column value.
If sorting numbers gives 1, 10, 2, the column is stored as text.
seoTitle: Power Apps sort gallery by column header (ascending/descending)
seoDescription: Make a Power Apps gallery sortable by clicking column headers with SortByColumns and two variables, keeping the query delegable.
primaryKeyword: Power Apps sort gallery by column

faqs.question: Can SortByColumns take the column name from a variable?
faqs.answer: Yes. That is what makes header sorting possible. Sort does not allow it, because it takes a formula instead of a name.

faqs.question: Why can't I sort by a choice column?
faqs.answer: SharePoint cannot sort complex columns such as choice, lookup and person on the server, so Power Apps shows a delegation warning.

faqs.question: Should the sort go inside or outside Filter?
faqs.answer: Outside. Filter first, then sort the result.

title: Generate rows, dates and repeats with the Sequence function
shortDescription: Create a table of numbers on the fly to build calendars, pickers and repeated rows.
fullDescription: Sequence returns a single-column table of numbers. Combined with ForAll or AddColumns it produces date ranges, time slots, numbered rows and loops with a counter, without a helper list.
problemStatement: Power Fx has no for loop, so makers build helper lists of numbers or dates in SharePoint just to drive a dropdown or a calendar.
whenToUse: Dropdowns of years, quantities or time slots
Creating a set number of rows
whenNotToUse: Looping over existing records, where ForAll over the table is enough
Very large ranges. Sequence returns at most 50,000 rows.
stepByStepInstructions: Decide how many rows you need, the starting number and the step.
Call Sequence with those values. The column is named Value.
Wrap it in ForAll to turn each number into the record you need.
Use the result as Items for a dropdown or gallery, or collect it.
For dates, add the number to a start date with DateAdd.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that Sequence starts at 1 unless you pass a start value.
Using Sequence where ForAll over the real table would do.
Building a helper list in SharePoint for numbers or dates.
Expecting more than 50,000 rows.
troubleshooting: If the range is off by one, check the start argument. Sequence(5) gives 1 to 5 and Sequence(5, 0) gives 0 to 4.
If Value is ambiguous inside nested ForAll calls, name the outer record with As.
If a calendar shows the wrong last day, calculate the month length from the first of next month minus one day, as shown.
If Index reports an error, the position is larger than the table. Sequence over CountRows of the same table.
seoTitle: Power Apps Sequence function: examples for dates and loops
seoDescription: Power Apps Sequence function examples: year dropdowns, date ranges, time slots, calendar days, numbered rows and loops with a counter.

faqs.question: Does Power Apps have a for loop?
faqs.answer: Not as such. ForAll over Sequence(n) does the same job, running a formula n times with a counter in Value.

faqs.question: How do I add a row number to a gallery?
faqs.answer: Loop over Sequence(CountRows(table)) and use Index to reach each row, as in the last example.

faqs.question: What is the maximum size of a Sequence?

title: Build a responsive canvas app with layout containers
shortDescription: Make one app fit phone, tablet and desktop using horizontal and vertical containers and screen size breakpoints.
fullDescription: Responsive canvas apps turn off scaling and let containers decide where controls go. This pattern gives the settings to change, a standard screen skeleton, and the formulas that switch layout at a breakpoint.
problemStatement: An app built at a fixed size shows black bars on wide monitors and tiny text on phones, and positioning every control with X and Y formulas is fragile.
whenToUse: Apps used on both desktop and mobile
New apps, where layout can be planned from the start
Screens with a header, side panel and content area
whenNotToUse: Apps used on one known device size
Retrofitting a large fixed-layout app in one pass. Convert screen by screen.
stepByStepInstructions: Turn off Scale to fit in the app's display settings. Lock aspect ratio turns off with it.
Add one vertical container per screen that fills the screen.
Add a fixed-height header container and a flexible body container inside it.
Split the body into child containers with fill portions and minimum widths, and turn on wrap.
Place controls inside containers and set their width to Parent.Width or to stretch.
Switch layout direction or visibility with App.ActiveScreen.Size, then test by resizing the browser.
commonMistakes: Leaving Scale to fit on, which scales the whole canvas instead of reflowing it.
Mixing manually positioned controls with containers on the same screen.
Setting fixed widths on controls inside a horizontal container, so nothing can shrink.
Testing only in Studio. Check the published app on a real phone.
troubleshooting: If controls overflow on a phone, set a minimum width on the child containers and turn on wrap on the parent.
If a container collapses to nothing, it has flexible height with no content height. Give it a minimum height.
If the breakpoint never triggers, check the screen's SizeBreakpoints property and that Scale to fit is off.
If scrollbars appear inside a container, set its vertical overflow to scroll deliberately or reduce the content.
seoTitle: Power Apps responsive design with containers
seoDescription: Make a Power Apps canvas app responsive: turn off scale to fit, structure screens with horizontal and vertical containers, and switch layout by screen size.

faqs.question: What does turning off Scale to fit do?
faqs.answer: The app stops scaling a fixed canvas and instead reports the real screen size, so your containers and formulas decide the layout.

faqs.question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical containers?
faqs.answer: A horizontal container places its children side by side, and a vertical container stacks them. Both can stretch children and distribute spare space.

faqs.question: How do I detect a phone?
faqs.answer: Compare App.ActiveScreen.Size with ScreenSize.Small. It is based on the screen's width breakpoints.

title: Check Microsoft 365 group membership in Power Apps
shortDescription: Show admin features only to members of a group, checked once when the app starts.
fullDescription: Group membership is easier to maintain than a list of email addresses in a formula. This pattern checks whether the signed-in user belongs to a Microsoft 365 group using the Office 365 Groups connector and stores the result in a named formula.
problemStatement: Admin emails are hard-coded in formulas across the app, and every staffing change needs a new published version.
whenToUse: Admin or approver features for a known team
Apps on SharePoint, where there is no security role to check
Organizations that already manage access with groups
whenNotToUse: Protecting data. Set permissions on the list or table as well.
Very large groups, where listing members is slow. Use a security list or a flow instead.
stepByStepInstructions: Create or choose a Microsoft 365 group for each role and note its object ID.
Add the Office 365 Groups connector to the app.
Add the named formulas above, with your group IDs.
Bind Visible or DisplayMode of admin features to the flags.
Restrict the underlying list or library to the same group, so the data is protected too.
Test with a member and a non-member account.
commonMistakes: Hiding buttons but leaving the SharePoint list editable by everyone.
Comparing email addresses without Lower, so case differences fail the match.
Calling the connector in several control properties instead of once in a named formula.
Using a security group that is not mail-enabled, which this connector may not return.
troubleshooting: If the check is always false, show CountRows of the member list in a label. Zero means the group ID is wrong or the user cannot read the group.
If guests are not matched, compare userPrincipalName as well as mail.
If the group has more than 999 members, the list is cut off. Use a smaller role group or a different check.
If users are asked to consent to a new connector, that is expected the first time the app opens after the change.
seoTitle: Power Apps: check if user is in a Microsoft 365 group
seoDescription: Check Microsoft 365 group membership in Power Apps with Office365Groups.ListGroupMembers and named formulas to show admin features to the right people.
primaryKeyword: Power Apps check user group membership
secondaryKeywords: check if user is in group

faqs.question: Can Power Apps check an Entra security group?
faqs.answer: The Office 365 Groups connector is designed for Microsoft 365 groups. For plain security groups, use a flow or the Microsoft Entra ID connector, which is premium.

faqs.question: Does hiding a screen secure the data?
faqs.answer: No. Also restrict the list, library or table so only the same group can change it.

faqs.question: Why use a named formula for this?
faqs.answer: The membership call runs once when first needed and is reused everywhere, which keeps the app fast.

title: Work with SharePoint lists over 5,000 items
shortDescription: Design columns, indexes and queries so large lists keep working in views, Power Apps and Power Automate.
fullDescription: SharePoint lists can hold millions of items, but any single query that has to examine more than 5,000 items is blocked. This pattern explains what triggers the limit and how to design a list, its views, and the apps and flows on top of it to stay under it.
problemStatement: A list that worked for months suddenly shows "The attempted operation is prohibited because it exceeds the list view threshold", and flows and apps on top of it start failing.
whenToUse: Any list expected to pass 5,000 items
Lists that already show threshold errors
Before building an app or flow on a growing list
whenNotToUse: Small reference lists
Data that needs relational queries or very high volume, where Dataverse or SQL is the better store
formulaOrCode:
Design rules for large lists

Indexes (List settings > Indexed columns)
  [ ] Index every column used to filter or sort: Status, DueDate, AssignedTo, Created
  [ ] Add indexes BEFORE the list passes 5,000 items where possible
  [ ] Maximum 20 indexes per list

Views
  [ ] First filter is on an indexed column and returns fewer than 5,000 items
  [ ] Use AND between filters. OR on the first filter breaks the index.
  [ ] No grouping or totals on non-indexed columns
  [ ] Default view: Status = Active, sorted by an indexed column

Power Apps
  Filter(Requests, Status.Value = "Open" && DueDate >= dpFrom.SelectedDate)
  // delegable operators only: =, <>, <, >, <=, >=, StartsWith, And, Or
  // avoid: Search, in, IsBlank on columns, Not, functions around a column

Power Automate (Get items)
  Filter Query : Status eq 'Open' and DueDate ge '2026-01-01'
  Top Count    : 5000
  Settings     : Pagination On, Threshold 100000
  // the first condition must be on an indexed column

Archive
  [ ] Move closed items older than N months to an archive list on a schedule
  [ ] Keep the active list as small as the process allows
stepByStepInstructions: List every column the views, apps and flows filter or sort on.
Create an index for each in List settings, Indexed columns.
Rewrite views so the first filter uses an indexed column and narrows the result below 5,000.
Check Power Apps formulas for delegation warnings and fix each one.
Add a filter query to every Get items action and turn on pagination where more than 5,000 rows are expected.
Schedule a flow to archive old items.
commonMistakes: Assuming the limit is on list size. It is on the number of items one query must examine.
Filtering on an indexed column with a value that still matches more than 5,000 items.
Using OR in the first view filter, which bypasses the index.
Relying on Get items without a filter and raising Top Count.
troubleshooting: If you cannot add an index because the list is already too large, SharePoint Online usually creates it in the background. Try again later, or add it in a quieter period.
If a view still fails, check its sort and group settings. Sorting on a non-indexed column triggers the limit.
If a flow's Get items returns only 100 rows, set Top Count or turn on pagination.
If Power Apps returns incomplete results with no error, look for a delegation warning. Non-delegable formulas only read the first 500 to 2,000 rows.
seoTitle: SharePoint 5,000 item list view threshold: how to fix it
seoDescription: Fix and avoid the SharePoint list view threshold: indexed columns, view filters, delegable Power Apps formulas, Get items pagination and archiving.

faqs.question: Can a SharePoint list hold more than 5,000 items?
faqs.answer: Yes, up to 30 million. The 5,000 limit applies to how many items a single query can examine, not to how many the list stores.

faqs.question: Can the threshold be raised in SharePoint Online?
faqs.answer: No. It is fixed in SharePoint Online. The fix is indexes and filters that keep each query under the limit.

faqs.question: Which column should I index first?
faqs.answer: The one your default view and main app filter on, usually a status or date column.

title: Get more than 5,000 SharePoint items in Power Automate
shortDescription: Use pagination and a filter query to read large lists reliably with Get items.
fullDescription: Get items returns 100 rows unless told otherwise. This pattern shows the three settings that control how many rows come back, how to keep the query under the list view threshold, and how to process the result without a slow loop.
problemStatement: A flow processes only the first 100 items of a list, or fails with a threshold error once the list grows past 5,000.
whenToUse: Scheduled flows that read a whole list or a large slice of it
Any Get items action on a list that will grow
whenNotToUse: Flows that need one item. Use Get item, or a filter with Top Count 1.
Reading everything in order to filter in the flow. Filter in the query instead.
formulaOrCode:
Get items
  Site Address : <site>
  List Name    : Requests
  Filter Query : Status eq 'Open' and Created ge '@{addDays(utcNow(), -90)}'
  Order By     : ID asc
  Top Count    : 5000
  Limit Columns by View : a view with only the columns you need

Settings (the three dots > Settings)
  Pagination : On
  Threshold  : 100000

How the numbers combine
  Top Count only          -> up to 5,000 rows, one request
  Pagination only         -> pages of 100 until the threshold is reached
  Top Count 5000 + Pagination -> pages of 5,000 until the threshold (fastest)

Count the result
  length(body('Get_items')?['value'])

Process without Apply to each where possible
  Select       -> reshape every row in one action
  Filter array -> keep a subset
  Create CSV table / Create HTML table -> output directly
stepByStepInstructions: Add a filter query so SharePoint returns only the rows you need, starting with an indexed column.
Set Top Count to 5000.
Open the action's settings, turn on Pagination and set a threshold above the largest expected result.
Choose a view in Limit Columns by View to reduce the payload, especially on lists with many lookup columns.
Check the count with a Compose using length().
Use Select or Filter array on the result instead of looping where you can.
commonMistakes: Leaving Top Count empty and wondering why only 100 rows arrive.
Setting the pagination threshold but no filter, then hitting the list view threshold on a non-indexed sort.
Looping over 20,000 rows with Apply to each, which takes hours.
Selecting every column of a list with more than 12 lookup, person or choice columns, which fails.
troubleshooting: "The attempted operation is prohibited because it exceeds the list view threshold" means the filter or order column is not indexed. Index it or filter on an indexed column first.
"The query cannot be completed because the number of lookup columns it contains exceeds the lookup column threshold" is fixed by Limit Columns by View.
If the result stops at 5,000, pagination is off.
If the threshold you can set is capped at 5,000, the flow owner's licence limits pagination. Run it under a licensed account or page manually with a filter on ID.
seoTitle: Power Automate Get items: more than 5,000 SharePoint items
seoDescription: Read more than 100 or 5,000 SharePoint items in Power Automate with Top Count, pagination and a filter query, and avoid list view threshold errors.
primaryKeyword: Power Automate get more than 5000 items

faqs.question: Why does Get items return only 100 items?
faqs.answer: That is the default page size. Set Top Count, turn on pagination, or both.

faqs.question: What is the maximum for Top Count?
faqs.answer: 5,000 per request. Pagination repeats the request until the threshold you set is reached.

faqs.question: How high can the pagination threshold go?
faqs.answer: Up to 100,000 on standard licences that include full Power Automate rights. Lower-tier plans are capped at 5,000.

title: Replace Apply to each and Condition with Filter array
shortDescription: Pick the rows you need from an array in one action instead of looping with a condition inside.
