seoDescription: Stop makers overwriting each other in a shared Dev environment by giving each a personal developer environment, a branch and a build from source.
primaryKeyword: Power Platform developer environment per maker branching

faqs.question: Should every maker have their own environment?
faqs.answer: For teams of several makers on one solution, yes. It isolates unfinished work, provided changes are merged through source control.

faqs.question: Are developer environments free?
faqs.answer: Each user can have up to three developer environments under the Power Apps Developer Plan, for building and testing only.

faqs.question: Can two people edit the same canvas app?
faqs.answer: Studio supports co-authoring in one environment, but parallel edits in separate environments cannot be merged reliably. Assign one owner at a time.

title: Add an approval step before a Power Platform pipeline deploys to production
shortDescription: Turn on the pre-deployment step for a pipeline stage and use a flow to request approval, then complete or reject the deployment from the result.
fullDescription: Power Platform pipelines can pause before a stage deploys and wait for an external decision. A cloud flow in the pipelines host environment receives the request, runs an approval and calls an action to continue or stop. This gives a recorded sign-off for production without leaving the product.
problemStatement: Any maker with access to the pipeline can push a solution to production at any time, with no second pair of eyes and no record of who agreed.
whenToUse: Change control that requires a named approver
whenNotToUse: Development-to-test stages, where a gate only slows feedback
Using approval as the only control when makers also hold admin rights in production
formulaOrCode:
Turn on the gate
  Deployment Pipeline Configuration app (in the pipelines host environment)
    Pipelines > open the pipeline > Deployment Stages > open the Production stage
      Pre-Deployment Step Required: Yes
      (optional) Pre-Export Step Required: Yes       runs before the solution is exported from Dev
      (optional) Is Delegated Deployment: Yes        deploy as a service principal or stage owner instead of the maker

Flow (create it in the host environment, in a solution)
  Trigger: Microsoft Dataverse > When an action is performed
    Catalog: Microsoft Dataverse Common        Category: Power Platform Pipelines
    Table name: (none)
    Action name: OnPreDeploymentStarted
  Useful trigger outputs (OutputParameters):
    StageRunId, DeploymentPipelineName, DeploymentStageName, ArtifactName, ArtifactVersion, DeploymentNotes

  Condition: only handle the production stage
    triggerOutputs()?['body/OutputParameters/DeploymentStageName']   is equal to   Production
    (If no: Terminate, Succeeded. Other stages with the step enabled need their own handling.)

  Get the requester
    Dataverse > Get a row by ID: Deployment Stage Runs, Row ID = StageRunId, Expand: createdby($select=fullname,internalemailaddress)

  Approvals > Start and wait for an approval (Approve/Reject - First to respond)
    Title:   Deploy @{ArtifactName} @{ArtifactVersion} to Production
    Assigned to: release-approvers@contoso.com
    Details: Requested by @{outputs('Get_stage_run')?['body/createdby/fullname']}
             Notes: @{triggerOutputs()?['body/OutputParameters/DeploymentNotes']}
    Item link: link to the stage run or the work item

  Condition: Outcome is equal to Approve
    Yes > Dataverse > Perform an unbound action
            Action name: UpdatePreDeploymentStepStatus
            StageRunId: @{triggerOutputs()?['body/OutputParameters/StageRunId']}
            PreDeploymentStepStatus: 20                  (20 = Completed, 30 = Failed)
    No  > same action with PreDeploymentStepStatus: 30
            Comments from the approver can be written to the stage run's notes.

  Timeout: Start and wait > Settings > Timeout P3D. Configure run after "has timed out" > set status 30.

What the maker sees
  After choosing Deploy, the stage shows "Pending pre-deployment step". On approval it continues without
  further action. On rejection it shows Failed with the pre-deployment step as the reason.

Other triggers in the same category
  OnDeploymentRequested, OnPreDeploymentStarted, OnPreDeploymentCompleted, OnDeploymentStarted,
  OnDeploymentCompleted          use the last one to post release notes to Teams or tag the Git commit.

Automated checks before approval
  In the same flow, before the approval: confirm the version is higher than production, that solution checker
  results have no critical issues, and that a change ticket number is present in the notes. Fail fast with status 30.

Permissions
  Approvers do not need access to the target environment. The flow's Dataverse connection needs the Deployment
  Pipeline Administrator role in the host.
stepByStepInstructions: Open the pipeline's production stage in the configuration app and require the pre-deployment step.
Create a flow in the host environment triggered by OnPreDeploymentStarted.
Filter to the stage you want to gate.
Start an approval with the solution name, version and notes.
Call UpdatePreDeploymentStepStatus with 20 on approval or 30 on rejection.
Handle timeouts so deployments never wait indefinitely.
commonMistakes: Enabling the step with no flow, which leaves deployments pending.
Not filtering by stage, so one flow answers for every pipeline.
Letting the requester approve their own deployment.
No timeout path.
troubleshooting: If deployments stay pending, check the flow ran and that the unbound action received the right StageRunId.
If the trigger never fires, the flow is in the wrong environment. It must be in the pipelines host.
If the action fails with privileges, give the connection's user the pipeline administrator role.
If approvers cannot see the request, check the Approvals connector's environment and their email addresses.
seoTitle: Add an approval step before a Power Platform pipeline deploys to production
seoDescription: Turn on the pre-deployment step for a pipeline stage and use a flow to request approval, then complete or reject the deployment from the result.

faqs.question: Can Power Platform pipelines require approval?
faqs.answer: Yes. Enable the pre-deployment step on a stage and use a flow to approve or reject the deployment.

faqs.question: Where does the approval flow live?
faqs.answer: In the pipelines host environment, triggered by the OnPreDeploymentStarted Dataverse action.

faqs.question: What is delegated deployment?
faqs.answer: A stage setting that runs the deployment as a service principal or the stage owner, so makers do not need rights in production.

title: Ship an urgent production fix without releasing unfinished work
shortDescription: A hotfix route for managed solutions: rebuild production's version in a clean environment, apply the fix, deploy it and merge it back into development.
fullDescription: When production has a fault, the development environment usually already contains next month's half-finished features. Exporting from it would ship them. A hotfix needs a copy of exactly what is in production, a minimal change, a fast test and a guaranteed merge back so the fix is not lost at the next release.
problemStatement: A flow fails in production. The fix takes five minutes in Dev, but Dev also holds an unfinished form redesign, so exporting the solution would release that too.
whenToUse: Urgent faults in production between planned releases
Teams whose development environment runs ahead of production
Managed solutions with source control or stored release zips
whenNotToUse: Problems that can wait for the next scheduled release
Editing production directly, which creates unmanaged layers and is lost or hidden later
formulaOrCode:
Prerequisites that make hotfixes possible
  Every release's managed AND unmanaged zip is kept (pipeline artefacts or a release library), or the unpacked
  source is tagged in Git:  git tag v1.4.0.0
  A spare sandbox, or the ability to create or reset one quickly.

Route A: from source control (preferred)
  1. Branch from the production tag
       git checkout -b hotfix/1.4.0.1 v1.4.0.0
  2. Build a hotfix environment
       pac admin reset --environment https://contoso-hotfix.crm.dynamics.com   (or create a new sandbox)
       pac solution pack   --folder src/RequestHub --zipfile out/RequestHub.zip --packagetype Unmanaged
       pac solution import --path out/RequestHub.zip --environment https://contoso-hotfix.crm.dynamics.com --publish-changes
  3. Make the fix in the hotfix environment. Change only what is needed.
  4. Set version 1.4.0.1, export, unpack, commit to the hotfix branch
       pac solution online-version --solution-name RequestHub --solution-version 1.4.0.1
       pac solution export --name RequestHub --path out/RequestHub.zip
       pac solution export --name RequestHub --path out/RequestHub_managed.zip --managed
       pac solution unpack --zipfile out/RequestHub.zip --folder src/RequestHub --allowDelete
  5. Import managed to Test (or a copy of production), run the smoke test and the specific case.
  6. Import managed to Production as an update.
  7. Merge the hotfix branch into main, and apply the same change in Dev (import or repeat by hand).
       git checkout main && git merge hotfix/1.4.0.1

Route B: no source control, release zips kept
  Import the unmanaged zip of the production version into a clean sandbox, then continue from step 3.

Route C: a solution patch
  In an environment holding the production version unmanaged: Solutions > select > Clone a patch.
  Add only the fixed component, export managed, import to production. Version 1.4.1.0 style numbering.
  The next full release must be at a higher version and include the fix. Patches lock the parent solution
  against edits in that environment until rolled up, which is why Route A is usually simpler.

Route D: fix forward from Dev (only when Dev equals production plus the fix)
  Acceptable just after a release when nothing else has changed. Check with a diff of unpacked source.

Emergency mitigation while the fix is built
  Turn off the failing flow, or use a feature flag (environment variable) to hide the broken feature.
  Document any direct production change and remove its unmanaged layer after the hotfix lands.

Version numbers
  major.minor.build.revision: planned releases raise build, hotfixes raise revision.
  1.4.0.0 (release) > 1.4.0.1 (hotfix) > 1.5.0.0 (next release, must include the fix).

After the hotfix
  Confirm the fix is in main and in Dev before the next export. A regression test for the fault is added to
  the smoke test list. Record the incident and the release in the release notes.
stepByStepInstructions: Keep each release's source tag or zips so production's version can be rebuilt.
Create a hotfix environment from the production version.
Make the smallest change that fixes the fault and raise the revision number.
Test the managed build against the failing case and the smoke tests.
Import to production as an update.
Merge the fix back into main and development before the next release.
commonMistakes: Exporting from Dev and shipping unfinished work.
Fixing directly in production and forgetting the unmanaged layer.
Not merging the hotfix back, so the next release reintroduces the fault.
Skipping test because the change is small.
troubleshooting: If you cannot rebuild the production version, note that a managed solution cannot be exported as unmanaged. Restore a copy of Dev from a backup taken at release time.
If the next release fails to import, its version is lower than the hotfix. Raise it.
If the fix disappears after the next release, it was never merged into main.
If an unmanaged layer hides the hotfix in production, remove the active layer on that component.
seoTitle: Ship an urgent production fix without releasing unfinished work
seoDescription: A hotfix route for managed solutions: rebuild production's version in a clean environment, apply the fix, deploy it and merge it back into development.

faqs.question: How do I hotfix a managed solution?
faqs.answer: Rebuild the production version in a clean environment, apply the fix, export it as managed with a higher revision and import it as an update.

faqs.question: Can I just fix it in production?
faqs.answer: Only as a recorded emergency mitigation. Direct edits create an unmanaged layer that hides later releases until removed.

faqs.question: How do I avoid losing the hotfix?
faqs.answer: Merge the hotfix branch into main and apply the change in development before the next export.

title: Write repeatable tests for a canvas app with Test Studio
shortDescription: Record and write test cases for a canvas app's key journeys, assert on results with Power Fx and run the suite from a link or a pipeline before each release.
fullDescription: Test Studio stores test cases inside the canvas app. Each case is a list of Power Fx steps that set control values, select buttons and assert what should be true. Suites can be played in the browser or opened by URL from a pipeline, which makes a regression check before release a matter of minutes.
problemStatement: Before each release someone clicks through the app by hand, skips the parts that seem unchanged, and a broken submit button reaches production.
whenToUse: Apps with a few critical journeys such as submit, approve and search
Apps maintained by more than one maker
whenNotToUse: Visual layout checking, which tests cannot judge
Flows and server logic, which need their own tests
Apps built mostly from unsupported controls or nested galleries
formulaOrCode:
Open
  Power Apps Studio > Advanced tools > Open tests          (the app must be saved and published once)

Structure
  Test suite: "Request submission"
    Test case: "Submit a valid request"
    Test case: "Required title blocks submit"
  Each step is one Power Fx formula. Record adds steps as you use the app. Edit them afterwards.

Functions available in tests
  SetProperty(Control.Property, value)        set an input
  Select(Control)  /  Select(Gallery, row, ChildControl)
  Assert(condition, "message when it fails")
  Trace("message", TraceSeverity.Information)  appears in results and Monitor

Test case: Submit a valid request
  Step 1  Select(btnNewRequest)
  Step 2  SetProperty(txtTitle.Text, "Test request " & Text(Now(), "yyyymmdd-hhmmss"))
  Step 3  SetProperty(drpCategory.Selected, LookUp(Categories, Title = "Hardware"))
  Step 4  SetProperty(txtAmount.Text, "250")
  Step 5  Assert(btnSubmit.DisplayMode = DisplayMode.Edit, "Submit should be enabled when the form is valid")
  Step 6  Select(btnSubmit)
  Step 7  Assert(lblConfirmation.Visible, "Confirmation should show after submit")
  Step 8  Assert(!IsBlank(LookUp(Requests, Title = txtTitle.Text)), "The request should exist in the data source")

Test case: Required title blocks submit
  Step 1  Select(btnNewRequest)
  Step 2  SetProperty(txtTitle.Text, "")
  Step 3  Assert(btnSubmit.DisplayMode = DisplayMode.Disabled, "Submit should be disabled without a title")
  Step 4  Assert(lblTitleError.Visible, "Title error should be visible")

Gallery row
  Select(galRequests, 1, btnOpen)
  Assert(lblDetailTitle.Text = First(colVisibleRequests).Title, "Detail should show the selected request")

Set-up and results (Test > properties)
  OnTestCaseStart:   Set(gblTestMode, true)                         let the app skip emails or use a test list
  OnTestCaseComplete: Patch(TestResults, Defaults(TestResults), { Title: TestCaseResult.TestCaseName,
                        Passed: TestCaseResult.Success, Message: TestCaseResult.TestFailureMessage })
  OnTestSuiteComplete: Notify("Suite finished: " & TestSuiteResult.TestsPassed & " passed, " &
                        TestSuiteResult.TestsFailed & " failed")

Run
  Test Studio > Play: opens the published app in a new tab and runs the steps.
  Copy play link: a URL that runs the suite. Open it in a pipeline with a browser automation step, then read the
  outcome from the TestResults list written by OnTestCaseComplete.
  Publish the app after changing tests. Play runs the published version.

Keep test data clean
  Create rows with a recognisable title prefix and remove them in a final step:
  RemoveIf(Requests, StartsWith(Title, "Test request "))

Limits
  No support for every control (some modern controls, code components, media and some nested galleries).
  Tests run as the signed-in user, with that user's permissions.

Power Apps Test Engine
  For pipeline-first testing: YAML test plans run with pac test run against canvas and model-driven apps, using
  the same Power Fx assertions with browser automation underneath.
stepByStepInstructions: Name the controls used in the app's main journeys.
Open Test Studio and create a suite for each journey.
Record the steps, then replace recorded values with deliberate test data.
Add Assert steps for each expected result.
Write results to a list in OnTestCaseComplete.
Publish and run the suite before each release.
commonMistakes: Recording without adding assertions, so the test cannot fail.
Depending on existing data that changes.
Forgetting to publish after editing tests.
Letting test runs send real emails or approvals.
troubleshooting: If a step fails on a control, check the control is supported and visible on the current screen.
If the test passes when the feature is broken, the Assert checks the wrong thing. Assert on the data source.
If timing causes failures, assert on a variable the app sets when the operation finishes.
If test rows pile up, add a clean-up step or a separate test list.
seoTitle: Write repeatable tests for a canvas app with Test Studio
seoDescription: Record and write test cases for a canvas app's key journeys, assert on results with Power Fx and run the suite from a link or a pipeline before each release.

faqs.question: Can I automate testing of a Power Apps canvas app?
faqs.answer: Yes. Test Studio records and plays Power Fx test steps with assertions, and Test Engine runs YAML test plans from a pipeline.

faqs.question: Do tests run against the editor version of the app?
faqs.answer: No. They run against the published version, so publish after changing the app or its tests.

faqs.question: Can Test Studio test flows?
faqs.answer: Not directly. It can assert on what a flow changed in the data source once the app triggers it.

title: Run a smoke test after every deployment
shortDescription: A flow that checks the essentials straight after an import: solution version, flows turned on, environment variables set, connections healthy and a test row processed.
fullDescription: A successful import only means the files went in. A smoke test confirms the system actually works: the right version is installed, flows are running, settings have values and one end-to-end case completes. Run automatically after deployment, it finds a broken release in minutes instead of when users report it.
problemStatement: The import reports success on Friday evening. On Monday it emerges that the approval flow was off and an environment variable was empty all weekend.
whenToUse: Every deployment to test and production
Solutions with several flows and environment-specific settings
whenNotToUse: Replacing proper acceptance testing of new features
Checks that create visible noise for real users, such as real approval emails
formulaOrCode:
Trigger
  Manual (run by the release owner), or an HTTP request called by the pipeline's last step, or the pipelines
  host trigger OnDeploymentCompleted.
  Input: expectedVersion (text), for example 1.5.0.0

Initialise  varResults (Array)       each check appends { "check": "...", "ok": true/false, "detail": "..." }

Check 1: solution version
  Dataverse > List rows: Solutions      Filter rows: uniquename eq 'RequestHub'      Select: version,ismanaged
  ok:  first(body('List_solutions')?['value'])?['version'] equals expectedVersion  and  ismanaged is true

Check 2: flows are on
  Dataverse > List rows: Processes
    Filter rows: category eq 5 and statecode ne 1 and _solutionid_value ne null
    Fetch XML alternative: join solutioncomponent on objectid where solution uniquename = RequestHub
  ok:  length(body('List_flows_off')?['value']) equals 0        detail: join of the names that are off

Check 3: environment variables have values
  Dataverse > List rows: Environment Variable Definitions
    Filter rows: startswith(schemaname,'cnt_')
    Expand Query: environmentvariabledefinition_environmentvariablevalue($select=value)
  For each definition: effective value = coalesce(first(values)?['value'], defaultvalue)
  ok:  no definition with an empty effective value

Check 4: connections work (one cheap read per connector)
  SharePoint > Get items, Top Count 1 on the app's main list
  Dataverse > List rows, Row count 1 on the main table
  Office 365 Users > Get my profile
  Put each in its own Scope. A following action with run after "has failed" appends ok: false.

Check 5: end-to-end case
  Dataverse > Add a new row: Service Requests
    Title: SMOKE TEST @{utcNow()}       Category: Test       cnt_issmoketest: Yes
  Delay 2 minutes (or Do until status changes, limit 10 checks, 30 seconds apart)
  Get a row by ID > ok: status equals the value your automation should have set (for example Assigned)
  Clean up: Delete the row. Automations should skip notifications when cnt_issmoketest is Yes.

Check 6: app is reachable
  Power Apps for Admins > Get App (or List rows: Canvas Apps filtered by name) > ok: the app exists and its
  last published time is after the deployment started.

Report
  Filter array: varResults where ok is false
  Create HTML table from varResults
  Teams > Post message in a channel:
    @{if(equals(length(body('Filter_failed')),0),'PASSED','FAILED')}: RequestHub @{expectedVersion} in Production
    followed by the table
  If any failed: Terminate with status Failed, so a calling pipeline stage fails as well.

Run it
  Azure DevOps or GitHub: call the flow's HTTP trigger after the import step and fail the job when the
  response reports failures. Keep the trigger URL in a secret variable.

Keep it short
  Target under five minutes and under ten checks. Add a check whenever an incident shows a gap.
stepByStepInstructions: List what must be true for the system to work after a release.
Build a flow that runs each check and records pass or fail.
Include one end-to-end test row that automations treat as a test.
Post the results to the release channel.
Fail the flow when any check fails.
Call the flow from the pipeline or run it straight after each import.
commonMistakes: Treating a successful import as proof the release works.
Smoke tests that send real approvals or emails to users.
No clean-up of test rows.
A test so long that nobody waits for it.
troubleshooting: If the flows check reports false failures, exclude flows that are intentionally off by name.
If the end-to-end check times out, lengthen the wait or check that the trigger flow is on.
If the smoke test itself is off after import, it is in the same solution. Keep it in a separate solution in each environment.
If results are ignored, make the pipeline stage depend on the result.
seoTitle: Run a smoke test after every deployment
seoDescription: A flow that checks the essentials straight after an import: solution version, flows turned on, environment variables set, connections healthy and a test row processed.
primaryKeyword: Power Platform post deployment smoke test

faqs.question: What should a Power Platform smoke test check?
faqs.answer: The installed solution version, that flows are on, that environment variables have values, that connections work and that one end-to-end case completes.

faqs.question: When should it run?
faqs.answer: Immediately after every import to test and production, ideally triggered by the pipeline.

faqs.question: Should the smoke test be part of the solution?
faqs.answer: Keep it in its own small solution so a failed deployment of the main solution cannot disable the check.
